docs.title: ursus: DataFrames for Go
docs.text:
A dataframe library for Go, modelled on Polars. Lazy queries with a query optimizer, Apache Arrow memory, SIMD kernels, and execution that spills to disk instead of running out of memory. Pure Go: no cgo, no C++ toolchain, no Python.

Get started Coming from Polars API reference

go get github.com/advenn/ursus

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Sum().Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.Len().Alias("orders"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("revenue"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ region  │ revenue │ orders │
│ String  │ Float64 │ Uint64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ "south" │ 46.5    │ 3      │
│ "north" │ 30.75   │ 2      │
│ "east"  │ 18      │ 1      │
└─────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Nothing runs until Collect. The optimizer reads only the columns the query uses, the group-by runs on every core, and the same query runs under a memory limit by spilling to disk.

  • Lazy and optimized

    A query is a plan until it is collected. Filters and projections are pushed into the scans and through joins, constants are folded, and a subtree used twice runs once.

    Lazy and eager

  • Polars' expressions, in Go

    Col("qty").Mul(Col("price")).Sum().Over(Col("region")): the same expressions, contexts and names as Polars, checked against Polars' answers on the same inputs.

    Expressions

  • Out of core

    Sort, group-by, join, unique and window functions spill to disk under a memory limit and give the answer they give in memory. An operator that cannot spill fails with an error naming itself.

    Memory and spilling

  • Pure Go

    go get is the whole install. It cross-compiles and links into a static binary like any other Go dependency, and Go functions run inside a query as UDFs.

    Installation

  • Parquet, CSV and Arrow

    Read and write Parquet and CSV from files, memory, or any io.ReaderAt, with row groups pruned by statistics. Arrow records go in and out, zero-copy out.

    Quick start

  • Checked against other engines

    Every TPC-H (PDS-H) and h2o.ai benchmark answer is validated against DuckDB's, and the test suite runs at four SIMD widths and with SIMD off.

    Benchmarks

docs.title: Is ursus for you?
docs.text:
It is pure Go, and that is the reason to pick it. The cost should be just as plain: ursus is slower than the serious analytical engines. On the h2o.ai benchmark at ten million rows it takes about 1.3 times Polars' time over Parquet and 1.6 times over CSV; on TPC-H at scale factor 1, about 2 times.

A good fit:

  • data where the speed difference is small in absolute terms: up to tens of millions of rows, it is half a second against a tenth of one. Larger data still runs, spilling to disk past the memory limit, but there the same ratio is seconds or minutes, and a spilled query pays for its disk too;
  • a Go service that needs real dataframe work, joins, group-bys and window functions, and cannot take on cgo, a Python sidecar or a large C++ dependency to get it;
  • anywhere the deployment story is worth more than the last multiple of speed.

Not a good fit:

  • interactive analytics over hundreds of millions of rows: use DuckDB or Polars;
  • anywhere you can link cgo freely: duckdb-go is a binding to a mature engine and about twice as fast on TPC-H;
  • anything production-critical today. ursus is at 0.6, and its API still changes between releases, as the changelog records.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
ursus is slower than Polars and DuckDB, and says by how much. Everything that measures it lives in bench/: TPC-H (as Polars' PDS-H) and the h2o.ai database-like suite, against DuckDB, Polars, pandas, DataFusion, chDB, Arrow-Go, Gota and QFrame.

Every answer is validated against DuckDB's, and an engine that answers wrongly is struck through in the report rather than reported as a fast number. ursus passes all 22 PDS-H queries and all 15 h2o.ai queries.

docs.title: Against Polars
docs.text:
Geometric means over each suite's queries, ursus and Polars run together in one session on 8 threads:

Suite ursus Polars ursus / Polars h2o.ai, 10M rows, Parquet 697 ms 531 ms 1.3× h2o.ai, 10M rows, CSV 1,784 ms 1,088 ms 1.6× TPC-H, scale factor 1 158 ms 79 ms 2.0× TPC-H, scale factor 0.1 20 ms 9 ms 2.3× TPC-H SF=1, peak memory 0.83 GB 0.92 GB 0.9×

Over the releases, ursus's time against Polars' has come down from 3.3× to 1.3× on h2o.ai over Parquet, and from 10.8× to 2.0× on TPC-H at scale factor 1.

docs.title: How they were taken
docs.text:
The figures are v0.6.4's, from a laptop under real conditions, so a small difference is noise and the ordering is the signal. Later 0.6 releases changed no plan the suites run, which a byte-for-byte diff of all 37 queries' optimized plans checks at each release, so the figures stand. The full report, with every engine, every query, the caveats and peak memory, is bench/results/REPORT.md.

To run them yourself:

cd bench
make preflight   # refuses to run without the free memory it needs
make setup
make bench       # generate, compute DuckDB's answers, run, validate, report

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text: An expression says how to compute a column: Col("qty").Mul(Col("price")). It holds no data, and it is computed only where a query puts it. The same expression gives a column per row in Select and WithColumns, one value per group in Agg, and keeps rows in Filter. These are Polars' contexts, and ursus follows them.

docs.title: The same expression, three ways
docs.text:
ctx := context.Background()
revenue := ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price"))

perRow, err := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), revenue.Alias("revenue")).
    Head(3).
    Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
total, err := sales().Select(revenue.Sum().Alias("revenue")).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
byRegion, err := sales().GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(revenue.Sum().Alias("revenue")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(perRow)
fmt.Println(total)
fmt.Println(byRegion)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌──────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ revenue │
│ Int64    │ Float64 │
├──────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 15      │
│ 2        │ 6       │
│ 3        │ 15.75   │
└──────────┴─────────┘

shape: (1, 1)
┌─────────┐
│ revenue │
│ Float64 │
├─────────┤
│ 108.75  │
└─────────┘

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ revenue │
│ String  │ Float64 │
├─────────┼─────────┤
│ "east"  │ 22.5    │
│ "north" │ 39.75   │
│ "south" │ 46.5    │
└─────────┴─────────┘
  • in a Select of row-wise expressions, revenue is a value per row;
  • its Sum() is an aggregate: in a Select it is one value for the frame;
  • in GroupBy(...).Agg, the same aggregate is one value per group.

GroupBy() with no keys also aggregates the whole frame, as one group.

docs.title: Windows: an aggregate beside the rows
docs.text:
Over computes an expression within each group of rows and gives the answer back on every row of the group, so the frame keeps its height. A sum over a region beside each order, and each order's rank within its region:

df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("order_id"),
        ursus.Col("region"),
        ursus.Col("qty"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Over(ursus.Col("region")).Alias("region_qty"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Rank(ursus.RankDense, true).
            Over(ursus.Col("region")).Alias("rank"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region")), ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("rank"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 5)
┌──────────┬─────────┬───────┬────────────┬────────┐
│ order_id │ region  │ qty   │ region_qty │ rank   │
│ Int64    │ String  │ Int64 │ Int128     │ Uint32 │
├──────────┼─────────┼───────┼────────────┼────────┤
│ 6        │ "east"  │ 12    │ 14         │ 1      │
│ 4        │ "east"  │ 2     │ 14         │ 2      │
│ 1        │ "north" │ 10    │ 20         │ 1      │
│ 3        │ "north" │ 7     │ 20         │ 2      │
│ 7        │ "north" │ 3     │ 20         │ 3      │
│ 5        │ "south" │ 9     │ 19         │ 1      │
│ 8        │ "south" │ 6     │ 19         │ 2      │
│ 2        │ "south" │ 4     │ 19         │ 3      │
└──────────┴─────────┴───────┴────────────┴────────┘

Window functions include the cumulative ones (CumSum, CumMax, ...), Shift, Diff, Rank, RollingMean and the other rolling windows by rows or by time, and the exponentially weighted EwmMean and its kin.

docs.title: Many columns at once
docs.text:
Col takes several names, and All() and Exclude(...) select by what to leave out. An expression over several columns is one expression per column, and Suffix or Prefix names them:

df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("product"),
        ursus.Col("qty", "price").Mul(int64(2)).Suffix("_x2"),
    ).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬────────┬──────────┐
│ product │ qty_x2 │ price_x2 │
│ String  │ Int64  │ Float64  │
├─────────┼────────┼──────────┤
│ "apple" │ 20     │ 3        │
│ "apple" │ 8      │ 3        │
│ "pear"  │ 14     │ 4.5      │
└─────────┴────────┴──────────┘

A selection inside a function across columns is that function's operands, as in Polars: SumHorizontal, MaxHorizontal and their kin, ConcatStr, Struct, ConcatList, Coalesce and HashRows answer one column over every column selected (since 0.6.7; before, the whole function was repeated a column at a time):

scores := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("name", []string{"ada", "ben"}),
    ursus.Values("maths", []int64{90, 60}),
    ursus.Values("art", []int64{70, 85}),
    ursus.Values("music", []int64{80, 75}),
)
show(scores.Select(
    ursus.Col("name"),
    ursus.SumHorizontal(ursus.ColDType(ursus.Int64)).Alias("total"),
    ursus.MaxHorizontal(ursus.ColDType(ursus.Int64)).Alias("best"),
))
Output
shape: (2, 3)
┌────────┬────────┬───────┐
│ name   │ total  │ best  │
│ String │ Int128 │ Int64 │
├────────┼────────┼───────┤
│ "ada"  │ 240    │ 90    │
│ "ben"  │ 220    │ 85    │
└────────┴────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Methods for one kind of column sit behind a namespace:

Namespace For For example Str() text Contains, Replace, Split, ToUpper, Strptime, Slice Dt() dates and times Year, Weekday, Truncate, OffsetBy, ConvertTimeZone List() lists Len, Get, Contains, Sum, Eval, Sort, Unique Struct() structs Field, WithFields, RenameFields, JsonEncode Bin() binary Contains, StartsWith, Encode, Size Cat() enums GetCategories, LenBytes, Slice 
df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("product").Str().ToUpper().Alias("product"),
        ursus.Col("date").Dt().Weekday().Alias("weekday"),
        ursus.Col("product").Str().Contains("p", true).Alias("has_p"),
    ).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ product │ weekday │ has_p │
│ String  │ Int32   │ Bool  │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ "APPLE" │ 6       │ true  │
│ "APPLE" │ 6       │ true  │
│ "PEAR"  │ 7       │ true  │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
When(cond).Then(a).Otherwise(b) is a conditional column, and When may follow Then for further conditions, the first true one winning:

ursus.When(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(10)).Then("large").
    When(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(5)).Then("medium").
    Otherwise("small")

Comparisons give a Bool column, combined with And, Or and Not under SQL's three-valued logic: null.And(false) is false, and null.And(true) is null. A condition that is null counts as false, so its row falls to the next When, or to Otherwise, as in Polars and SQL's CASE WHEN (since 0.6.7; before, the row was null). Write Otherwise(ursus.Null(...)) where a null is wanted.

docs.title: Literals
docs.text:
A Go value is a literal wherever an expression goes: Col("qty").Gt(3), Then("bulk"), FillNullWith(0.0). Lit(v) makes a literal expression of its own, and a Go slice is a List literal.

A literal has its Go value's type. A Go integer constant is an int, an Int64, and a float constant a Float64, so Col("a").Add(3) of an Int32 column is an Int64 column, and Col("f").Mul(2.5) of a Float32 one a Float64. Write Add(int32(3)) to stay at Int32. Polars' literals take the column's type instead. The fills are the exception: FillNullWith, FillNan and their kin meet the column, so FillNullWith(0) of an Int32 column stays Int32, and only a fill with a fraction widens an integer column.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
An expression is named after the leftmost column it reads: Col("qty").Mul(Col("price")) is named qty. Alias names it, and goes last, since an alias inside an expression does not name the whole.

New in 0.6.7: Meta() asks an expression about itself, as Polars' meta does: RootNames the columns it reads by name, OutputName its name, HasMultipleOutputs, IsColumn, IsColumnSelection, IsLiteral and IsRegexProjection; UndoAliases the expression without its names, Eq whether two are one computation, Pop the outermost operation's inputs, and TreeFormat a drawing of it.

docs.title: A query is a plan
docs.text:
A LazyFrame is a query, not data. ScanCSV, Filter, GroupBy and the rest each add a step to a plan, and nothing is read or computed until the plan runs:

  • Collect(ctx) runs it and gives a DataFrame, the answer, held in memory;
  • CollectBatches(ctx) runs it and gives the answer a batch at a time;
  • Count(ctx) runs it and gives the number of rows;
  • WriteParquet(ctx, w) and WriteCSV(ctx, w) run it into a writer.

Because the whole query is known before it runs, ursus can check it first and then rewrite it.

docs.title: Checked before it runs
docs.text:
When a query is collected, ursus resolves every column's type, expands each selection of several columns, and type-checks every expression, before any data is read. A mistake is reported then, with what was meant:

lf := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("prodcut")). // a typo: nothing has run, so nothing fails yet
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3)))

_, err := lf.Collect(context.Background())
fmt.Println(err)
Output
ursus: select: unknown column "prodcut"
  did you mean: "product"?
  available: order_id, date, region, product, qty, price
  at Project

The Select with the typo did not fail when it was written. A query being built never fails: the first error is kept, the chain goes on, and Collect returns it. So a long chain has one if err != nil, at the end.

docs.title: Rewritten before it runs
docs.text:
The optimizer rewrites the plan into one that gives the same answer for less work:

  • predicate pushdown: a filter moves toward the scan, through joins, so fewer rows travel;
  • projection pushdown: a scan reads only the columns the query uses;
  • limit and top-k pushdown: a Head after a Sort becomes a top-k;
  • constant folding and simplification;
  • common subplans: a subtree used twice runs once.

A subtree used twice runs once when it joins, aggregates or sorts, which is worth the fence it puts around it: a filter above one use stops there. New in 0.6.7: Cache() asks it of any query, as Polars' cache does, a scan read twice or a Go function's answer; a query used once is not cached.

Explain shows the plan. Optimized(false) shows it as written:

q := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty"))

written, err := q.Explain(context.Background(), ursus.Optimized(false))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(written)
Output
PROJECT [col("product"), col("qty")]
  FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(3))]
    CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
      projection: * (6 cols)

and without the option, the plan that runs. The PROJECT is gone, and the scan reads two of six columns:

plan, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Explain(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(plan)
Output
FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(3))]
  CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
    projection: [product, qty] (2/6 cols)

Explain's output is stable on purpose: ursus's own tests compare plans as text, so a query that still gives the right answer while reading forty columns instead of two fails a test.

New in 0.6.7. Columns(ctx), DTypes(ctx) and Width(ctx) are a query's column names, their types and how many there are, as Polars' lazy columns, dtypes and width: read from CollectSchema, which types the plan without running it.

docs.title: Eager: a DataFrame
docs.text:
A DataFrame is an answer in memory, Arrow arrays underneath. Its methods mirror LazyFrame's, and each is a lazy query over the frame, collected at once. So each takes a context, which can cancel it:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := sales().Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
big, err := df.Filter(ctx, ursus.Col("qty").Ge(int64(9)))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(big.Shape())
Output
3 6

df.Lazy() turns a frame back into a query, for a chain of several steps optimized together.

Printed, a frame draws its first ten rows. New in 0.6.7: Show(n) draws its first n, every one, as Polars' show, and a query's Show(ctx, n) computes only those.

docs.title: Streaming the answer
docs.text:
CollectBatches is a Go iterator over the answer's batches, so an answer larger than memory never has to be held at once:

ctx := context.Background()
for batch, err := range sales().CollectBatches(ctx, ursus.WithBatchSize(3)) {
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println("a batch of", batch.Height(), "rows")
}
Output
a batch of 3 rows
a batch of 3 rows
a batch of 2 rows

Breaking out of the loop stops the query and removes any spill files it wrote.

docs.title: Order and threads
docs.text:
A query runs on every core by default; WithThreads(n) sets how many. A scan's rows come in the file's order at any thread count, a filter keeps its input's order, and a sort's is sorted. Two orders are not promised, as in Polars, and each has an option that promises one:

  • a group-by's groups: MaintainOrder() gives them in the order their keys first appear;
  • an inner join's rows, which follow whichever input ursus did not hash: JoinMaintainOrder(ursus.JoinOrderLeft) keeps the left frame's order, and JoinOrderRight the right's, for a join of any kind.

docs.title: Memory and spilling
docs.text: A query in ursus runs under a memory budget. When the operators that hold data across batches, a sort, a group-by, a join's build side, reach it, they write what they hold to disk and carry on, and the answer is the one they give in memory. An operator that cannot spill fails at the budget with an error naming itself, instead of growing until the operating system kills the process.

docs.title: The default budget
docs.text:
A query with no limit of its own is budgeted at half the memory the process can have: the smaller of its container's limit and the machine's memory on Linux, and the machine's memory on macOS and Windows. Half, because ursus's buffers live on the Go heap, which grows to about twice what is live before it collects.

Under that default, ursus also sets the Go runtime's soft memory limit near the same ceiling, so the heap's slack stays under it. GOMEMLIMIT, or calling ursus.LeaveProcessMemoryLimit() before the first query, keeps a program's own choice.

docs.title: A limit of your own
docs.text:
WithMemoryLimit sets the budget for one query, WithSpillDir where its files go, and WithMemoryStats reports what it held and how many files it wrote. A group-by over 25,000 keys under 256 KiB:

keys := make([]int64, 100_000)
for i := range keys {
    keys[i] = int64(i * 7919 % 25_000)
}
var stats ursus.MemoryStats
df, err := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("k", keys)).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("k")).Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("n")).
    Select(ursus.Len().Alias("groups"), ursus.Col("n").Max().Alias("largest")).
    Collect(context.Background(),
        ursus.WithMemoryLimit(256<<10),
        ursus.WithSpillDir(os.TempDir()),
        ursus.WithMemoryStats(&stats))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
fmt.Println("spilled:", stats.Spills > 0)
Output
shape: (1, 2)
┌────────┬─────────┐
│ groups │ largest │
│ Uint64 │ Uint64  │
├────────┼─────────┤
│ 25000  │ 4       │
└────────┴─────────┘

spilled: true

The spill files are removed when the query ends, on success, on an error, and when a loop over CollectBatches breaks early. WithMemoryLimit(0) turns the budget off.

docs.title: What spills
docs.text:
• sort, and a top-k with any k;
  • group-by, including the values a median, a quantile or an NUnique holds, and the pairs of a CorrSpearman;
  • join, both sides partitioned;
  • unique;
  • window functions, over many partitions or one huge one;
  • keyed Rolling and GroupByDynamic;
  • tail and reverse.

JoinAsOf, MergeSorted and HStack stream their input, as Rolling and GroupByDynamic do, so they hold little to begin with. Changed in 0.6.7: a CorrSpearman over a group larger than the limit spills its pairs, in a group-by, a window or a temporal group, where it failed.

docs.title: What does not
docs.text:
A few answers are as large as their input, and cannot be divided across files: Implode holds every value of a group as its answer, for one. Each such operator fails at the budget, and its error says what it holds, why it cannot spill, and what the alternatives are:

keys := make([]int64, 100_000)
_, err := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("k", keys)).
    Select(ursus.Col("k").Implode()).
    Collect(context.Background(),
        ursus.WithMemoryLimit(64<<10),
        ursus.WithSpillDir(os.TempDir()))
fmt.Println(err)
Output
ursus: group_by: memory limit of 64.0KiB exceeded: the query is holding 105.2KiB, 105.2KiB of it in this operator
  group_by holds one entry per distinct key, and implode holds every VALUE as its answer — which partitioning to disk cannot divide, because it divides across keys (quantile, median, n_unique and corr_spearman spill their values); raise the limit with WithMemoryLimit
  sort, group_by, join, unique, over, reverse and tail spill to disk; join_asof, merge_sorted, hstack, rolling and group_by_dynamic stream their input; an over computing a rolling window by time one of whose periods holds more than the limit fails rather than exceed it, and so does implode over one group larger than it

Collect itself holds its whole answer, by definition. An answer larger than memory goes through CollectBatches, or WriteParquet and WriteCSV, which stream it.

docs.title: A larger-than-memory query
docs.text:
A sort of more Parquet than fits in memory, written to a file as it comes out of the sort, holding at most 512 MiB:

ctx := context.Background()
err := ursus.ScanParquet("events/*.parquet").
    Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("ts"))).
    SinkParquet(ctx, "sorted.parquet",
        ursus.WithMemoryLimit(512<<20),
        ursus.WithSpillDir("/var/tmp/ursus"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Each path that spills is tested under a limit far below its input, against its answer without one.

docs.title: Types and nulls
docs.text:
Every column has one type, and a frame's schema is its columns' names and types, known before a query runs:

df, err := sales().Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df.Schema())
Output
{order_id: Int64, date: Date, region: String, product: String, qty: Int64, price: Float64}

docs.title: The types
docs.text:
Type Go value Notes Bool bool Int8 … Int64, Uint8 … Uint64 int8 … uint64 Int128 ursus.Int128Value what an integer sum gives Float32, Float64 float32, float64 Decimal(p, s) 128-bit; exact +, -, * and Sum, refused past 38 digits String, Binary string, []byte Date time.Time a calendar day Datetime(unit, zone) time.Time a unit of s, ms, us or ns, and an IANA zone or none Duration(unit) time.Duration TimeOf(unit) a time of day Enum(...) string fixed categories, sorted in their order List(T) a slice a list of values a row StructOf(fields...) a struct named fields a row

ursus.Int64, ursus.Date and the rest name the types, and Datetime, Duration, TimeOf, Decimal, List, Enum and StructOf make one. A type is a comparable value, so it can key a map.

docs.title: Null is not NaN
docs.text:
Null is a missing value, and any type can hold one. NaN is a float that is not a number, the answer to 0.0 / 0.0. They are different, and ursus keeps them apart everywhere:

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("x",
        []float64{1, math.NaN(), 0},
        []bool{true, true, false}),
).Select(
    ursus.Col("x"),
    ursus.Col("x").IsNull().Alias("is_null"),
    ursus.Col("x").IsNan().Alias("is_nan"),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ x       │ is_null │ is_nan │
│ Float64 │ Bool    │ Bool   │
├─────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 1       │ false   │ false  │
│ NaN     │ false   │ true   │
│ null    │ true    │ null   │
└─────────┴─────────┴────────┘

A null's test is IsNull, a NaN's IsNan; FillNull and FillNan repair them, and DropNulls and DropNans drop their rows.

docs.title: Nulls in aggregates
docs.text:
An aggregate skips nulls. Count counts the values that are there, Len the rows, and a mean is the sum of the values over their count, not over the rows:

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("score", []float64{4, 0, 8}, []bool{true, false, true}),
).Select(
    ursus.Len().Alias("rows"),
    ursus.Col("score").Count().Alias("count"),
    ursus.Col("score").NullCount().Alias("nulls"),
    ursus.Col("score").Mean().Alias("mean"),
    ursus.Col("score").FillNullWith(0.0).Mean().Alias("mean_as_zero"),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐
│ rows   │ count  │ nulls  │ mean    │ mean_as_zero │
│ Uint64 │ Uint64 │ Uint64 │ Float64 │ Float64      │
├────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┼──────────────┤
│ 3      │ 2      │ 1      │ 6       │ 4            │
└────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘

Two rules follow SQL rather than Polars, because a null can become a number but a number cannot become a null again:

  • the Sum of a group with no values is null, not 0;
  • the Mean of a group with no values is null, not NaN.

docs.title: Casts
docs.text:
Cast converts a column to another type and refuses a value it cannot convert, naming it. CastLossy turns such values into nulls instead:

ctx := context.Background()
text := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("n", []string{"12", "7", "seven"}))

_, err := text.Select(ursus.Col("n").Cast(ursus.Int64)).Collect(ctx)
fmt.Println(err)

df, err := text.Select(ursus.Col("n").CastLossy(ursus.Int64)).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
ursus: cast: cannot parse "seven" as Int64 at row 2
  use CastLossy to turn unparseable values into nulls instead
shape: (3, 1)
┌───────┐
│ n     │
│ Int64 │
├───────┤
│ 12    │
│ 7     │
│ null  │
└───────┘

A cast never loses a value silently: an integer that does not fit a narrower type is refused by Cast, and a float rounds only when the target is a float. A float with a fraction is refused as an integer, where Polars truncates it; Truncate(0) first says that is what you want.

New in 0.6.7. ToPhysical is a column as it is stored, as Polars' to_physical: a Date's days as an Int32, a Datetime's, a Duration's and a Time's ticks as an Int64, a Decimal's unscaled units as an Int128, an Enum's category as the smallest unsigned integer that holds them. Reinterpret(signed) reads an integer's bits as the integer of its width and the other sign, so a UInt64's maximum is an Int64's -1.

docs.title: A frame's casts
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. Cast casts columns by name, CastTypes every column of a type, and CastAll every column, the rest left as they are, in their places, as Polars' frame cast does. CastStrict(false) turns what does not convert into nulls, as CastLossy does.

lines := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("price")).
    Head(2)
show(lines.Cast(map[string]ursus.DataType{
    "qty":   ursus.Int32,
    "price": ursus.Float32,
}))
show(lines.CastTypes(map[ursus.DataType]ursus.DataType{ursus.Int64: ursus.Int16}))
show(lines.Select(ursus.Col("price").Truncate(0).Cast(ursus.Int64)))
Output
shape: (2, 3)
┌──────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Int32 │ Float32 │
├──────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 4     │ 1.5     │
└──────────┴───────┴─────────┘

shape: (2, 3)
┌──────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int16    │ Int16 │ Float64 │
├──────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 4     │ 1.5     │
└──────────┴───────┴─────────┘

shape: (2, 1)
┌───────┐
│ price │
│ Int64 │
├───────┤
│ 1     │
│ 1     │
└───────┘

A Datetime key matches its unit and zone exactly, so a frame of two units needs a key for each, where Polars' pl.Datetime matches both.

docs.title: A frame made to a schema
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. MatchToSchema(schema, options) makes a frame's columns a schema's: its columns, in its order, of its types, as Polars' match_to_schema does. By default every difference is refused, the first type that does not meet first; the options say what to do instead:

want := ursus.MustSchema(
    ursus.Of("order_id", ursus.Int64),
    ursus.Of("qty", ursus.Int64),
    ursus.Of("discount", ursus.Float64),
)
drifted := sales().Head(2).Select(
    ursus.Col("qty").Cast(ursus.Int32), ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("product"))

_, err := drifted.
    MatchToSchema(want, ursus.MatchOptions{}).
    Collect(context.Background())
fmt.Println(err)

show(drifted.MatchToSchema(want, ursus.MatchOptions{
    MissingColumns: ursus.MatchInsert,
    ExtraColumns:   ursus.MatchIgnore,
    IntegerCast:    ursus.MatchUpcast,
}))
Output
ursus: match_to_schema: qty is Int32, and the schema's is Int64
  MatchOptions{IntegerCast: ursus.MatchUpcast} widens it
shape: (2, 3)
┌──────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │ discount │
│ Int64    │ Int64 │ Float64  │
├──────────┼───────┼──────────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │ null     │
│ 2        │ 4     │ null     │
└──────────┴───────┴──────────┘
Option MatchRaise / MatchForbid, the default or MissingColumns refuse a schema column the frame lacks MatchInsert, as nulls ExtraColumns refuse a frame column the schema lacks MatchIgnore, dropped MissingStructFields, ExtraStructFields the same, for a struct's fields MatchInsert, MatchIgnore IntegerCast, FloatCast refuse a narrower number MatchUpcast, widened

MatchUpcast widens only where nothing can be lost: an Int32 to an Int64, a UInt32 to an Int64, a Float32 to a Float64; never an integer to a float, an Int64 to an Int32, or a UInt64 to an Int64. A struct's fields are matched by name, at any depth, and a list's element widens as a column does.

Columns sets any option for one column, and ColumnMatch.Fill computes a missing column from the others. A fill's answer meets the schema's type as a column of the frame would; Polars keeps the expression's own type, so its answer can be of a type the schema did not ask for.

docs.title: Values from Go
docs.text:
ursus.Values makes a column from a slice of a Go type, []time.Time a Datetime(ns, "UTC") one, and ursus.ValuesNullable one with nulls, from the values and whether each is present.

Going the other way, a null never comes back as a zero mistaken for a value:

  • df.At[T](row, name) and a Series[T]'s Get give the value and whether it is present;
  • df.Rows[T]() decodes a null into a pointer field as nil; declare the field *int64 where a column can be null.

docs.title: Coming from Polars
docs.text:
ursus is modelled on Polars: the same expressions, the same contexts, mostly the same names, and its answers are tested against Polars 1.44's on the same inputs. What changes is what Go asks for.

Polars (Python)ursus (Go) 
import polars as pl

df = (
    pl.scan_csv("sales.csv")
    .filter(pl.col("qty") > 3)
    .group_by("region")
    .agg(
        (pl.col("qty") * pl.col("price")).sum().alias("revenue"),
        pl.len().alias("orders"),
    )
    .sort("revenue", descending=True)
    .collect()
)

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(3)).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Sum().Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.Len().Alias("orders"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("revenue"))).
    Collect(ctx)

docs.title: What Go changes
docs.text:
• Methods, not operators. Go has no operator overloading, so pl.col("a") > 3 is Col("a").Gt(3), and a * b is a.Mul(b).
  • Lazy is the real API. A LazyFrame is a query and Collect runs it. A DataFrame's methods are a lazy query collected at once, so each takes a context.Context: df.Filter(ctx, pred).
  • Errors come at the end. A query being built never fails: an unknown column or a type mismatch is kept and returned by Collect, with a hint, so a chain stays a chain.
  • Values come back typed. df.Column[int64]("qty") is a Series[int64], and df.Rows[Sale]() a []Sale, through Go 1.27's generic methods.
  • Options are functions. Join(other, JoinOn(Col("k")), JoinHow(JoinLeft)) where Polars takes keyword arguments.

docs.title: Where ursus answers differently
docs.text:
These are deliberate, and each is documented beside the method:

  • An integer sum is an Int128, as DuckDB's is, so it cannot overflow. Polars' sum of Int64 is an Int64.
  • The sum of an all-null group is null, not 0, and its product null, not 1: a null can be filled with 0 afterwards, but a 0 cannot be told from a real one.
  • Count(ctx) of a frame is its number of rows. Polars' frame count() is each column's non-null count; in ursus that is Select(ursus.All().Count()).
  • NUnique does not count null as a value; Polars counts it.
  • Round rounds half away from zero; Polars rounds half to even, which RoundHalfToEven selects.
  • Max and Min propagate NaN; Polars' max ignores it, and its nan_max propagates it, as NanMax does here.
  • A literal has its Go value's type: Col("a").Add(3) of an Int32 column is an Int64, since a Go integer constant is an int; write int32(3) to keep Int32. Polars' literals take the column's type, as a fill value's does here.
  • A cast is exact or refused: a float with a fraction cast to an integer is an error, or null when lossy, where Polars truncates it toward zero. Truncate(0) first for Polars' answer.
  • Div and Pow always give a float.
  • An expression is named after its leftmost column. Col("a").Alias("x").Add(1) is x in Polars and a here: put the alias last.
  • Remove drops a row whose condition is null, as Filter does; Polars' remove keeps it.
  • GroupByDynamic keeps empty windows, a row of Len 0 for a period with no rows; Polars leaves them out.
  • ToInteger, ToDate and ToDatetime give null for what does not parse; Polars' fail by default.
  • Cut and Hist give text, where Polars gives a Categorical, which ursus does not have yet.
  • A Time takes a unit, where Polars' is nanoseconds.

The full list, with the step that made each choice, is in feature-gaps.md §9, and what Polars has that ursus does not yet is in the rest of that file.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go get github.com/advenn/ursus

That is the whole install. ursus is pure Go, with Apache Arrow's Go library as its one direct dependency besides golang.org/x/text: no cgo, no C or C++ toolchain, no Python runtime and no sidecar process. It cross-compiles like any other Go module.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Go 1.27 or newer. Two of its changes are load-bearing:

  • generic methods are why df.Column[int64]("qty"), df.Rows[Sale]() and Series[T].Map[U] exist at all;
  • a generic method still cannot satisfy an interface, so every public type is a concrete struct, and the polymorphism is kept in unexported interfaces.

docs.title: Your first program
docs.text:
Make a module and add ursus to it:

mkdir hello && cd hello
go mod init hello
go get github.com/advenn/ursus

Put this in main.go and go run .:

main.go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/advenn/ursus"
)

func main() {
    df, err := ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("name", []string{"ursus", "polars", "pandas"}),
        ursus.Values("language", []string{"Go", "Rust", "Python"}),
    ).Filter(ursus.Col("language").Eq("Go")).Collect(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(df)
}
Output
shape: (1, 2)
┌─────────┬──────────┐
│ name    │ language │
│ String  │ String   │
├─────────┼──────────┤
│ "ursus" │ "Go"     │
└─────────┴──────────┘

docs.title: SIMD kernels
docs.text:
ursus's compute kernels have SIMD versions for amd64, behind Go's simd experiment. They are optional: switch them on when you build,

GOEXPERIMENT=simd go build ./...

and without the experiment, or on another architecture, every kernel falls back to its scalar twin. That fallback is not a promise but a test: CI runs the whole suite with the experiment off on every push, as it runs it at four vector widths with it on. The flag buys speed, not correctness.

GOAMD64=v3 lets the Go compiler use AVX2, FMA and BMI in ordinary code too. ursus's own builds and benchmarks use it; any amd64 machine from the last decade has them.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: ursus runs wherever Go does. Its memory limit, on by default at half the memory the machine or the container allows, reads that allowance on Linux (cgroups included), macOS and Windows.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
ursus is on ZeroVer, at 0.6, and a stable 1.0 is not expected yet. Go's rule for v0 applies: a release may rename, remove or reshape an API, and the changelog lists each release's breaks with their replacements. Pin a version in your go.mod, and read the changelog before you move.

These docs are versioned too: the selector at the top of the page switches between releases, and dev is the development branch.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This tour builds a frame, reads a file, and runs the queries most programs need. Every block of code on this site is a Go example that the test suite runs, and the output under it is what it printed.

The examples read sales.csv, eight orders:

order_id,date,region,product,qty,price
1,2026-01-03,north,apple,10,1.50
2,2026-01-03,south,apple,4,1.50
3,2026-01-04,north,pear,7,2.25
4,2026-01-05,east,pear,2,2.25
5,2026-01-05,south,fig,9,3.00
6,2026-01-06,east,apple,12,1.50
7,2026-01-07,north,fig,3,3.00
8,2026-01-07,south,pear,6,2.25

docs.title: A frame from Go values
docs.text:
Frame builds a frame from columns, and Values makes a column from a Go slice. Its type follows the slice's: []int64 is an Int64 column, []string a String one.

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("city", []string{"Oslo", "Lima", "Pune"}),
    ursus.Values("population", []int64{709_000, 10_151_000, 7_764_000}),
    ursus.Values("coastal", []bool{true, true, false}),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌────────┬────────────┬─────────┐
│ city   │ population │ coastal │
│ String │ Int64      │ Bool    │
├────────┼────────────┼─────────┤
│ "Oslo" │ 709000     │ true    │
│ "Lima" │ 10151000   │ true    │
│ "Pune" │ 7764000    │ false   │
└────────┴────────────┴─────────┘

Frame gives a LazyFrame, a query. Collect runs it and gives a DataFrame, the answer.

docs.title: Reading a file
docs.text:
ScanCSV reads a CSV and infers its columns' types; an option overrides one. Here the dates become a Date:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv",
    ursus.WithSchemaOverrides(map[string]ursus.DataType{"date": ursus.Date}),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 6)
┌──────────┬────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ date       │ region  │ product │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Date       │ String  │ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├──────────┼────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 2026-01-03 │ "north" │ "apple" │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 2026-01-03 │ "south" │ "apple" │ 4     │ 1.5     │
│ 3        │ 2026-01-04 │ "north" │ "pear"  │ 7     │ 2.25    │
│ 4        │ 2026-01-05 │ "east"  │ "pear"  │ 2     │ 2.25    │
│ 5        │ 2026-01-05 │ "south" │ "fig"   │ 9     │ 3       │
│ 6        │ 2026-01-06 │ "east"  │ "apple" │ 12    │ 1.5     │
│ 7        │ 2026-01-07 │ "north" │ "fig"   │ 3     │ 3       │
│ 8        │ 2026-01-07 │ "south" │ "pear"  │ 6     │ 2.25    │
└──────────┴────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

ScanParquet reads Parquet the same way, and ScanCSVReader, ScanParquetBytes, ScanCSVFrom and ScanParquetFrom read from memory or from any reader you open, an object store's included.

docs.title: Selecting and filtering
docs.text:
Filter keeps the rows where an expression is true, and Select keeps or computes columns:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("region").Eq("north")).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬───────┐
│ product │ qty   │
│ String  │ Int64 │
├─────────┼───────┤
│ "apple" │ 10    │
│ "pear"  │ 7     │
│ "fig"   │ 3     │
└─────────┴───────┘

Columns are named with Col, and an expression's methods build on it: Eq, Gt, Ge, And, Or, IsNull. Methods have names because Go has no operator overloading: Col("qty").Gt(3), not qty > 3.

docs.title: Adding columns
docs.text:
WithColumns adds columns, or replaces those of the same name. When, Then and Otherwise choose a value by a condition:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    WithColumns(
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.When(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(int64(8))).
            Then("bulk").
            Otherwise("single").
            Alias("kind"),
    ).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("revenue"), ursus.Col("kind")).
    Head(4).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (4, 3)
┌──────────┬─────────┬──────────┐
│ order_id │ revenue │ kind     │
│ Int64    │ Float64 │ String   │
├──────────┼─────────┼──────────┤
│ 1        │ 15      │ "bulk"   │
│ 2        │ 6       │ "single" │
│ 3        │ 15.75   │ "single" │
│ 4        │ 4.5     │ "single" │
└──────────┴─────────┴──────────┘

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text:
GroupBy takes the keys, and Agg the aggregates to compute for each group:

df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("product")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty"),
        ursus.Col("price").Max().Alias("price"),
        ursus.Col("region").NUnique().Alias("regions"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("product"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ product │ qty    │ price   │ regions │
│ String  │ Int128 │ Float64 │ Uint64  │
├─────────┼────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ "apple" │ 26     │ 1.5     │ 3       │
│ "fig"   │ 12     │ 3       │ 2       │
│ "pear"  │ 15     │ 2.25    │ 3       │
└─────────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

A sum of integers is an Int128, so it cannot overflow; cast it if you need an Int64. Groups come out in no promised order: sort them, or call MaintainOrder() for the order their keys first appear in.

docs.title: Joining
docs.text:
Join matches rows by keys. JoinHow picks the kind: inner by default, and left, right, full, semi, anti and cross. A row with no match on the other side takes nulls:

managers := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("region", []string{"north", "south"}),
    ursus.Values("manager", []string{"Ada", "Grace"}),
)
df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Join(managers,
        ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("region")),
        ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinLeft)).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("manager")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 3)
┌──────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ region  │ manager │
│ Int64    │ String  │ String  │
├──────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ "north" │ "Ada"   │
│ 2        │ "south" │ "Grace" │
│ 3        │ "north" │ "Ada"   │
│ 4        │ "east"  │ null    │
│ 5        │ "south" │ "Grace" │
│ 6        │ "east"  │ null    │
│ 7        │ "north" │ "Ada"   │
│ 8        │ "south" │ "Grace" │
└──────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: Back into Go
docs.text:
Rows decodes a frame into a slice of structs, matching fields to columns by an ursus tag, by name, or by name ignoring case:

type sale struct {
    ID      int64  `ursus:"order_id"`
    Product string `ursus:"product"`
    Qty     int64  `ursus:"qty"`
}
df, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(int64(9))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
sales, err := df.Rows[sale]()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, s := range sales {
    fmt.Printf("%+v\n", s)
}
Output
{ID:1 Product:apple Qty:10}
{ID:5 Product:fig Qty:9}
{ID:6 Product:apple Qty:12}

df.Column[T](name) gives one column as a typed Series[T], and df.At[T](row, name) one value and whether it was null.

docs.title: What will run
docs.text:
Explain shows the plan the optimizer made. Here the scan reads two of the file's six columns, and the Select is gone, because the scan already gives just those two:

plan, err := ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv").
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(int64(3))).
    Select(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Explain(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(plan)
Output
FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(3))]
  CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
    projection: [product, qty] (2/6 cols)

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Coming from Polars: the names you know, and where ursus differs.
  • Lazy and eager: when a query runs, and how to stream its answer.
  • Expressions: the same expression per row, per group and over a window.
  • Memory and spilling: running a query bigger than memory.
  • The user guide: twelve chapters, from selecting and joining to Go functions and Parquet.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
Each chapter takes one kind of work and shows it in code that runs: every block is a Go example the test suite runs, and the output under it is what it printed. The examples read the quick start's sales.csv, eight orders, its dates read as dates, unless a chapter says otherwise:

func sales() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/sales.csv",
        ursus.WithSchemaOverrides(map[string]ursus.DataType{"date": ursus.Date}))
}

  • Selecting and filtering

    Columns by name, pattern or type; rows by predicates; sorting, top-k, unique rows and slices.

  • Aggregation and group-by

    Aggregates per group and over the whole frame, conditional aggregates, lists per group, and summaries.

  • Window functions

    An aggregate beside every row, cumulative and shifted values, ranks, rolling windows by rows and by time, and exponential averages.

  • Joins

    Every join kind, keys, suffixes and validation, as-of joins, joins on a condition, and filters by another frame.

  • Reshaping

    Pivot and unpivot, explode and unnest, concatenating frames, and transpose.

  • Strings

    Cleaning, matching with regular expressions, extracting, replacing, splitting, and parsing numbers and dates.

  • Lists and structs

    List columns and the questions to ask of them, expressions over their elements, sets, and struct fields.

  • Dates and times

    Parsing, calendar arithmetic, time zones, ranges, and groups by day, week or a rolling period.

  • Missing data

    Counting nulls, filling them from a value or the neighbours, coalescing, interpolating, and dropping.

  • Go values in and out

    Frames from Go slices, typed columns as Series, rows into structs, and streaming an answer a batch at a time.

  • Go functions

    Go functions inside a query, a value or a batch at a time, with nulls, errors and concurrency.

  • CSV, Parquet and Arrow

    Scans and their options, globs, object storage, pushdown into Parquet, sinks, and Arrow in and out.

docs.title: Aggregation and group-by
docs.text: GroupBy(keys...) splits the rows by their keys, and Agg(exprs...) computes each expression once per group: one row per group comes out, its keys and its aggregates.

docs.title: The aggregates
docs.text:
df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("sum"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Mean().Alias("mean"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Median().Alias("median"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Min().Alias("min"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Max().Alias("max"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Std(1).Round(2).Alias("std"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 7)
┌─────────┬────────┬───────────────────┬─────────┬───────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ sum    │ mean              │ median  │ min   │ max   │ std     │
│ String  │ Int128 │ Float64           │ Float64 │ Int64 │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼────────┼───────────────────┼─────────┼───────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ "east"  │ 14     │ 7                 │ 7       │ 2     │ 12    │ 7.07    │
│ "north" │ 20     │ 6.666666666666667 │ 7       │ 3     │ 10    │ 3.51    │
│ "south" │ 19     │ 6.333333333333333 │ 6       │ 4     │ 9     │ 2.52    │
└─────────┴────────┴───────────────────┴─────────┴───────┴───────┴─────────┘

The usual statistics are all there:

  • Sum, Mean, Median, Min and Max;
  • Std(ddof) and Var(ddof);
  • Quantile(q, interpolation);
  • Product;
  • Skew, Kurtosis and Entropy;
  • Corr, Cov and CorrSpearman of two columns.

Every aggregate skips nulls. A mean is over the values that are there, and a group with no values sums to null, not 0. An integer sum is an Int128, so it cannot overflow: cast it to Int64 if you want Polars' type.

Counting has several forms, each one value per group:

df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("product")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Len().Alias("orders"),
        ursus.Col("region").NUnique().Alias("regions"),
        ursus.Col("region").First().Alias("first"),
        ursus.Col("region").Last().Alias("last"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("product"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 5)
┌─────────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ product │ orders │ regions │ first   │ last    │
│ String  │ Uint64 │ Uint64  │ String  │ String  │
├─────────┼────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ "apple" │ 3      │ 3       │ "north" │ "east"  │
│ "fig"   │ 2      │ 2       │ "south" │ "north" │
│ "pear"  │ 3      │ 3       │ "north" │ "south" │
└─────────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
  • Len() counts a group's rows;
  • Count() counts a column's values that are not null;
  • NUnique() counts its distinct values, a null not among them;
  • First() and Last() are its first and last value in the rows' order.

New in 0.6.7: Item(allowEmpty) is a group's one value, as Polars' item, and refuses a group of several, or of none unless allowEmpty, which makes it null. LowerBound() and UpperBound() are the least and greatest value of the column's type. IsSorted(descending, nullsLast) says whether a group's values come in order, NaN the greatest and the nulls all first, or all last; it reads the rows in their order, so a group-by holding it runs on one worker.

New in 0.6.7. First and Last take a value that may be null, so that First(a) and First(b) come from one row. FirstNonNull() and LastNonNull() skip the nulls, as Polars' first(ignore_nulls=True), so two of them may come from different rows. A group-by has each as a shorthand over every column, and All() gathers each column's values a group into a list, as Polars' group_by().all():

temps, read := []float64{0, 21.5, 22.0, 0}, []bool{false, true, true, false}
readings := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("sensor", []string{"a", "a", "a", "b"}),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("temp", temps, read),
)
g := readings.GroupBy(ursus.Col("sensor")).MaintainOrder()
show(g.Agg(
    ursus.Col("temp").First().Alias("first"),
    ursus.Col("temp").FirstNonNull().Alias("first_seen"),
    ursus.Col("temp").LastNonNull().Alias("last_seen"),
))
show(g.All())
Output
shape: (2, 4)
┌────────┬─────────┬────────────┬───────────┐
│ sensor │ first   │ first_seen │ last_seen │
│ String │ Float64 │ Float64    │ Float64   │
├────────┼─────────┼────────────┼───────────┤
│ "a"    │ null    │ 21.5       │ 22        │
│ "b"    │ null    │ null       │ null      │
└────────┴─────────┴────────────┴───────────┘

shape: (2, 2)
┌────────┬──────────────────┐
│ sensor │ temp             │
│ String │ List(Float64)    │
├────────┼──────────────────┤
│ "a"    │ [null, 21.5, 22] │
│ "b"    │ [null]           │
└────────┴──────────────────┘

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
A key is any expression, not only a column. Alias a computed key to name it:

df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("qty").Ge(8).Alias("bulk")).
    Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("orders"), ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("bulk"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (2, 3)
┌───────┬────────┬────────┐
│ bulk  │ orders │ qty    │
│ Bool  │ Uint64 │ Int128 │
├───────┼────────┼────────┤
│ false │ 5      │ 22     │
│ true  │ 3      │ 31     │
└───────┴────────┴────────┘

Several keys group by their combinations:

df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("product")).
    Agg(ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region")), ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("product"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ region  │ product │ qty    │
│ String  │ String  │ Int128 │
├─────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ "east"  │ "apple" │ 12     │
│ "east"  │ "pear"  │ 2      │
│ "north" │ "apple" │ 10     │
│ "north" │ "fig"   │ 3      │
│ "north" │ "pear"  │ 7      │
│ "south" │ "apple" │ 4      │
│ "south" │ "fig"   │ 9      │
│ "south" │ "pear"  │ 6      │
└─────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Groups come out in no promised order: they are built on every core at once. Sort the answer, as these examples do, or ask for the order the keys first appear in with MaintainOrder():

df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("product")).
    MaintainOrder().
    Agg(ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬────────┐
│ product │ qty    │
│ String  │ Int128 │
├─────────┼────────┤
│ "apple" │ 26     │
│ "pear"  │ 15     │
│ "fig"   │ 12     │
└─────────┴────────┘

A null key is a group of its own, as in SQL's GROUP BY and Polars.

docs.title: Conditional aggregates
docs.text:
An aggregate's input is an expression, so it can be narrowed or computed first:

df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("qty").Filter(ursus.Col("product").Eq("apple")).Sum().
            Alias("apple_qty"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Ge(8).Sum().Alias("bulk_orders"),
        ursus.Col("product").MaxBy(ursus.Col("qty")).Alias("biggest"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬───────────┬─────────────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ apple_qty │ bulk_orders │ biggest │
│ String  │ Int128    │ Int128      │ String  │
├─────────┼───────────┼─────────────┼─────────┤
│ "east"  │ 12        │ 1           │ "apple" │
│ "north" │ 10        │ 1           │ "apple" │
│ "south" │ 4         │ 1           │ "fig"   │
└─────────┴───────────┴─────────────┴─────────┘
  • Filter(pred) before an aggregate keeps a group's rows where pred is true: apple_qty sums only the apples;
  • a Bool sums as 0 and 1, so the sum of a condition counts the rows that meet it;
  • MaxBy(other) and MinBy(other) take a column's value where another column is largest or smallest: each region's biggest order's product.
  • New in 0.6.7: TopKBy(other, k) and BottomKBy(other, k) take k of them, a list a group, as Polars' top_k_by and bottom_k_by: each region's three biggest orders' products. A null in other comes last, and rows that tie on it are ordered by their values, the greater first for TopKBy, where Polars' sort orders them as it finds them.

docs.title: Lists per group
docs.text:
Implode gathers a group's values into a list. Unique, Sort, Head and the other expressions that give several values give a list per group too:

df, err := sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(
        ursus.Col("order_id").Implode().Alias("orders"),
        ursus.Col("product").Unique().Sort().Alias("products"),
    ).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ region  │ orders      │ products                 │
│ String  │ List(Int64) │ List(String)             │
├─────────┼─────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ "east"  │ [4, 6]      │ ["apple", "pear"]        │
│ "north" │ [1, 3, 7]   │ ["apple", "fig", "pear"] │
│ "south" │ [2, 5, 8]   │ ["apple", "fig", "pear"] │
└─────────┴─────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

New in 0.6.7: any expression that is not an aggregate is each group's values as a list, as Polars answers it: Agg(Col("qty")) is each group's quantities, Agg(Col("qty").Mul(2)) doubled, and a window runs a group at a time, Agg(Col("qty").CumSum(false)) each group's running total, and Agg(Col("qty").CumSum(false).Max()) its greatest. An expression that mixes an aggregate with a row's value, Col("qty").Sub(Col("qty").Mean()), is each row's value less its group's mean, a list a group.

New in 0.6.7: an aggregate's input may hold another aggregate, computed over the group first, as Polars computes it: Col("qty").Sub(Col("qty").Mean()).Abs().Sum() is each group's sum of distances from its mean, and in a Select the frame's. Col("t").SortBy(Col("qty").Sub(Col("qty").Mean())).First() sorts by the same distances.

A list column can be exploded back into rows, or asked questions with List().

docs.title: Filtering groups: having
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. Having(predicates...) keeps the groups whose predicates all hold, each an aggregate of its group, as Polars' having and SQL's HAVING: the regions with more than two orders, here. It filters what Agg gives, the shorthands, and Head and Tail; a group whose predicate is null is left out.

show(sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    MaintainOrder().
    Having(ursus.Len().Gt(2)).
    Agg(ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty")))
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌─────────┬────────┐
│ region  │ qty    │
│ String  │ Int128 │
├─────────┼────────┤
│ "north" │ 20     │
│ "south" │ 19     │
└─────────┴────────┘

A predicate must be an aggregate and Boolean. Polars casts a number to a Boolean, so that a sum keeps every group not 0; here it is refused.

docs.title: Each group's first and last rows
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. GroupBy(keys).Head(n) keeps each group's first n rows as rows rather than lists, as Polars' group_by().head(n), and Tail(n) its last n. The key columns come first, the groups in the order each first appears, and each group's rows in the frame's order:

show(sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Tail(1))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ region  │ product │ qty   │
│ String  │ String  │ Int64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ "north" │ "fig"   │ 3     │
│ "south" │ "pear"  │ 6     │
│ "east"  │ "apple" │ 12    │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────┘

They are a window over the keys and a sort, so they spill past a memory limit and keep their order there. Head(0) is no rows, where Polars gives a row of nulls for each group.

docs.title: Every column at once
docs.text:
GroupBy(...) has shortcuts that aggregate every column but the keys:

  • Sum(), Mean(), Median() and Quantile(q, interpolation) take the numeric columns;
  • Min(), Max(), First(), Last() and NUnique() take every column;
  • Count() counts each group's rows into a column named count, and Len(name) under a name of your own.
df, err := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("price")).
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Max().
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ qty   │ price   │
│ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ "east"  │ 12    │ 2.25    │
│ "north" │ 10    │ 3       │
│ "south" │ 9     │ 3       │
└─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

docs.title: The whole frame
docs.text:
An aggregate in Select is one value for the whole frame, so a Select of aggregates is one row. GroupBy() with no keys is the same, written as a group-by:

df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Len().Alias("orders"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty"),
        ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Sum().Alias("revenue"),
        ursus.Col("date").Max().Alias("last_day"),
    ).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (1, 4)
┌────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────────┐
│ orders │ qty    │ revenue │ last_day   │
│ Uint64 │ Int128 │ Float64 │ Date       │
├────────┼────────┼─────────┼────────────┤
│ 8      │ 53     │ 108.75  │ 2026-01-07 │
└────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────┘

New in 0.6.7. A frame's own Sum, Mean, Median, Min, Max, Std(ddof), Var(ddof), Quantile(q, interpolation), Product and NullCount aggregate every column at once, one row, as Polars' frame methods do. A column the aggregate does not take is kept, as a null: the mean of text is null, and a Boolean's mean is the share of its trues.

lines := sales().Select(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("price"))
show(lines.Mean())
show(lines.Max())
Output
shape: (1, 3)
┌────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ region │ qty     │ price   │
│ String │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ null   │ 6.625   │ 2.15625 │
└────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

shape: (1, 3)
┌─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ qty   │ price   │
│ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ "south" │ 12    │ 3       │
└─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

New in 0.6.7. Corr(ctx) is each pair of columns' Pearson correlation, a Float64 column a column, as Polars' frame corr, which NumPy computes: a column holding a null is NaN throughout, where Corr of two expressions skips the rows holding one. SumHorizontal(ctx, ignoreNulls), MeanHorizontal(ctx, ignoreNulls), MinHorizontal and MaxHorizontal are each row's reduction across every column, named sum, mean, min and max, and Fold(ctx, fn) folds a function across the columns from the first, as Polars' frame methods do.

ValueCounts(exprs...) counts the rows of each distinct value, most frequent first, ties in the order their values first appear:

df, err := sales().ValueCounts(ursus.Col("product")).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬────────┐
│ product │ count  │
│ String  │ Uint64 │
├─────────┼────────┤
│ "apple" │ 3      │
│ "pear"  │ 3      │
│ "fig"   │ 2      │
└─────────┴────────┘

and Describe summarizes each column, as Polars' describe does:

df, err := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("price")).
    Describe(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (9, 3)
┌──────────────┬───────────────────┬────────────────────┐
│ statistic    │ qty               │ price              │
│ String       │ Float64           │ Float64            │
├──────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ "count"      │ 8                 │ 8                  │
│ "null_count" │ 0                 │ 0                  │
│ "mean"       │ 6.625             │ 2.15625            │
│ "std"        │ 3.543101950067402 │ 0.6258922202972101 │
│ "min"        │ 2                 │ 1.5                │
│ "25%"        │ 4                 │ 1.5                │
│ "50%"        │ 7                 │ 2.25               │
│ "75%"        │ 9                 │ 2.25               │
│ "max"        │ 12                │ 3                  │
└──────────────┴───────────────────┴────────────────────┘

docs.title: A group's rows as a frame
docs.text: New in 0.6.7. Groups(ctx) gives each group's rows as a frame beside its key, a Go iterator, as Polars' for key, df in df.group_by(...): the groups in the order each first appears, each frame the rows as the frame holds them, and the key a one-row frame named as the key expressions are, so a key computed from a column is the key's and never changes the rows. MapGroups(ctx, fn) runs a Go function over each group's frame and stacks the answers, which must agree in their columns and types, as Polars' map_groups, for what an aggregation cannot say. Both run the query and hold its answer, a frame a group, as PartitionBy does.

docs.title: Under a memory limit
docs.text: A group-by spills to disk when its groups outgrow the query's memory budget, a median's, a quantile's and an NUnique's values included, and gives the answer it gives in memory. Implode cannot divide its answer, and fails at the limit with an error that says so. See Memory and spilling.

docs.title: Dates and times
docs.text:
Type Holds Date a calendar day Datetime(unit, zone) an instant, to the second, ms, us or ns, in an IANA zone or none Duration(unit) a length of time TimeOf(unit) a time of day

A Go time.Time is a Datetime(ns, "UTC") in Values, and a literal anywhere an expression goes. Methods for these types sit behind Dt().

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
Str().Strptime(type, format, strict) parses text with a strftime format; not strict, what does not parse is null:

logs := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("at", []string{"2026-03-08 06:30", "2026-03-08 07:45", "oops"}),
)
utc := ursus.Datetime(ursus.Micro, "UTC")
show(logs.Select(
    ursus.Col("at"),
    ursus.Col("at").Str().Strptime(utc, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M", false).Alias("instant"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ at                 │ instant                     │
│ String             │ Datetime(us, UTC)           │
├────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ "2026-03-08 06:30" │ 2026-03-08T06:30:00.000000Z │
│ "2026-03-08 07:45" │ 2026-03-08T07:45:00.000000Z │
│ "oops"             │ null                        │
└────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

A CSV column is read as a date when the scan is told so: WithSchemaOverrides(map[string]ursus.DataType{"date": ursus.Date}), as the guide's sales does.

docs.title: The parts of a date
docs.text:
The examples here read three days:

func days() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("day", []string{"2024-02-29", "2026-01-03", "2026-12-31"}),
    ).Select(ursus.Col("day").Str().ToDate())
}

d := ursus.Col("day").Dt()
show(days().Select(
    ursus.Col("day"),
    d.Year().Alias("year"),
    d.Month().Alias("month"),
    d.Weekday().Alias("weekday"),
    d.Week().Alias("week"),
    d.Quarter().Alias("quarter"),
    d.OrdinalDay().Alias("day_of_year"),
    d.IsLeapYear().Alias("leap"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 8)
┌────────────┬───────┬───────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┬─────────────┬───────┐
│ day        │ year  │ month │ weekday │ week  │ quarter │ day_of_year │ leap  │
│ Date       │ Int32 │ Int32 │ Int32   │ Int32 │ Int32   │ Int32       │ Bool  │
├────────────┼───────┼───────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┼─────────────┼───────┤
│ 2024-02-29 │ 2024  │ 2     │ 4       │ 9     │ 1       │ 60          │ true  │
│ 2026-01-03 │ 2026  │ 1     │ 6       │ 1     │ 1       │ 3           │ false │
│ 2026-12-31 │ 2026  │ 12    │ 4       │ 53    │ 4       │ 365         │ false │
└────────────┴───────┴───────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┴─────────────┴───────┘

Weekday is ISO's, Monday 1 to Sunday 7, and Week the ISO week: 2026's last day is in its week 53. Datetimes add Hour, Minute, Second and the fractions, Date and Time.

docs.title: Arithmetic
docs.text:
A date minus a date is a Duration; TotalDays and its kin turn it into a number. OffsetBy moves by a calendar interval, so a month after January 31 is February 28, not March 3:

invoices := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("issued", []string{"2026-01-31", "2026-02-10"}),
    ursus.Values("paid", []string{"2026-02-14", "2026-02-11"}),
).Select(ursus.Col("issued").Str().ToDate(), ursus.Col("paid").Str().ToDate())
issued := ursus.Col("issued").Dt()
show(invoices.Select(
    ursus.Col("issued"),
    ursus.Col("paid").Sub(ursus.Col("issued")).Dt().TotalDays().
        Alias("days_to_pay"),
    issued.OffsetBy(ursus.Every("1mo")).Alias("plus_a_month"),
    issued.MonthEnd().Alias("month_end"),
    issued.AddBusinessDays(5, ursus.RollForward).Alias("plus_5_business"),
))
Output
shape: (2, 5)
┌────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┬────────────┬─────────────────┐
│ issued     │ days_to_pay │ plus_a_month │ month_end  │ plus_5_business │
│ Date       │ Int64       │ Date         │ Date       │ Date            │
├────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┼────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ 2026-01-31 │ 14          │ 2026-02-28   │ 2026-01-31 │ 2026-02-09      │
│ 2026-02-10 │ 1           │ 2026-03-10   │ 2026-02-28 │ 2026-02-17      │
└────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┴────────────┴─────────────────┘

MonthStart and MonthEnd move to a month's ends. AddBusinessDays(n, roll) counts business days, Monday to Friday unless a BusinessCalendar gives other weekdays and its holidays; roll says what a start on a day off does: RollForward, RollBackward, or RollRaise, the default, to refuse it. IsBusinessDay tests one.

docs.title: Truncating and formatting
docs.text:
Truncate(every) moves each value to the start of its interval: a week starts on Monday, as in Polars. Round moves it to the nearest. Strftime(format) formats it:

date := ursus.Col("date").Dt()
show(sales().Select(
    ursus.Col("date"),
    date.Truncate(ursus.Every("1w")).Alias("week"),
    date.Truncate(ursus.Every("1mo")).Alias("month"),
    date.Strftime("%a %d %b").Alias("label"),
).Unique())
Output
shape: (5, 4)
┌────────────┬────────────┬────────────┬──────────────┐
│ date       │ week       │ month      │ label        │
│ Date       │ Date       │ Date       │ String       │
├────────────┼────────────┼────────────┼──────────────┤
│ 2026-01-03 │ 2025-12-29 │ 2026-01-01 │ "Sat 03 Jan" │
│ 2026-01-04 │ 2025-12-29 │ 2026-01-01 │ "Sun 04 Jan" │
│ 2026-01-05 │ 2026-01-05 │ 2026-01-01 │ "Mon 05 Jan" │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 2026-01-05 │ 2026-01-01 │ "Tue 06 Jan" │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 2026-01-05 │ 2026-01-01 │ "Wed 07 Jan" │
└────────────┴────────────┴────────────┴──────────────┘

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
A Datetime with a zone is an instant shown on that zone's clock. ConvertTimeZone shows the same instant on another clock; ReplaceTimeZone keeps the clock and changes the instant. New York's clocks moved forward an hour at 07:00 UTC on March 8, 2026, and the second row is on the other side of it:

at := []time.Time{
    time.Date(2026, 3, 8, 6, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC),
    time.Date(2026, 3, 8, 7, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC),
}
instants := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("utc", at)).
    Select(ursus.Col("utc").Cast(ursus.Datetime(ursus.Second, "UTC")))
show(instants.Select(
    ursus.Col("utc"),
    ursus.Col("utc").Dt().ConvertTimeZone("America/New_York").Alias("new_york"),
    ursus.Col("utc").Dt().ReplaceTimeZone("Asia/Tokyo").Alias("same_wall_in_tokyo"),
))
Output
shape: (2, 3)
┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
│ utc                  │ new_york                      │ same_wall_in_tokyo        │
│ Datetime(s, UTC)     │ Datetime(s, America/New_York) │ Datetime(s, Asia/Tokyo)   │
├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
│ 2026-03-08T06:30:00Z │ 2026-03-08T01:30:00-05:00     │ 2026-03-08T06:30:00+09:00 │
│ 2026-03-08T07:30:00Z │ 2026-03-08T03:30:00-04:00     │ 2026-03-08T07:30:00+09:00 │
└──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

ursus reads zones from the system's zone database, as Go's time package does, where Polars bundles its own. They agree but for a zone whose daylight time the system's database writes in the rearguard form, as Ubuntu's does for Dublin.

docs.title: Ranges
docs.text:
DateRange(start, end, every) makes a date for each step, ends included, and DatetimeRange and TimeRange the same for instants and times of day. DateRanges makes a list a row from columns:

from := ursus.Lit(time.Date(2026, 1, 30, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)).Cast(ursus.Date)
to := ursus.Lit(time.Date(2026, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC)).Cast(ursus.Date)
span := ursus.DateRange(from, to, ursus.Every("1d")).Alias("day")
show(ursus.Frame().Select(span))
Output
shape: (4, 1)
┌────────────┐
│ day        │
│ Date       │
├────────────┤
│ 2026-01-30 │
│ 2026-01-31 │
│ 2026-02-01 │
│ 2026-02-02 │
└────────────┘

docs.title: Upsampling
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. Upsample(time, every, groupBy...) puts a row at every step from each group's first instant to its last, as Polars' upsample. A row the frame has at a step is kept; where it has none, the new row is null but for the time and the group's keys, which a fill forward completes: the weekend below. A row that falls between two steps is left out, as Polars leaves it.

show(prices().
    Filter(ursus.Col("ticker").Eq("ACME")).
    Upsample("date", ursus.Every("1d"), "ticker").
    WithColumns(ursus.Col("close").FillNull(ursus.FillForward).Alias("filled")))
Output
shape: (8, 4)
┌────────────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ date       │ ticker │ close   │ filled  │
│ Date       │ String │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├────────────┼────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ "ACME" │ 10      │ 10      │
│ 2026-01-06 │ "ACME" │ 11      │ 11      │
│ 2026-01-07 │ "ACME" │ 10.5    │ 10.5    │
│ 2026-01-08 │ "ACME" │ 12      │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-09 │ "ACME" │ 12      │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-10 │ "ACME" │ null    │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-11 │ "ACME" │ null    │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-12 │ "ACME" │ 13.5    │ 13.5    │
└────────────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

It is a LazyFrame's too. The groups keep the order each first appears, and their rows the grid's, with or without a memory limit, so a fill after it reads the rows it should. Unlike Polars', the frame need not be sorted.

docs.title: Dynamic groups
docs.text:
GroupByDynamic(index, options) groups rows into windows of time cut from a sorted index: per day, per week, per hour. Every is how far apart windows start, and Period how long each is, Every when not given, so the windows tile the time.

show(prices().
    Filter(ursus.Col("ticker").Eq("ACME")).
    GroupByDynamic(ursus.Col("date"),
        ursus.DynamicOptions{Every: ursus.Every("1d")}).
    Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("rows"), ursus.Col("close").Mean().Alias("close")))
Output
shape: (8, 3)
┌────────────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ date       │ rows   │ close   │
│ Date       │ Uint64 │ Float64 │
├────────────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ 1      │ 10      │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 1      │ 11      │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 1      │ 10.5    │
│ 2026-01-08 │ 1      │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-09 │ 1      │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-10 │ 0      │ null    │
│ 2026-01-11 │ 0      │ null    │
│ 2026-01-12 │ 1      │ 13.5    │
└────────────┴────────┴─────────┘

Empty windows are rows, which Polars leaves out

ursus makes every window of the grid from the first instant to the last, so a day with no rows is a row with a count of 0: the weekend above. Polars' group_by_dynamic leaves those windows out. Filter rows > 0 for Polars' answer.

GroupBy cuts windows within each key; the index column comes first, then the keys, where Polars puts the keys first:

show(sales().
    GroupByDynamic(ursus.Col("date"), ursus.DynamicOptions{
        Every:   ursus.Every("1w"),
        GroupBy: []ursus.Expr{ursus.Col("region")},
    }).
    Agg(ursus.Col("qty").Sum().Alias("qty")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region")), ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("date"))))
Output
shape: (5, 3)
┌────────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ date       │ region  │ qty    │
│ Date       │ String  │ Int128 │
├────────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ "east"  │ 14     │
│ 2025-12-29 │ "north" │ 17     │
│ 2026-01-05 │ "north" │ 3      │
│ 2025-12-29 │ "south" │ 4      │
│ 2026-01-05 │ "south" │ 15     │
└────────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Offset shifts the grid, Closed says which end of a window holds its instant, Label what the index column shows, StartBy where the grid begins, and IncludeBoundaries adds each window's bounds.

docs.title: Rolling groups
docs.text:
Rolling(index, options) gives every row its own window, reaching back Period from its instant, and aggregates it: the rows and the high of the three days up to each close.

show(prices().
    Filter(ursus.Col("ticker").Eq("ACME")).
    Rolling(ursus.Col("date"), ursus.RollingOptions{Period: ursus.Every("3d")}).
    Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("rows"), ursus.Col("close").Max().Alias("high_3d")))
Output
shape: (6, 3)
┌────────────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ date       │ rows   │ high_3d │
│ Date       │ Uint64 │ Float64 │
├────────────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ 1      │ 10      │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 2      │ 11      │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 3      │ 11      │
│ 2026-01-08 │ 3      │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-09 │ 3      │ 12      │
│ 2026-01-12 │ 1      │ 13.5    │
└────────────┴────────┴─────────┘

A rolling group is a group-by with one row for each input row. The rolling windows by time in Window functions answer the same question as a column beside the rows.

Offset places each window as Polars' offset does: from the row's instant plus the offset, a period long, (t + Offset, t + Offset + Period]. Unset, it is minus the period, the window up to the row; NoOffset() is a window wholly after it, Polars' offset="0d". Changed in 0.6.7: Offset moved the window's end before.

docs.title: An integer index
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. An index can be a count rather than an instant: a step, a sequence number. An Int32 or Int64 index counts by Polars' integer unit, so Every("5i") is five of it, and its windows are cut from its values, as from time's:

readings := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("step", []int64{1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 12}),
    ursus.Values("load", []float64{3, 5, 2, 6, 4, 7}),
)
fives := ursus.DynamicOptions{Every: ursus.Every("5i")}
show(readings.GroupByDynamic(ursus.Col("step"), fives).
    Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("rows"), ursus.Col("load").Sum()))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ step  │ rows   │ load    │
│ Int64 │ Uint64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ 0     │ 3      │ 10      │
│ 5     │ 2      │ 10      │
│ 10    │ 1      │ 7       │
