└───────┴────────┴─────────┘

Dynamic and rolling groups take one, as do Upsample and the rolling windows and ewms by a column, and the index keeps its type. All but GroupByDynamic take a UInt32 or a UInt64 too, as Polars' do. An interval of time on an integer index is refused, and so is "i" where a date is moved: in Truncate, Round, OffsetBy, a range or an as-of tolerance, where Polars moves nothing, panics, or reads it as nanoseconds.

docs.title: Under a memory limit
docs.text: Dynamic and rolling groups stream their input and hand out each window when it closes, keyed ones too, so a long series runs under a memory budget.

docs.title: Go functions
docs.text: When no expression says what you need, a Go function can: it runs inside the query, on every core, beside the expressions. A function call in Go is cheap, so a user-defined function costs far less here than a Python function does in Polars.

docs.title: A value at a time: MapElements
docs.text:
MapElements(name, type, fn) calls fn on each value. The function's Go types are the column's in and the answer's out, inferred from fn by a generic method:

slug := ursus.Col("product").MapElements("slug", ursus.String,
    func(s string) (string, error) {
        return strings.ToUpper(s[:1]) + "-" + fmt.Sprint(len(s)), nil
    })
show(sales().Head(3).Select(ursus.Col("product"), slug.Alias("slug")))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬────────┐
│ product │ slug   │
│ String  │ String │
├─────────┼────────┤
│ "apple" │ "A-5"  │
│ "apple" │ "A-5"  │
│ "pear"  │ "P-4"  │
└─────────┴────────┘

An answer can be of any type, and a mapped column is an expression like any other, a group-by's key here:

band := ursus.Col("qty").MapElements("band", ursus.String,
    func(q int64) (string, error) {
        switch {
        case q >= 10:
            return "large", nil
        case q >= 5:
            return "medium", nil
        }
        return "small", nil
    })
show(sales().
    GroupBy(band.Alias("band")).
    Agg(ursus.Len().Alias("orders")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("band"))))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌──────────┬────────┐
│ band     │ orders │
│ String   │ Uint64 │
├──────────┼────────┤
│ "large"  │ 2      │
│ "medium" │ 3      │
│ "small"  │ 3      │
└──────────┴────────┘

Nulls pass through: fn is never called with one, so it cannot mistake a missing value for a zero. Three of the six rows were null, and the function ran three times:

var calls atomic.Int64
double := ursus.Col("temp").MapElements("double", ursus.Float64,
    func(t float64) (float64, error) {
        calls.Add(1)
        return 2 * t, nil
    })
show(readings().Select(ursus.Col("temp"), double.Alias("doubled")))
fmt.Println("calls:", calls.Load())
Output
shape: (6, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────┐
│ temp    │ doubled │
│ Float64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼─────────┤
│ 10      │ 20      │
│ null    │ null    │
│ null    │ null    │
│ 13      │ 26      │
│ 12      │ 24      │
│ null    │ null    │
└─────────┴─────────┘

calls: 3

docs.title: A column at a time: MapBatches
docs.text:
MapBatches(name, type, fn) calls fn with a batch of values and whether each is there, and takes back the same: the place to decide what a null means, or to call something that works on many values at once.

orZero := ursus.Col("temp").MapBatches("or_zero", ursus.Float64,
    func(vals []float64, valid []bool) ([]float64, []bool, error) {
        out, ok := make([]float64, len(vals)), make([]bool, len(vals))
        for i := range vals {
            if valid[i] {
                out[i] = vals[i]
            }
            ok[i] = true // a null becomes 0, a value of its own
        }
        return out, ok, nil
    })
show(readings().Select(ursus.Col("temp"), orZero.Alias("or_zero")))
Output
shape: (6, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────┐
│ temp    │ or_zero │
│ Float64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼─────────┤
│ 10      │ 10      │
│ null    │ 0       │
│ null    │ 0       │
│ 13      │ 13      │
│ 12      │ 12      │
│ null    │ 0       │
└─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: A window at a time: RollingMap
docs.text: New in 0.6.7. RollingMap(name, type, size, fn) calls fn on each row's window of size rows, as Polars' rolling_map: the window's values in its order and whether each is there, as MapBatches gives a batch, and the answer is the row's. A window of fewer values than MinSamples(k), size unless set, is null; RollingCenter() centres it on its row. It runs within each partition under Over, and streams past a memory limit as the rolling functions do.

docs.title: A row at a time: MapRows
docs.text: New in 0.6.7. A frame's MapRows(ctx, fn) calls fn on each row, as Polars' map_rows. A row is a struct, read as Rows reads one, or a []any of its values in the columns' order; a struct answer is a column a field, and any other answer one column named map. The rows are decoded and fn called once each, in order, on one goroutine, so an expression or MapBatches is the faster way where one can say it.

docs.title: A whole column: MapColumns
docs.text: New in 0.6.7. A frame's MapColumns(ctx, names, fn) replaces each named column with fn of it, as Polars' map_columns: the answer keeps the column's name and place, and is as long as the frame, or one value, which every row takes.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
An error fn returns fails the query, naming the function, the value and the row of its batch. A panic in fn is reported the same way, rather than ending the program.

dozens := ursus.Col("qty").MapElements("dozens", ursus.Float64,
    func(q int64) (float64, error) {
        if q > 10 {
            return 0, errors.New("more than ten is a wholesale order")
        }
        return float64(q) / 12, nil
    })
_, err := sales().Select(dozens).Collect(context.Background())
fmt.Println(err)
Output
ursus: map_elements: udf "dozens" failed on 12, row 5 of its batch of column "qty"
  caused by: more than ten is a wholesale order

docs.title: The name
docs.text:
The name is how Explain and every error show a function, since a closure prints as nothing. Two different functions given one name are refused before the query runs:

slug := ursus.Col("product").MapElements("slug", ursus.String,
    func(s string) (string, error) { return strings.ToUpper(s), nil })
plan, err := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(5)).
    Select(slug).
    Explain(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(plan)
Output
PROJECT [col("product").map_elements("slug" -> String)]
  FILTER [(col("qty") > lit(5))]
    CSV SCAN testdata/sales.csv
      projection: [product, qty] (2/6 cols)

A function used twice should be built once and held in a variable, so it is one function under one name.

docs.title: What the function must do
docs.text:
• Be safe to call from several goroutines. A query runs on every core, and there is no opting one expression out: a closure over a shared map is a data race. Count with sync/atomic, as the null example does.
  • Not depend on the order it is called in. The answer's order is the rows', the calls' is not.
  • Answer the type it declares. The declared type is the column's from the plan's start; an answer of another type fails the query.

docs.title: Into a frame
docs.text:
Values(name, slice) makes a column from a Go slice, its type the slice's, and ValuesNullable(name, slice, valid) one with nulls where valid is false. A slice of structs becomes a frame a field at a time:

type order struct {
    ID     int64
    Placed time.Time
    Total  float64
    Note   *string // nil: no note
}
note := "gift wrap"
in := []order{
    {1, time.Date(2026, 1, 3, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC), 15, nil},
    {2, time.Date(2026, 1, 4, 14, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC), 27, &note},
}

ids, totals := make([]int64, len(in)), make([]float64, len(in))
placed := make([]time.Time, len(in))
notes, hasNote := make([]string, len(in)), make([]bool, len(in))
for i, o := range in {
    ids[i], placed[i], totals[i] = o.ID, o.Placed, o.Total
    if o.Note != nil {
        notes[i], hasNote[i] = *o.Note, true
    }
}
show(ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", ids),
    ursus.Values("placed", placed),
    ursus.Values("total", totals),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("note", notes, hasNote),
))
Output
shape: (2, 4)
┌───────┬────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬─────────────┐
│ id    │ placed                         │ total   │ note        │
│ Int64 │ Datetime(ns, UTC)              │ Float64 │ String      │
├───────┼────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────────┤
│ 1     │ 2026-01-03T09:00:00.000000000Z │ 15      │ null        │
│ 2     │ 2026-01-04T14:30:00.000000000Z │ 27      │ "gift wrap" │
└───────┴────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴─────────────┘

New in 0.6.7: FromRows(rows) does that in one call, as Polars builds a frame from dataclasses, a column a field named as Rows reads it, its ursus tag or its own name. A pointer field is nullable, a slice a List, and a struct a Struct:

type order struct {
    ID     int64     `ursus:"id"`
    Placed time.Time `ursus:"placed"`
    Total  float64   `ursus:"total"`
    Note   *string   `ursus:"note"` // nil: no note
}
note := "gift wrap"
show(ursus.FromRows([]order{
    {1, time.Date(2026, 1, 3, 9, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC), 15, nil},
    {2, time.Date(2026, 1, 4, 14, 30, 0, 0, time.UTC), 27, &note},
}))
Output
shape: (2, 4)
┌───────┬────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬─────────────┐
│ id    │ placed                         │ total   │ note        │
│ Int64 │ Datetime(ns, UTC)              │ Float64 │ String      │
├───────┼────────────────────────────────┼─────────┼─────────────┤
│ 1     │ 2026-01-03T09:00:00.000000000Z │ 15      │ null        │
│ 2     │ 2026-01-04T14:30:00.000000000Z │ 27      │ "gift wrap" │
└───────┴────────────────────────────────┴─────────┴─────────────┘
Go slice Column []bool Bool []int8 … []int64, []int Int8 … Int64, Int64 []uint8 … []uint64, []uint Uint8 … Uint64, Uint64 []float32, []float64 Float32, Float64 []string, [][]byte String, Binary []time.Time Datetime(ns, "UTC"); cast to Date for days []time.Duration Duration(ns)

Arrow records come in through ScanArrowRecords; see CSV, Parquet and Arrow.

docs.title: A column out: Series
docs.text:
df.Column[T](name) is a column as a Series[T], typed by a generic method, so no assertion is needed at the call site. A Series answers in Go:

df, err := sales().Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
qty, err := df.Column[int64]("qty")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(qty.Name(), qty.Len(), qty.NullCount())
fmt.Println(qty.Values())

total := qty.Fold(int64(0), func(acc, v int64) int64 { return acc + v })
fmt.Println("total:", total)

kinds := qty.Map[string](func(v int64) string {
    if v >= 8 {
        return "bulk"
    }
    return "single"
})
fmt.Println(kinds)
Output
qty 8 0
[10 4 7 2 9 12 3 6]
total: 53
[bulk single single single bulk bulk single single]
  • Values() is the values that are not null, as a slice;
  • Map[U](fn) maps each value to a Go slice of another type, and MapErr with a function that can fail;
  • Fold(init, fn) reduces the values left to right;
  • Name, DType, Len and NullCount.

New in 0.6.7: a Series has Polars' operations on one column: Sort, SortDesc, Unique, Reverse, DropNulls, FillNull, Cast[U], and the aggregates Min, Max, Sum, Mean, Median, Std and Var with their degrees of freedom, Count and NUnique, each run through the engine as a one-column frame; Head, Tail, Slice and Rename share the column; and ToDummies makes its dummy columns, as a frame's (see Reshaping).

A null is never a zero mistaken for a value. All() iterates each value with whether it is there, and Get(i) and df.At[T](row, name) answer one:

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("score", []int64{90, 0, 75}, []bool{true, false, true}),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
score, err := df.Column[int64]("score")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for v, present := range score.All() {
    fmt.Println(v, present)
}
v, ok := score.Get(1)
fmt.Println("row 1:", v, ok)
Output
90 true
0 false
75 true
row 1: 0 false

T must match the column: int64 for Int64, float64 for Float64, string for String, ursus.Int128Value for an Int128 sum. A mismatch is an error naming both. A Date is viewed as its int32 days and a Datetime as its int64 ticks; Rows, below, decodes either into a time.Time.

docs.title: Rows out: structs
docs.text:
df.Rows[T]() decodes every row into a struct. A field takes the column its ursus tag names, else its own name, else its name ignoring case; ursus:"-" skips it:

type sale struct {
    ID      int64     `ursus:"order_id"`
    Day     time.Time `ursus:"date"`
    Product string
    Qty     int64
    Revenue float64 `ursus:"-"` // filled by the program, not read
}
df, err := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("region").Eq("east")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
rows, err := df.Rows[sale]()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, r := range rows {
    fmt.Println(r.ID, r.Day.Format("Jan 2"), r.Product, r.Qty)
}
Output
4 Jan 5 pear 2
6 Jan 6 apple 12

A field with no column is an error, not a zero left behind: a typo would otherwise be a wrong number in a report. A pointer field is how a struct sees a null, nil:

type reading struct {
    Hour int64
    Temp *float64 // nil where the reading is null
}
df, err := readings().Head(3).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
rows, err := df.Rows[reading]()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, r := range rows {
    if r.Temp == nil {
        fmt.Println(r.Hour, "no reading")
        continue
    }
    fmt.Println(r.Hour, *r.Temp)
}
Output
0 10
1 no reading
2 no reading

The mapping of fields to columns is worked out once, so decoding costs a setter call a field a row, not a reflection lookup.

New in 0.6.7: RowsByKey[K, T](key) groups the rows by a column, as Polars' rows_by_key, a key's rows in the frame's order, and ToMaps() is each row a map[string]any, as Polars' to_dicts: an int64 for an Int64, a time.Time for an instant, a []any for a List, nil for a null. IterRows[T] streams a query's rows as structs, a batch at a time, as Polars' iter_rows, so an answer larger than memory can be read row by row.

docs.title: A large answer, a batch at a time
docs.text:
CollectBatches streams an answer as frames of WithBatchSize rows, a Go iterator, so an answer larger than memory reaches Go without being held at once:

type sale struct {
    ID  int64 `ursus:"order_id"`
    Qty int64
}
ctx := context.Background()
total := int64(0)
for batch, err := range sales().CollectBatches(ctx, ursus.WithBatchSize(3)) {
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    rows, err := batch.Rows[sale]()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    for _, r := range rows {
        total += r.Qty
    }
    fmt.Println("batch of", len(rows), "- running total", total)
}
Output
batch of 3 - running total 21
batch of 3 - running total 44
batch of 2 - running total 53

Breaking out of the loop stops the query and removes its spill files.

docs.title: CSV, Parquet and Arrow
docs.text: Every reader is a scan: it gives a LazyFrame, and reads only when the query runs, only the columns the query uses.

docs.title: CSV
docs.text:
ScanCSV(path, options...) reads a file, and ScanCSVReader(bytes, name) text already in memory. The types are inferred from the first rows, and the options say the rest:

data := []byte("id;name;score\n1;Ada;90\n2;Ben;NA\n3;Cai;75\n")
show(ursus.ScanCSVReader(data, "scores.csv",
    ursus.WithSeparator(';'),
    ursus.WithNullValues("NA"),
    ursus.WithSchemaOverrides(map[string]ursus.DataType{"score": ursus.Float64}),
))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ id    │ name   │ score   │
│ Int64 │ String │ Float64 │
├───────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ 1     │ "Ada"  │ 90      │
│ 2     │ "Ben"  │ null    │
│ 3     │ "Cai"  │ 75      │
└───────┴────────┴─────────┘
Option For WithSeparator(c), WithQuote(c), WithComment(prefix) the dialect WithHasHeader(b), WithColumnNames(names...), WithSkipRows(n) the header WithSchema(s), WithSchemaOverrides(m), WithInferRows(n) the types WithNullValues(vals...) the text that means null WithTruncateRaggedLines(b), WithMaxRecordSize(n) malformed input

ScanCSVGlob(pattern) reads every file a pattern matches as one frame, in their names' order, and ScanCSVFiles(paths) a list:

show(ursus.ScanCSVGlob("testdata/parts/revenue-*.csv").
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("month")).
    Agg(ursus.Col("revenue").Sum().Alias("revenue")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("month"))))
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌───────────┬─────────┐
│ month     │ revenue │
│ String    │ Float64 │
├───────────┼─────────┤
│ "2026-01" │ 86.25   │
│ "2026-02" │ 79.25   │
└───────────┴─────────┘

WriteCSV(ctx, w, options...) writes a query's answer to any io.Writer, and SinkCSV(ctx, path) to a file:

var out bytes.Buffer
err := readings().Head(3).
    WriteCSV(context.Background(), &out, ursus.WithNullValue("NA"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Print(out.String())
Output
hour,temp,backup
0,10.0,9.0
1,NA,11.0
2,NA,NA

docs.title: Parquet
docs.text:
ScanParquet(path) reads the footer when the query is planned, and at run time only the column chunks the query needs. A filter on a column with statistics skips whole row groups that cannot hold a match:

ctx := context.Background()
var file bytes.Buffer
if err := sales().WriteParquet(ctx, &file, ursus.WithRowGroupRows(4)); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
q := ursus.ScanParquetBytes(file.Bytes(), "sales.parquet").
    Filter(ursus.Col("order_id").Gt(6)).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("product"))
plan, err := q.Explain(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(plan)
show(q)
Output
FILTER [(col("order_id") > lit(6))]
  PARQUET SCAN sales.parquet
    projection: [order_id, product] (2/6 cols)
    predicate: [(col("order_id") > lit(6))]

shape: (2, 2)
┌──────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ product │
│ Int64    │ String  │
├──────────┼─────────┤
│ 7        │ "fig"   │
│ 8        │ "pear"  │
└──────────┴─────────┘

projection is the columns read, two of six, and predicate the filter the reader tests against each row group's statistics, skipping every row group that cannot hold a match.

  • ScanParquetGlob(pattern), ScanParquetFiles(paths) and ScanParquetBytes(b, name) read several files, or bytes in memory;
  • List and Struct columns are read and written, in the encoding PyArrow and Polars use;
  • WriteParquet(ctx, w) and SinkParquet(ctx, path) write, with WithCompression, Snappy by default, WithRowGroupRows and WithStatistics.

docs.title: From object storage
docs.text:
ursus has no S3 or GCS client of its own: each store wants its vendor's SDK, and ursus takes on none. ScanParquetFrom reads through any io.ReaderAt you open instead, so a ReadAt over ranged GETs reaches any store, and only the footer and the needed column chunks travel:

ctx := context.Background()
var file bytes.Buffer
if err := sales().WriteParquet(ctx, &file); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
stored := file.Bytes() // standing in for an object in a bucket

lf := ursus.ScanParquetFrom([]ursus.ParquetFile{{
    Name: "s3://shop/sales.parquet",
    Open: func(ctx context.Context) (io.ReaderAt, int64, error) {
        return bytes.NewReader(stored), int64(len(stored)), nil
    },
}})
n, err := lf.Filter(ursus.Col("region").Eq("south")).Count(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(n, "orders from the south")
Output
3 orders from the south

ScanCSVFrom takes a stream the same way, and the writers take any io.Writer, an upload included.

docs.title: Arrow
docs.text:
df.Record() exports a frame as an Arrow record without copying, and lf.CollectRecords(ctx) streams records. ScanArrowRecords(records...) imports records, and ScanArrow(fn) any array.RecordReader: an IPC stream, Flight, the C Data Interface. Import copies, so nothing released afterwards reaches a frame.

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Head(3).
    Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
rec, err := df.Record() // the frame's memory, shared with arrow-go
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(rec.NumRows(), "rows,", rec.Schema().Field(1).Type)

back := ursus.ScanArrowRecords(rec) // copies, so rec can be released
rec.Release()
show(back.WithColumns(ursus.Col("qty").Mul(2).Alias("double")))
Output
3 rows, int64
shape: (3, 3)
┌──────────┬───────┬────────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │ double │
│ Int64    │ Int64 │ Int64  │
├──────────┼───────┼────────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │ 20     │
│ 2        │ 4     │ 8      │
│ 3        │ 7     │ 14     │
└──────────┴───────┴────────┘

38 of Arrow's 45 types map to ursus's; Decimal256, intervals, unions and run-end encoding are refused by name.

New in 0.6.7: Arrow IPC, as Polars reads and writes it. ScanIPC(path) reads an IPC file, Feather version 2, the format of Polars' write_ipc, and ScanIPCStream(path) an IPC stream, write_ipc_stream's; both read string views, large lists and compressed buffers, which Polars writes. WriteIPC(ctx, w), WriteIPCStream(ctx, w) and SinkIPC(ctx, path) write them, uncompressed as Polars' are by default, or with WithIPCCompression(ursus.IPCLZ4) or IPCZstd. ReadIPCSchema(path) and ReadParquetSchema(ctx, path) read a file's schema from its footer alone.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7: ScanNDJSON(path) reads newline-delimited JSON, an object a line, as Polars' scan_ndjson and read_ndjson. ScanNDJSONFiles(paths) and ScanNDJSONGlob(pattern) read several files as one frame, the schema the first's; ScanNDJSONFrom(files) reads files you open, from an object store, say; and ScanNDJSONBytes(b, name) reads NDJSON in memory. A key is a column, in the order the keys are first seen, and its type is inferred from the first 100 lines as Polars infers it: an integer is an Int64, or an Int128 past it; a number with a fraction or an exponent a Float64; an array a List, and an object a Struct. A key holding text and anything else is a String, the other value as Polars writes it: 1.5 for 1.50, and an array as JSON. WithInferSchemaLines(n) infers from more lines, 0 from all of them; WithNDJSONSchema(s) reads the lines as a schema you give, of any type, a Date from its text; and WithNDJSONIgnoreErrors(true) reads a value its column cannot take as a null, as Polars' ignore_errors. An error names the line and the key. A file is read in blocks, each cut into a part a thread and the parts parsed at once, and only the columns a query uses are built.

New in 0.6.7: WriteNDJSON(ctx, w) writes each row as a JSON object on a line of its own, as Polars' write_ndjson, and WriteJSON(ctx, w) one array of them, as write_json; SinkNDJSON(ctx, path) streams to a file, whole or not at all. Each value is written as Polars writes it: a float in Polars' text, NaN and the infinities null; a Decimal, a date and an instant quoted, "2024-01-02 03:04:05.123456", a zoned instant with its offset, "2024-01-02T03:04:05+05:00"; a duration in ISO 8601's seconds, "PT90S"; a List an array and a Struct an object. A Binary column is refused, as Polars refuses it.

docs.title: Larger than memory
docs.text: A sink streams: a query whose answer is larger than memory writes it with SinkParquet or SinkCSV, the spilling operators under a memory limit, as Memory and spilling shows.

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
Join(other, options...) matches this frame's rows with other's by equal keys. The examples join five orders with four customers: customer 2, Ben, has no order, and order 13's customer, 5, is not a customer.

func customers() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("customer_id", []int64{1, 2, 3, 4}),
        ursus.Values("name", []string{"Ada", "Ben", "Cai", "Dee"}),
    )
}

func orders() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("order", []int64{10, 11, 12, 13, 14}),
        ursus.Values("customer_id", []int64{1, 3, 1, 5, 4}),
        ursus.Values("amount", []float64{25, 40, 10, 99, 15}),
    )
}

and show collects a query and prints it:

func show(lf *ursus.LazyFrame) {
    df, err := lf.Collect(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(df)
}

docs.title: The kinds
docs.text:
JoinOn names the keys, and JoinHow the kind; inner is the default.

InnerLeftRightFullSemiAntiCross

Pairs of rows whose keys match. Order 13 and Ben are left out.

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(orders().Join(customers(), on, ursus.JoinMaintainOrder(ursus.JoinOrderLeft)))
Output
shape: (4, 4)
┌───────┬─────────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ order │ customer_id │ amount  │ name   │
│ Int64 │ Int64       │ Float64 │ String │
├───────┼─────────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 10    │ 1           │ 25      │ "Ada"  │
│ 11    │ 3           │ 40      │ "Cai"  │
│ 12    │ 1           │ 10      │ "Ada"  │
│ 14    │ 4           │ 15      │ "Dee"  │
└───────┴─────────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Every row of the left frame, with nulls where the right has no match.

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(orders().Join(customers(), on, ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinLeft)))
Output
shape: (5, 4)
┌───────┬─────────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ order │ customer_id │ amount  │ name   │
│ Int64 │ Int64       │ Float64 │ String │
├───────┼─────────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 10    │ 1           │ 25      │ "Ada"  │
│ 11    │ 3           │ 40      │ "Cai"  │
│ 12    │ 1           │ 10      │ "Ada"  │
│ 13    │ 5           │ 99      │ null   │
│ 14    │ 4           │ 15      │ "Dee"  │
└───────┴─────────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Every row of the right frame, with nulls where the left has no match.

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(orders().Join(customers(), on, ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinRight)))
Output
shape: (5, 4)
┌───────┬─────────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ order │ customer_id │ amount  │ name   │
│ Int64 │ Int64       │ Float64 │ String │
├───────┼─────────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 10    │ 1           │ 25      │ "Ada"  │
│ 11    │ 3           │ 40      │ "Cai"  │
│ 12    │ 1           │ 10      │ "Ada"  │
│ 14    │ 4           │ 15      │ "Dee"  │
│ null  │ 2           │ null    │ "Ben"  │
└───────┴─────────────┴─────────┴────────┘

Every row of both, each key column kept, since either side's can be null.

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(orders().Join(customers(), on, ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinFull)))
Output
shape: (6, 5)
┌───────┬─────────────┬─────────┬───────────────────┬────────┐
│ order │ customer_id │ amount  │ customer_id_right │ name   │
│ Int64 │ Int64       │ Float64 │ Int64             │ String │
├───────┼─────────────┼─────────┼───────────────────┼────────┤
│ 10    │ 1           │ 25      │ 1                 │ "Ada"  │
│ 11    │ 3           │ 40      │ 3                 │ "Cai"  │
│ 12    │ 1           │ 10      │ 1                 │ "Ada"  │
│ 13    │ 5           │ 99      │ null              │ null   │
│ 14    │ 4           │ 15      │ 4                 │ "Dee"  │
│ null  │ null        │ null    │ 2                 │ "Ben"  │
└───────┴─────────────┴─────────┴───────────────────┴────────┘

The left rows that have a match, once each, and only the left's columns: the customers who ordered.

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(customers().Join(orders(), on, ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinSemi)))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────────┬────────┐
│ customer_id │ name   │
│ Int64       │ String │
├─────────────┼────────┤
│ 1           │ "Ada"  │
│ 3           │ "Cai"  │
│ 4           │ "Dee"  │
└─────────────┴────────┘

The left rows that have no match: the customers who never ordered.

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(customers().Join(orders(), on, ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinAnti)))
Output
shape: (1, 2)
┌─────────────┬────────┐
│ customer_id │ name   │
│ Int64       │ String │
├─────────────┼────────┤
│ 2           │ "Ben"  │
└─────────────┴────────┘

Every pair of rows, with no keys.

sizes := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("size", []string{"S", "M"}))
colours := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("colour", []string{"red", "blue", "green"}))
show(sizes.Join(colours, ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinCross)))
Output
shape: (6, 2)
┌────────┬─────────┐
│ size   │ colour  │
│ String │ String  │
├────────┼─────────┤
│ "S"    │ "red"   │
│ "S"    │ "blue"  │
│ "S"    │ "green" │
│ "M"    │ "red"   │
│ "M"    │ "blue"  │
│ "M"    │ "green" │
└────────┴─────────┘

Row order. An inner join's order is not promised, as in Polars: ursus hashes the smaller input and the rows follow the other. JoinMaintainOrder keeps an order, as Polars' maintain_order does, for every kind: JoinOrderLeft the left frame's, each row's matches in the right frame's order, as the inner example does, and JoinOrderRight the right frame's. Changed in 0.6.7: it took a Boolean, and kept an inner join's left order alone. Left, semi, anti and full joins keep the left frame's order without it while they fit in memory; JoinMaintainOrder keeps it when they spill too.

A right join's order and columns are not Polars'

A right join here keeps the left frame's row order, with the right rows that matched nothing after them, and keeps the key where the left frame has it. Polars gives a right join's rows in the right frame's order, and its key among the right frame's columns. JoinMaintainOrder(ursus.JoinOrderRight) gives Polars' rows; Select the columns in the order you want them.

docs.title: Merged keys
docs.text:
A key named the same on both sides appears once, for every kind but full, which keeps both, customer_id and customer_id_right. JoinCoalesce(true) merges them, the left's where a row has a left side and the right's where it does not:

on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id"))
show(orders().Join(customers(), on,
    ursus.JoinHow(ursus.JoinFull),
    ursus.JoinCoalesce(true)))
Output
shape: (6, 4)
┌───────┬─────────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ order │ customer_id │ amount  │ name   │
│ Int64 │ Int64       │ Float64 │ String │
├───────┼─────────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 10    │ 1           │ 25      │ "Ada"  │
│ 11    │ 3           │ 40      │ "Cai"  │
│ 12    │ 1           │ 10      │ "Ada"  │
│ 13    │ 5           │ 99      │ null   │
│ 14    │ 4           │ 15      │ "Dee"  │
│ null  │ 2           │ null    │ "Ben"  │
└───────┴─────────────┴─────────┴────────┘

docs.title: Keys of different names
docs.text:
JoinLeftOn and JoinRightOn name the keys on each side, paired by position. Both key columns are kept, customer_id and id: merging them would delete a column you named. Polars drops the right one; JoinCoalesce(true) does here too.

people := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", []int64{1, 3}),
    ursus.Values("name", []string{"Ada", "Cai"}),
)
show(orders().
    Join(people,
        ursus.JoinLeftOn(ursus.Col("customer_id")),
        ursus.JoinRightOn(ursus.Col("id"))).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("order"))))
Output
shape: (3, 5)
┌───────┬─────────────┬─────────┬───────┬────────┐
│ order │ customer_id │ amount  │ id    │ name   │
│ Int64 │ Int64       │ Float64 │ Int64 │ String │
├───────┼─────────────┼─────────┼───────┼────────┤
│ 10    │ 1           │ 25      │ 1     │ "Ada"  │
│ 11    │ 3           │ 40      │ 3     │ "Cai"  │
│ 12    │ 1           │ 10      │ 1     │ "Ada"  │
└───────┴─────────────┴─────────┴───────┴────────┘

Several keys match on all of them: JoinOn(Col("a"), Col("b")).

docs.title: Columns of the same name
docs.text:
A right column whose name the left frame already has takes a suffix, _right unless JoinSuffix says otherwise:

shipped := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("order", []int64{10, 11, 12}),
    ursus.Values("amount", []float64{25, 38, 10}),
)
show(orders().
    Join(shipped,
        ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("order")),
        ursus.JoinSuffix("_shipped"),
        ursus.JoinMaintainOrder(ursus.JoinOrderLeft)).
    Select(ursus.Col("order"), ursus.Col("amount"), ursus.Col("amount_shipped")))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬────────────────┐
│ order │ amount  │ amount_shipped │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64        │
├───────┼─────────┼────────────────┤
│ 10    │ 25      │ 25             │
│ 11    │ 40      │ 38             │
│ 12    │ 10      │ 10             │
└───────┴─────────┴────────────────┘

docs.title: Null keys
docs.text:
A null key matches nothing, as in SQL, unless JoinNullsEqual(true) makes nulls equal:

key := ursus.ValuesNullable("k", []int64{1, 0}, []bool{true, false}) // 1 and null
left := ursus.Frame(key, ursus.Values("l", []string{"a", "b"}))
right := ursus.Frame(key, ursus.Values("r", []string{"x", "y"}))
on := ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("k"))
ordered := ursus.JoinMaintainOrder(ursus.JoinOrderLeft)
show(left.Join(right, on, ordered))
show(left.Join(right, on, ordered, ursus.JoinNullsEqual(true)))
Output
shape: (1, 3)
┌───────┬────────┬────────┐
│ k     │ l      │ r      │
│ Int64 │ String │ String │
├───────┼────────┼────────┤
│ 1     │ "a"    │ "x"    │
└───────┴────────┴────────┘

shape: (2, 3)
┌───────┬────────┬────────┐
│ k     │ l      │ r      │
│ Int64 │ String │ String │
├───────┼────────┼────────┤
│ 1     │ "a"    │ "x"    │
│ null  │ "b"    │ "y"    │
└───────┴────────┴────────┘

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A join whose keys repeat where you expected them unique multiplies rows silently. JoinValidate checks the keys' cardinality and fails the query when the data breaks it:

twice := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("customer_id", []int64{1, 1}),
    ursus.Values("name", []string{"Ada", "Ada Lovelace"}),
)
_, err := orders().
    Join(twice,
        ursus.JoinOn(ursus.Col("customer_id")),
        ursus.JoinValidate(ursus.ValidateManyToOne)).
    Collect(context.Background())
fmt.Println(err)
Output
ursus: join: validate=m:1 requires unique keys on the right side, but a key is duplicated
  first duplicate at right row 1
  key: col("customer_id")
  each duplicate multiplies every matching row on the other side
  de-duplicate with .Unique(...), or pass JoinValidate(ursus.ValidateManyToMany)

The checks are ValidateOneToOne, ValidateOneToMany, ValidateManyToOne and ValidateManyToMany, the first side named being the left: ValidateManyToOne on orders.Join(customers) asks for each customer once.

docs.title: As-of joins
docs.text:
JoinAsOf matches each left row with the nearest right row before it, rather than an equal one: each trade with the quote in force when it happened. AsOfBy matches within equal keys first, and AsOfTolerance limits how far back a match may be:

at := func(s int) time.Time { return time.Date(2026, 1, 5, 9, 0, s, 0, time.UTC) }
trades := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("time", []time.Time{at(1), at(5), at(9)}),
    ursus.Values("ticker", []string{"ACME", "BOLT", "ACME"}),
    ursus.Values("qty", []int64{100, 50, 70}),
)
quotes := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("time", []time.Time{at(0), at(2), at(4), at(6)}),
    ursus.Values("ticker", []string{"ACME", "BOLT", "ACME", "BOLT"}),
    ursus.Values("bid", []float64{10.0, 20.0, 10.1, 20.2}),
)
show(trades.JoinAsOf(quotes,
    ursus.AsOfOn(ursus.Col("time")),
    ursus.AsOfBy(ursus.Col("ticker")),
    ursus.AsOfTolerance(ursus.Every("3s")),
))
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌────────────────────────────────┬────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ time                           │ ticker │ qty   │ bid     │
│ Datetime(ns, UTC)              │ String │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 2026-01-05T09:00:01.000000000Z │ "ACME" │ 100   │ 10      │
│ 2026-01-05T09:00:05.000000000Z │ "BOLT" │ 50    │ 20      │
│ 2026-01-05T09:00:09.000000000Z │ "ACME" │ 70    │ null    │
└────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────┴─────────┘

The 09:00:09 ACME trade's last quote is five seconds old, past the three-second tolerance, so its bid is null.

  • It is a left join: every left row comes back, its right columns null when nothing is near enough.
  • AsOfStrategyOpt(AsOfForward) takes the nearest row after, and AsOfNearest the nearest either way.
  • Both frames must be sorted by the as-of key, and ursus checks that they are rather than trusting it: an unsorted side fails with an error.
  • New in 0.6.7: a numeric key's tolerance is a number, AsOfTolerance(5), and a tolerance of zero admits only an exact match, as Polars'. AsOfCoalesce(false) keeps the right frame's key too, ts_right; a key named apart on the two sides is kept on both, as in Polars.

docs.title: Joins on a condition
docs.text:
JoinWhere(other, predicates...) pairs the rows that satisfy every predicate, such as an interval: each order with the promotion running on its date. An equality among the predicates becomes a hash join's key; without one, every pair is tested. JoinWhereSuffix(other, suffix, predicates...) names a colliding right column with another suffix, which the predicates use.

promotions := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("promotion", []string{"new year", "mid week"}),
    ursus.Values("from", []string{"2026-01-01", "2026-01-06"}),
    ursus.Values("to", []string{"2026-01-04", "2026-01-07"}),
).WithColumns(ursus.Col("from").Str().ToDate(), ursus.Col("to").Str().ToDate())
show(sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("date")).
    JoinWhere(promotions,
        ursus.Col("date").Ge(ursus.Col("from")),
        ursus.Col("date").Le(ursus.Col("to"))).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("date"), ursus.Col("promotion")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("order_id"))))
Output
shape: (6, 3)
┌──────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
│ order_id │ date       │ promotion  │
│ Int64    │ Date       │ String     │
├──────────┼────────────┼────────────┤
│ 1        │ 2026-01-03 │ "new year" │
│ 2        │ 2026-01-03 │ "new year" │
│ 3        │ 2026-01-04 │ "new year" │
│ 6        │ 2026-01-06 │ "mid week" │
│ 7        │ 2026-01-07 │ "mid week" │
│ 8        │ 2026-01-07 │ "mid week" │
└──────────┴────────────┴────────────┘

docs.title: Updating from another frame
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. Update(other, options) writes another frame's values over this one's, in the columns both have, matched by keys, as Polars' update: a null in other leaves the value unless IncludeNulls, and the frame keeps its rows, its columns and their order.

prices := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("sku", []string{"a", "b", "c"}),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("price", []float64{9.5, 3, 0}, []bool{true, true, false}),
)
fixes := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("sku", []string{"c", "a"}),
    ursus.Values("price", []float64{4.25, 9.75}),
)
show(prices.Update(fixes, ursus.UpdateOptions{On: []string{"sku"}}))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌────────┬─────────┐
│ sku    │ price   │
│ String │ Float64 │
├────────┼─────────┤
│ "a"    │ 9.75    │
│ "b"    │ 3       │
│ "c"    │ 4.25    │
└────────┴─────────┘

How keeps the frame's every row, UpdateLeft, the default; only those other matches, UpdateInner; or also other's unmatched ones, as new rows, UpdateFull. Without keys, rows are matched by their places. A column whose types differ takes the type that holds both. It is a join, so it spills as one does and keeps its order.

docs.title: Filtering by another frame
docs.text:
WhereExists(other, predicates...) keeps this frame's rows that have at least one row in other satisfying every predicate, once each, with only this frame's columns: SQL's EXISTS. WhereNotExists keeps those that have none. The predicates name other's columns as a join would, with the suffix where a name collides:

show(customers().WhereExists(orders(),
    ursus.Col("customer_id").Eq(ursus.Col("customer_id_right")),
    ursus.Col("amount").Gt(20.0)))
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌─────────────┬────────┐
│ customer_id │ name   │
│ Int64       │ String │
├─────────────┼────────┤
│ 1           │ "Ada"  │
│ 3           │ "Cai"  │
└─────────────┴────────┘

A semi or anti join asks the same question when the condition is equal keys alone.

docs.title: Under a memory limit
docs.text: Equi-joins spill both sides to disk under a memory budget, and give the answer they give in memory; under a limit a join's row order is promised only with JoinMaintainOrder. An as-of join streams both sides, whatever its strategy. See Memory and spilling.

docs.title: Lists and structs
docs.text: A List column holds a list of values a row, all of one type; a Struct column holds named fields a row. Both come from Parquet and Arrow as they are, and are built from other columns as below.

docs.title: Building lists
docs.text:
Str().Split makes a list a row, as does any aggregation that gives several values, Implode among them:

func baskets() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("order", []int64{1, 2, 3}),
        ursus.Values("items", []string{"pear,apple,fig", "fig", "apple,pear"}),
        ursus.Values("prices", []string{"2.25,1.5,3", "3", "1.5,2.25"}),
    ).WithColumns(
        ursus.Col("items").Str().Split(","),
        ursus.Col("prices").Str().Split(",").
            List().Eval(ursus.Element().Cast(ursus.Float64)),
    )
}

show(baskets())
show(sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(ursus.Col("qty").Implode().Alias("qtys")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬──────────────────────────┬────────────────┐
│ order │ items                    │ prices         │
│ Int64 │ List(String)             │ List(Float64)  │
├───────┼──────────────────────────┼────────────────┤
│ 1     │ ["pear", "apple", "fig"] │ [2.25, 1.5, 3] │
│ 2     │ ["fig"]                  │ [3]            │
│ 3     │ ["apple", "pear"]        │ [1.5, 2.25]    │
└───────┴──────────────────────────┴────────────────┘

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────────┐
│ region  │ qtys        │
│ String  │ List(Int64) │
├─────────┼─────────────┤
│ "east"  │ [2, 12]     │
│ "north" │ [10, 7, 3]  │
│ "south" │ [4, 9, 6]   │
└─────────┴─────────────┘

ConcatList(exprs...) joins columns and lists into one list a row, and a Go slice is a List literal: ursus.Lit([]string{"apple", "pear"}).

docs.title: Questions of each list
docs.text:
Methods for lists sit behind List(), and each answers once per row:

items, prices := ursus.Col("items").List(), ursus.Col("prices").List()
show(baskets().Select(
    ursus.Col("order"),
    items.Len().Alias("n"),
    items.Get(0).Alias("first"),
    items.Contains("fig").Alias("has_fig"),
    prices.Sum().Alias("total"),
    prices.Max().Alias("dearest"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 6)
┌───────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order │ n      │ first   │ has_fig │ total   │ dearest │
│ Int64 │ Uint32 │ String  │ Bool    │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1     │ 3      │ "pear"  │ true    │ 6.75    │ 3       │
│ 2     │ 1      │ "fig"   │ true    │ 3       │ 3       │
│ 3     │ 2      │ "apple" │ false   │ 3.75    │ 2.25    │
└───────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
  • Len, Get(i), First and Last; Get is null past the end;
  • Contains(v) and CountMatches(v);
  • Sum, Mean, Min, Max, Median, Std, Var, Quantile and NUnique;
  • Any and All for lists of Bool.

docs.title: Transforming lists
docs.text:
Sort, Reverse, Unique, Head, Tail, Slice, Shift and Diff give a list back; Join(sep) joins a list of text into one string. Eval(expr) runs any expression over each list's elements, Element() naming the element:

items := ursus.Col("items").List()
show(baskets().Select(
    ursus.Col("order"),
    items.Sort().Alias("sorted"),
    items.Join(" + ").Alias("joined"),
    ursus.Col("prices").List().Eval(ursus.Element().Mul(2)).Alias("doubled"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌───────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬───────────────┐
│ order │ sorted                   │ joined               │ doubled       │
│ Int64 │ List(String)             │ String               │ List(Float64) │
├───────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────────┤
│ 1     │ ["apple", "fig", "pear"] │ "pear + apple + fig" │ [4.5, 3, 6]   │
│ 2     │ ["fig"]                  │ "fig"                │ [6]           │
│ 3     │ ["apple", "pear"]        │ "apple + pear"       │ [3, 4.5]      │
└───────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴───────────────┘

Filter(pred) keeps the elements a predicate holds for, and in Eval a window or a rank is over the list's elements:

prices := ursus.Col("prices").List()
show(baskets().Select(
    ursus.Col("order"),
    prices.Filter(ursus.Element().Ge(2.0)).Alias("from_2"),
    prices.Eval(ursus.Element().Rank(ursus.RankDense, true)).Alias("rank"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐
│ order │ from_2        │ rank         │
│ Int64 │ List(Float64) │ List(Uint32) │
├───────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤
│ 1     │ [2.25, 3]     │ [2, 3, 1]    │
│ 2     │ [3]           │ [1]          │
│ 3     │ [2.25]        │ [2, 1]       │
└───────┴───────────────┴──────────────┘

docs.title: Set operations
docs.text:
SetIntersection, SetUnion, SetDifference and SetSymmetricDifference combine two lists a row, in the order elements first appear:

items := ursus.Col("items")
fruit := ursus.Lit([]string{"apple", "pear"})
show(baskets().Select(
    ursus.Col("order"),
    items.List().SetIntersection(fruit).Alias("in_both"),
    items.List().SetDifference(fruit).Alias("only_here"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬───────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ order │ in_both           │ only_here    │
│ Int64 │ List(String)      │ List(String) │
├───────┼───────────────────┼──────────────┤
│ 1     │ ["pear", "apple"] │ ["fig"]      │
│ 2     │ []                │ ["fig"]      │
│ 3     │ ["apple", "pear"] │ []           │
└───────┴───────────────────┴──────────────┘

docs.title: Back into rows
docs.text:
Explode gives every element its own row, several list columns zipped together; see Reshaping:

show(baskets().Explode("items", "prices"))
Output
shape: (6, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order │ items   │ prices  │
│ Int64 │ String  │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1     │ "pear"  │ 2.25    │
│ 1     │ "apple" │ 1.5     │
│ 1     │ "fig"   │ 3       │
│ 2     │ "fig"   │ 3       │
│ 3     │ "apple" │ 1.5     │
│ 3     │ "pear"  │ 2.25    │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: Structs
docs.text:
Struct(exprs...) packs columns into one struct column, a field for each, named as its expression:

show(sales().Head(3).Select(
    ursus.Col("order_id"),
    ursus.Struct(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).Alias("line"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌──────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ order_id │ line                                │
│ Int64    │ Struct(product: String, qty: Int64) │
├──────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1        │ {product: "apple", qty: 10}         │
│ 2        │ {product: "apple", qty: 4}          │
│ 3        │ {product: "pear", qty: 7}           │
└──────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘

Methods for structs sit behind Struct():

line := ursus.Struct(ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).Alias("line")
l := ursus.Col("line").Struct()
lines := sales().Head(2).Select(line)
show(lines.Select(
    l.Field("product").Alias("product"),
    l.WithFields(l.Field("qty").Mul(10).Alias("qty")).Alias("scaled"),
))
show(lines.Select(l.JsonEncode().Alias("json")))
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌─────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ product │ scaled                              │
│ String  │ Struct(product: String, qty: Int64) │
├─────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "apple" │ {product: "apple", qty: 100}        │
│ "apple" │ {product: "apple", qty: 40}         │
└─────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘

shape: (2, 1)
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│ json                                 │
│ String                               │
├──────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "{\"product\":\"apple\",\"qty\":10}" │
│ "{\"product\":\"apple\",\"qty\":4}"  │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Field(name) reads one field, and Field of several names reads each as a column;
  • WithFields(exprs...) replaces fields of the same names and adds new ones; read a field inside it through Field, as anywhere;
  • RenameFields(names...) renames them in order, and new in 0.6.7, Name().PrefixFields, SuffixFields and MapFields rename each from its name;
  • new in 0.6.7, Drop(names...) leaves fields out, as Polars' struct.drop, and refuses a name that is no field;
  • JsonEncode writes each struct as JSON text, and Str().JsonDecode(type) reads it back;
  • Unnest turns the fields into columns, as the frame's Unnest does.

A struct is also how ursus gives several values a row: SplitExact, ExtractGroups, ValueCounts of an expression, and Rle.

docs.title: What is not here yet
docs.text: An Array type, a fixed-size list, is not, and neither are lists of lists or of structs, which are refused by name. A List or a Struct cannot be a group-by, join or Unique key. The scope records each in feature-gaps.md.

docs.title: Missing data
docs.text:
A missing value is a null, in a column of any type. It is not NaN, a float that is not a number, and ursus keeps the two apart everywhere: see Types and nulls. The examples read six hours of temperatures with gaps, and a backup reading for some of them:

func readings() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    ok := []bool{true, false, false, true, true, false}
    return ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("hour", []int64{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}),
        ursus.ValuesNullable("temp", []float64{10, 0, 0, 13, 12, 0}, ok),
        ursus.ValuesNullable("backup", []float64{9, 11, 0, 0, 0, 14},
            []bool{true, true, false, false, false, true}),
    )
}

docs.title: Counting
docs.text:
NullCount counts a column's nulls, and over All() every column's:

show(readings().Select(ursus.All().NullCount()))
Output
shape: (1, 3)
┌────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ hour   │ temp   │ backup │
│ Uint64 │ Uint64 │ Uint64 │
├────────┼────────┼────────┤
│ 0      │ 3      │ 3      │
└────────┴────────┴────────┘

IsNull and IsNotNull test each value, for a Filter or a When.

docs.title: Filling with a value
docs.text:
FillNullWith(v) fills with a value, FillNull(strategy) with one the column gives: FillMean, FillMin, FillMax, FillZero or FillOne. Coalesce(exprs...) takes each row's first value that is not null, here the temperature, else the backup, else −1:

temp := ursus.Col("temp")
show(readings().Select(
    ursus.Col("hour"),
    temp,
    temp.FillNullWith(0.0).Alias("zero"),
    temp.FillNull(ursus.FillMean).Alias("mean"),
    ursus.Coalesce(temp, ursus.Col("backup"), ursus.Lit(-1.0)).Alias("coalesced"),
))
Output
shape: (6, 5)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────────────────┬───────────┐
│ hour  │ temp    │ zero    │ mean               │ coalesced │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │ Float64            │ Float64   │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┼────────────────────┼───────────┤
│ 0     │ 10      │ 10      │ 10                 │ 10        │
│ 1     │ null    │ 0       │ 11.666666666666666 │ 11        │
│ 2     │ null    │ 0       │ 11.666666666666666 │ -1        │
│ 3     │ 13      │ 13      │ 13                 │ 13        │
│ 4     │ 12      │ 12      │ 12                 │ 12        │
│ 5     │ null    │ 0       │ 11.666666666666666 │ 14        │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┴────────────────────┴───────────┘

A fill meets the column's type: FillNullWith(0) of an Int32 column stays Int32, and so does FillNullWith(2.0), a whole number. A fill with a fraction, 0.5, widens an integer column to Float64. Polars widens it for any float.

docs.title: Filling from the neighbours
docs.text:
FillForward carries the last value forward and FillBackward the next one back; ForwardFill(limit) and BackwardFill(limit) fill at most that many rows of a gap. Interpolate draws a straight line across a gap, and leaves a gap at either end as it is:

temp := ursus.Col("temp")
show(readings().Select(
    ursus.Col("hour"),
    temp,
    temp.FillNull(ursus.FillForward).Alias("forward"),
    temp.ForwardFill(1).Alias("forward_1"),
    temp.FillNull(ursus.FillBackward).Alias("backward"),
    temp.Interpolate().Alias("interpolated"),
))
Output
shape: (6, 6)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┬───────────┬──────────┬──────────────┐
│ hour  │ temp    │ forward │ forward_1 │ backward │ interpolated │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │ Float64   │ Float64  │ Float64      │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┼───────────┼──────────┼──────────────┤
│ 0     │ 10      │ 10      │ 10        │ 10       │ 10           │
│ 1     │ null    │ 10      │ 10        │ 13       │ 11           │
│ 2     │ null    │ 10      │ null      │ 13       │ 12           │
│ 3     │ 13      │ 13      │ 13        │ 13       │ 13           │
│ 4     │ 12      │ 12      │ 12        │ 12       │ 12           │
│ 5     │ null    │ 12      │ 12        │ null     │ null         │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┴───────────┴──────────┴──────────────┘

They run in the rows' order; under Over(keys...), within each partition, so a sensor's gap is never filled from another sensor's readings.

New in 0.6.7. InterpolateBy(by) draws the line at each row's by, a time or a number, where Interpolate steps by rows, as Polars' interpolate_by: readings at hours 0, 1 and 4, the middle one missing, fill it a quarter of the way along. by need not be sorted, and a null in it is refused, as Polars refuses it.

New in 0.6.7. A strategy takes a limit too, FillForward.Limit(n) and FillBackward.Limit(n), as Polars' fill_null(strategy=..., limit=n), for a column or for every column of a frame at once:

show(readings().FillNull(ursus.FillForward.Limit(1)))
Output
shape: (6, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ hour  │ temp    │ backup  │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 0     │ 10      │ 9       │
│ 1     │ 10      │ 11      │
│ 2     │ null    │ 11      │
│ 3     │ 13      │ null    │
│ 4     │ 12      │ null    │
│ 5     │ 12      │ 14      │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘

A limit is at least 1; leave it off for none. A limit on another strategy is refused, as Polars refuses it.

docs.title: Dropping
docs.text:
DropNulls(names...) drops the rows with a null in any of those columns, or in any column at all:

show(readings().DropNulls("temp"))
show(readings().DropNulls())
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ hour  │ temp    │ backup  │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 0     │ 10      │ 9       │
│ 3     │ 13      │ null    │
│ 4     │ 12      │ null    │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘

shape: (1, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ hour  │ temp    │ backup  │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 0     │ 10      │ 9       │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘

New in 0.6.7. DropNans(names...) drops the rows with a NaN in any of those columns, or in any float column. A null is not a NaN, and its row stays:

nan := math.NaN()
present := []bool{true, true, false, true} // the third is null
ratios := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", []int64{1, 2, 3, 4}),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("ratio", []float64{0.5, nan, 0, 2}, present),
)
show(ratios.DropNans())
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌───────┬─────────┐
│ id    │ ratio   │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┤
│ 1     │ 0.5     │
│ 3     │ null    │
│ 4     │ 2       │
└───────┴─────────┘

docs.title: The whole frame
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. A frame's Interpolate() interpolates every column it can: numbers, an integer becoming a Float64, and dates and times, which keep their type, as Polars' interpolate does. Text and Booleans are left as they are:

day := func(d int) time.Time { return time.Date(2026, 1, d, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC) }
ends := []bool{true, false, false, true} // two rows missing between
gappy := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("day", []time.Time{day(1), {}, {}, day(7)}, ends),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("level", []int64{10, 0, 0, 40}, ends),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("note", []string{"start", "", "", "end"}, ends),
).WithColumns(ursus.Col("day").Cast(ursus.Date))
show(gappy.Interpolate())
Output
shape: (4, 3)
┌────────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ day        │ level   │ note    │
│ Date       │ Float64 │ String  │
├────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 2026-01-01 │ 10      │ "start" │
│ 2026-01-03 │ 20      │ null    │
│ 2026-01-05 │ 30      │ null    │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 40      │ "end"   │
└────────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

A frame's FillNull(v) fills every column that can hold a null and that v can fill, chosen from the schema before any data is read. hour, built by Values, cannot hold a null, and is left as it is.

show(readings().FillNull(0.0))
Output
shape: (6, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ hour  │ temp    │ backup  │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 0     │ 10      │ 9       │
│ 1     │ 0       │ 11      │
│ 2     │ 0       │ 0       │
│ 3     │ 13      │ 0       │
│ 4     │ 12      │ 0       │
│ 5     │ 0       │ 14      │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: How nulls behave
docs.text:
• Arithmetic with a null is null, and so is a comparison.
  • Logic is three-valued, as SQL's: null.Or(true) is true, null.And(false) false.
  • A filter keeps the rows where its predicate is true, so a null drops a row.
  • An aggregate skips nulls; a group of nulls alone sums to null, not 0.
  • A group-by makes the nulls of a key one group, and a join matches no null key, unless JoinNullsEqual(true).
  • A sort puts nulls first, unless a key asks for NullsLast().

docs.title: Wide: pivot
docs.text:
Pivot spreads a column's values into columns of their own: a row for each distinct Index, and a column for each distinct On value, holding Values. Agg reduces the values that fall in one cell; without it, a cell of two values is refused.

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := sales().Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
wide, err := df.Pivot(ctx, ursus.PivotOptions{
    On:          []string{"product"},
    Index:       []string{"region"},
    Values:      []string{"qty"},
    Agg:         ursus.Expr.Sum,
    SortColumns: true,
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(wide)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ region  │ apple  │ fig    │ pear   │
│ String  │ Int128 │ Int128 │ Int128 │
├─────────┼────────┼────────┼────────┤
│ "north" │ 10     │ 3      │ 7      │
│ "south" │ 4      │ 9      │ 6      │
│ "east"  │ 12     │ null   │ 2      │
└─────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┘

A cell is Agg of the values that fall in it. East sold no figs, so its cell is the sum of nothing: Polars' sum gives 0 there; here, as for every sum of nothing, it is null (see Coming from Polars). A count of nothing is 0, as Polars' is (fixed in 0.6.7; before, every such cell was null). New columns come in the order their values first appear, or sorted with SortColumns.

New in 0.6.7. Pivot is a LazyFrame's too, as Polars' LazyFrame.pivot is, its new columns given in OnColumns, since a lazy plan knows its columns before it reads the data. A value given that the data never holds is a column of empty cells, plum here; one the data holds and OnColumns leaves out is left out, fig here. A DataFrame's pivot finds them itself. Either way a group-by of the index and the On values reduces the rows first, and spills past a memory limit as any group-by does.

products := ursus.Values("product", []string{"apple", "pear", "plum"})
wide := sales().Pivot(ursus.PivotOptions{
    On:        []string{"product"},
    OnColumns: []*ursus.Column{products},
    Index:     []string{"region"},
    Values:    []string{"qty"},
    Agg:       ursus.Expr.Sum,
})
show(wide)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ region  │ apple  │ pear   │ plum   │
│ String  │ Int128 │ Int128 │ Int128 │
├─────────┼────────┼────────┼────────┤
│ "north" │ 10     │ 7      │ null   │
│ "south" │ 4      │ 6      │ null   │
│ "east"  │ 12     │ 2      │ null   │
└─────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┘

New in 0.6.7. Several On columns name a new column by their values together, as Polars writes them, text quoted:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("shop", []string{"a", "a", "b", "b"}),
    ursus.Values("quarter", []string{"q1", "q2", "q1", "q1"}),
    ursus.Values("channel", []string{"web", "web", "store", "web"}),
    ursus.Values("sales", []int64{10, 12, 7, 3}),
).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
wide, err := df.Pivot(ctx, ursus.PivotOptions{
    On:     []string{"quarter", "channel"},
    Index:  []string{"shop"},
    Values: []string{"sales"},
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(wide)
Output
shape: (2, 4)
┌────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬────────────────┐
│ shop   │ {"q1","web"} │ {"q2","web"} │ {"q1","store"} │
│ String │ Int64        │ Int64        │ Int64          │
├────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼────────────────┤
│ "a"    │ 10           │ 12           │ null           │
│ "b"    │ 3            │ null         │ 7              │
└────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────┘

docs.title: Long: unpivot
docs.text:
Unpivot is the opposite: several columns become two, which column and what it held. Index names the columns carried along; empty, it is every column not in On.

quarters := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("region", []string{"north", "south"}),
    ursus.Values("q1", []int64{120, 80}),
    ursus.Values("q2", []int64{135, 95}),
)
show(quarters.Unpivot(ursus.UnpivotOptions{
    On:           []string{"q1", "q2"},
    Index:        []string{"region"},
    VariableName: "quarter",
    ValueName:    "sales",
}))
Output
shape: (4, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ region  │ quarter │ sales │
│ String  │ String  │ Int64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ "north" │ "q1"    │ 120   │
│ "north" │ "q2"    │ 135   │
│ "south" │ "q1"    │ 80    │
│ "south" │ "q2"    │ 95    │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────┘

New in 0.6.7. On may be left out instead: it is then every column not in Index, as Polars' on=None, and every column when Index is left out too. The melted columns share one value column, so their types must meet in one that holds each of them exactly: an Int32 beside an Int64 melts into an Int64, but text beside a number is refused, where Polars writes the numbers as text. Cast first.

quarters := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("region", []string{"north", "south"}),
    ursus.Values("q1", []int64{120, 80}),
    ursus.Values("q2", []int64{135, 95}),
    ursus.Values("q3", []int32{150, 90}),
)
show(quarters.Unpivot(ursus.UnpivotOptions{Index: []string{"region"}}))
Output
shape: (6, 3)
┌─────────┬──────────┬───────┐
│ region  │ variable │ value │
│ String  │ String   │ Int64 │
├─────────┼──────────┼───────┤
│ "north" │ "q1"     │ 120   │
│ "north" │ "q2"     │ 135   │
│ "north" │ "q3"     │ 150   │
│ "south" │ "q1"     │ 80    │
│ "south" │ "q2"     │ 95    │
│ "south" │ "q3"     │ 90    │
└─────────┴──────────┴───────┘

The row order is not Polars'

Polars gives every row's first column, then every row's second. ursus gives each row's columns together, then the next row's, because it unpivots a batch at a time and its order must not depend on the batches. Sort afterwards when the order matters.

docs.title: Lists into rows: explode
docs.text:
Explode gives each element of a list its own row, the other columns repeated:

posts := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("post", []int64{1, 2, 3}),
    ursus.Values("tags", []string{"go,data", "go", ""}),
).WithColumns(ursus.Col("tags").Str().Split(","))
show(posts)
show(posts.Explode("tags"))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌───────┬────────────────┐
│ post  │ tags           │
│ Int64 │ List(String)   │
├───────┼────────────────┤
│ 1     │ ["go", "data"] │
│ 2     │ ["go"]         │
│ 3     │ [""]           │
└───────┴────────────────┘

shape: (4, 2)
┌───────┬────────┐
│ post  │ tags   │
│ Int64 │ String │
├───────┼────────┤
│ 1     │ "go"   │
│ 1     │ "data" │
│ 2     │ "go"   │
│ 3     │ ""     │
└───────┴────────┘

Several columns explode together, zipped, so their lists must be the same length in each row. An empty list and a null list each become one row holding a null.

docs.title: Structs into columns: unnest
docs.text:
Unnest turns a struct column into a column for each of its fields:

points := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", []int64{1, 2}),
    ursus.Values("x", []float64{0.5, 2}),
    ursus.Values("y", []float64{1, -1}),
).Select(
    ursus.Col("id"),
    ursus.Struct(ursus.Col("x"), ursus.Col("y")).Alias("point"),
)
show(points)
show(points.Unnest("point"))
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌───────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id    │ point                          │
│ Int64 │ Struct(x: Float64, y: Float64) │
├───────┼────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1     │ {x: 0.5, y: 1}                 │
│ 2     │ {x: 2, y: -1}                  │
└───────┴────────────────────────────────┘

shape: (2, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ id    │ x       │ y       │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1     │ 0.5     │ 1       │
│ 2     │ 2       │ -1      │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┘

docs.title: Concatenating
docs.text:
Concat stacks frames' rows. By default each frame must have the same columns in the same order; an Int32 and an Int64 of one name meet at Int64.

january := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("day", []int64{30, 31}),
    ursus.Values("qty", []int64{4, 6}),
)
february := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("day", []int64{1, 2}),
    ursus.Values("qty", []int64{3, 8}),
)
show(ursus.Concat([]*ursus.LazyFrame{january, february}))
Output
shape: (4, 2)
┌───────┬───────┐
│ day   │ qty   │
│ Int64 │ Int64 │
├───────┼───────┤
│ 30    │ 4     │
│ 31    │ 6     │
│ 1     │ 3     │
│ 2     │ 8     │
└───────┴───────┘

WithConcatMode(ConcatDiagonal) takes the union of the columns instead, each frame's missing ones null:

old := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", []int64{1, 2}),
    ursus.Values("name", []string{"Ada", "Ben"}),
)
recent := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", []int64{3}),
    ursus.Values("email", []string{"cai@example.com"}),
)
show(ursus.Concat([]*ursus.LazyFrame{old, recent},
    ursus.WithConcatMode(ursus.ConcatDiagonal)))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬────────┬───────────────────┐
│ id    │ name   │ email             │
│ Int64 │ String │ String            │
├───────┼────────┼───────────────────┤
│ 1     │ "Ada"  │ null              │
│ 2     │ "Ben"  │ null              │
│ 3     │ null   │ "cai@example.com" │
└───────┴────────┴───────────────────┘

New in 0.6.7. ConcatRelaxed and ConcatDiagonalRelaxed meet a column's types where the default refuses them, at Polars' supertype: an Int64 beside a Float64 at Float64, which may round; a number beside text at text. The default meets types only where every value comes out as it went in.

counted := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("qty", []int64{4, 6}))
weighed := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("qty", []float64{2.5}))
show(ursus.Concat([]*ursus.LazyFrame{counted, weighed},
    ursus.WithConcatMode(ursus.ConcatRelaxed)))
Output
shape: (3, 1)
┌─────────┐
│ qty     │
│ Float64 │
├─────────┤
│ 4       │
│ 6       │
│ 2.5     │
└─────────┘

lf.Concat(others...) and VStack are the same for one frame. Concatenation streams: the frames are read one after another.

docs.title: Aligned by key
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. ConcatAlign puts frames side by side by key, as Polars' concat(how="align"): it joins them on the columns every frame has, a full join, and sorts by those columns. ConcatAlignInner, ConcatAlignLeft and ConcatAlignRight join so instead. A column in some frames but not every one would be two columns of one name, and is refused; Polars keeps the first frame's.

prices := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("day", []int64{3, 1, 2}),
    ursus.Values("close", []float64{10.5, 10.0, 11.0}),
)
volumes := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("day", []int64{2, 4, 1}),
    ursus.Values("volume", []int64{700, 900, 500}),
)
show(ursus.Concat([]*ursus.LazyFrame{prices, volumes},
    ursus.WithConcatMode(ursus.ConcatAlign)))
Output
shape: (4, 3)
┌───────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ day   │ close   │ volume │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ Int64  │
├───────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 1     │ 10      │ 500    │
│ 2     │ 11      │ 700    │
│ 3     │ 10.5    │ null   │
│ 4     │ null    │ 900    │
└───────┴─────────┴────────┘

The joins spill past a memory limit, and the rows come out in the same order with one or without, ties in each frame's order.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
HStack places frames side by side, row i of each together, as Concat with ConcatHorizontal does. The frames must be the same height and their column names distinct. New in 0.6.7: ConcatHorizontalExtend pads a shorter frame's columns with nulls instead, as Polars' horizontal_extend. Either reads its frames in step, holding a batch of each.

names := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("name", []string{"Ada", "Ben"}))
scores := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("score", []int64{90, 75}))
show(names.HStack(scores))
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌────────┬───────┐
│ name   │ score │
│ String │ Int64 │
├────────┼───────┤
│ "Ada"  │ 90    │
│ "Ben"  │ 75    │
└────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Transpose
docs.text:
Transpose turns rows into columns. IncludeHeader keeps the old column names as a column, and ColumnNames names the new ones. New in 0.6.7: ColumnNamesFrom takes their names from a text column instead, which is left out, as Polars' column_names given a column's name:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("metric", []string{"orders", "revenue"}),
    ursus.Values("north", []float64{3, 39.75}),
    ursus.Values("south", []float64{3, 46.5}),
).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
t, err := df.Transpose(ctx, ursus.TransposeOptions{
    IncludeHeader:   true,
    HeaderName:      "region",
    ColumnNamesFrom: "metric",
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(t)
Output
shape: (2, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ orders  │ revenue │
│ String  │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ "north" │ 3       │ 39.75   │
│ "south" │ 3       │ 46.5    │
└─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

Every column of the answer has the type its values meet at, Polars' supertype, so integers beside floats become floats and, new in 0.6.7, text beside numbers text, where it was refused. It is a DataFrame's only: its columns are the frame's rows, so its schema waits for the data.

docs.title: Dummies
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. ToDummies replaces a column with a Uint8 column for each of its distinct values, 1 where a row holds the value and 0 where it does not, as Polars' to_dummies. A null is a value of its own. Each dummy is named the column, a separator, _ by default, and the value as Polars displays it, so 1.0 is 1.0 and an instant 2024-01-02 03:04:05. A column's dummies stand in its place, ordered by name as Polars orders them, so 10 comes before 2:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("id", []int64{1, 2, 3, 4}),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("size", []int64{10, 2, 0, 10},
        []bool{true, true, false, true}),
).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
d, err := df.ToDummies(ctx, ursus.DummiesOptions{Columns: []string{"size"}})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(d)
Output
shape: (4, 4)
┌───────┬─────────┬────────┬───────────┐
│ id    │ size_10 │ size_2 │ size_null │
│ Int64 │ Uint8   │ Uint8  │ Uint8     │
├───────┼─────────┼────────┼───────────┤
│ 1     │ 1       │ 0      │ 0         │
│ 2     │ 0       │ 1      │ 0         │
│ 3     │ 0       │ 0      │ 1         │
│ 4     │ 1       │ 0      │ 0         │
└───────┴─────────┴────────┴───────────┘

DropFirst leaves out the first value to appear that is not null, which the others imply, and DropNulls the null. Columns names the columns to encode, every column when empty, and a Series has its own ToDummies. The values are numbered in one pass, as a group-by numbers its groups, so a column of many distinct values costs no more than one of few, beside the dummies it makes.

docs.title: Unstack
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. Unstack lays each column out as a grid without keys, as Polars' unstack. Vertically, a column x's values go Step at a time down new columns x_0, x_1 and on, Step rows high; with UnstackHorizontal, Step at a time across Step new columns:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("reading", []float64{1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5}),
).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
g, err := df.Unstack(ctx, ursus.UnstackOptions{Step: 3})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(g)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌───────────┬───────────┬───────────┐
│ reading_0 │ reading_1 │ reading_2 │
│ Float64   │ Float64   │ Float64   │
├───────────┼───────────┼───────────┤
│ 1.5       │ 3         │ 4.5       │
│ 2         │ 3.5       │ null      │
│ 2.5       │ 4         │ null      │
└───────────┴───────────┴───────────┘

The slots after the last value are null, or Fill, one value for every column or one for each, cast to the column's type as ExtendConstant casts it. Each suffix is zero-padded to the digits of the count of new columns, x_00 to x_12 for 13, as Polars pads it. A vertical column shares the old one's values, a slice of them.

docs.title: Split by key: partition
docs.text:
New in 0.6.7. PartitionBy splits a frame into a part for each distinct key, in the order the keys first appear, as Polars' partition_by. Each part has its Key, a one-row frame of the key's values, typed as the columns are, beside its Frame, the rows holding that key. Go has no map keyed by a tuple, so the parts are a slice where Polars' as_dict gives a dict. DropKey leaves the key columns out of each frame:

ctx := context.Background()
df, err := sales().Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
parts, err := df.PartitionBy(ctx, ursus.PartitionOptions{
    By:      []string{"region"},
    DropKey: true,
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
for _, p := range parts {
    region, _, _ := p.Key.At[string](0, "region")
    fmt.Println(region, p.Frame.Height())
}
fmt.Println(parts[0].Frame)
Output
north 3
south 3
east 2
shape: (3, 5)
┌──────────┬────────────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ date       │ product │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Date       │ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├──────────┼────────────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 2026-01-03 │ "apple" │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 3        │ 2026-01-04 │ "pear"  │ 7     │ 2.25    │
│ 7        │ 2026-01-07 │ "fig"   │ 3     │ 3       │
└──────────┴────────────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

Keys group as a group-by groups them: a null key is a part of its own, and -0 and 0 are one key. It is a DataFrame's, and its parts together hold what the frame did.

docs.title: Columns
docs.text:
Select keeps the columns it names, in its order. Col names columns, ColRegex matches them by a pattern, and ColDType by their type, so the same query adapts when the schema grows:

df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("order_id"),
        ursus.ColRegex("^(qty|price)$"),
        ursus.ColDType(ursus.String),
    ).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 5)
┌──────────┬───────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │ price   │ region  │ product │
│ Int64    │ Int64 │ Float64 │ String  │ String  │
├──────────┼───────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │ 1.5     │ "north" │ "apple" │
│ 2        │ 4     │ 1.5     │ "south" │ "apple" │
│ 3        │ 7     │ 2.25    │ "north" │ "pear"  │
└──────────┴───────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

Exclude is every column but the named ones:

df, err := sales().
    Select(ursus.Exclude("order_id", "date")).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ region  │ product │ qty   │ price   │
│ String  │ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ "north" │ "apple" │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ "south" │ "apple" │ 4     │ 1.5     │
│ "north" │ "pear"  │ 7     │ 2.25    │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

New in 0.6.7: package selector picks columns by what they are, as Polars' selectors do: Numeric, Integer, Float, Temporal, String and the other types; StartsWith, EndsWith, Contains and Matches by name; ByName, ByIndex, First and Last; and their Union, Intersect, Difference, SymmetricDifference and Complement, Polars' |, &, -, ^ and ~, named so that a selector's complement is never taken for an expression's negation, and Exclude. A selector's Expr is the expression of its columns, and Expand the names it selects in a schema:

every := selector.Numeric().Difference(selector.ByName("order_id"))
df, err := sales().Select(every.Expr()).Head(3).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌───────┬─────────┐
│ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┤
│ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 4     │ 1.5     │
│ 7     │ 2.25    │
└───────┴─────────┘

Drop removes columns and Rename renames them, from a map of old names to new:

df, err := sales().
    Drop("order_id", "date").
    Rename(map[string]string{"qty": "quantity", "price": "unit_price"}).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌─────────┬─────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
│ region  │ product │ quantity │ unit_price │
│ String  │ String  │ Int64    │ Float64    │
├─────────┼─────────┼──────────┼────────────┤
│ "north" │ "apple" │ 10       │ 1.5        │
│ "south" │ "apple" │ 4        │ 1.5        │
│ "north" │ "pear"  │ 7        │ 2.25       │
└─────────┴─────────┴──────────┴────────────┘

An expression is named after the first column it reads, and Alias gives it one name. New in 0.6.7: Name() has Polars' name functions, which name each column a multi-column expression makes: Prefix, Suffix and Map; ToLower and ToUpper; Replace, of a regular expression or of the text; and Keep, the first column's name through any alias:

c := ursus.Col
df, err := sales().
    Select(
        c("qty", "price").Name().Suffix("_x"),
        c("region").Name().ToUpper(),
        c("qty").Mul(c("price")).Alias("total").Name().Keep(),
    ).
    Head(3).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌───────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ qty_x │ price_x │ REGION  │ qty     │
│ Int64 │ Float64 │ String  │ Float64 │
├───────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 10    │ 1.5     │ "north" │ 15      │
│ 4     │ 1.5     │ "south" │ 6       │
│ 7     │ 2.25    │ "north" │ 15.75   │
└───────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

For a struct, PrefixFields, SuffixFields and MapFields rename its fields and leave the column's name, as Polars' name.prefix_fields and the rest do.

New in 0.6.7. InsertColumn(i, column) puts a column at a place, an expression or Go values, as Polars' insert_column does; a negative place counts from the end, −1 before the last column:

lines := sales().
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("price")).
    Head(3)
revenue := ursus.Col("qty").Mul(ursus.Col("price")).Alias("revenue")
show(lines.InsertColumn(1, revenue))
show(lines.InsertColumn(-1, ursus.Values("note", []string{"gift", "", "rush"})))
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌──────────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ revenue │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Float64 │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├──────────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 15      │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 6       │ 4     │ 1.5     │
│ 3        │ 15.75   │ 7     │ 2.25    │
└──────────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

shape: (3, 4)
┌──────────┬───────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │ note   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Int64 │ String │ Float64 │
├──────────┼───────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │ "gift" │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 4     │ ""     │ 1.5     │
│ 3        │ 7     │ "rush" │ 2.25    │
└──────────┴───────┴────────┴─────────┘

New in 0.6.7.
