ReplaceColumn(i, column) puts a column in place of the one at a place, and DropInPlace(name) gives a column and the frame without it, as Polars' replace_column and drop_in_place, each a new frame where Polars changes its own. GetColumnIndex(name) is a column's place, ToSeries(i) the column at one, and ToStruct(name) the whole frame as one Struct column.

Select can also compute columns, as WithColumns does: see Expressions. A pattern is explicit: ursus does not read Col("^qty$") as a regular expression, as Polars does, so a column named with a ^ can still be selected by name.

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
Filter keeps the rows where every predicate is true; several predicates are and-ed. IsIn tests membership and IsBetween a range, both ends included unless a Closed says otherwise:

df, err := sales().
    Filter(
        ursus.Col("product").IsIn("apple", "fig"),
        ursus.Col("qty").IsBetween(4, 10),
    ).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 6)
┌──────────┬────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ date       │ region  │ product │ qty   │ price   │
│ Int64    │ Date       │ String  │ String  │ Int64 │ Float64 │
├──────────┼────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ 2026-01-03 │ "north" │ "apple" │ 10    │ 1.5     │
│ 2        │ 2026-01-03 │ "south" │ "apple" │ 4     │ 1.5     │
│ 5        │ 2026-01-05 │ "south" │ "fig"   │ 9     │ 3       │
└──────────┴────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴───────┴─────────┘

Or, And and Not combine predicates into one:

df, err := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("region").Eq("east").Or(ursus.Col("price").Ge(3.0))).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("price")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (4, 3)
┌──────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ region  │ price   │
│ Int64    │ String  │ Float64 │
├──────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 4        │ "east"  │ 2.25    │
│ 5        │ "south" │ 3       │
│ 6        │ "east"  │ 1.5     │
│ 7        │ "north" │ 3       │
└──────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

An aggregate in a predicate is over the whole frame, so a filter can compare each row with the frame: here, the orders larger than the mean, 6.625.

df, err := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("qty").Gt(ursus.Col("qty").Mean())).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (4, 2)
┌──────────┬───────┐
│ order_id │ qty   │
│ Int64    │ Int64 │
├──────────┼───────┤
│ 1        │ 10    │
│ 3        │ 7     │
│ 5        │ 9     │
│ 6        │ 12    │
└──────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Nulls in a filter
docs.text:
A comparison with a null is null, neither true nor false, and Filter keeps only the rows where its predicate is true, as SQL's WHERE does. So Filter(p) and Filter(p.Not()) together can miss rows: the ones where p is null.

Remove is the opposite of Filter: it drops the rows where any predicate is true. It drops the rows where one is null too, so cai, with no score, is in neither:

ctx := context.Background()
scores := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("name", []string{"ana", "ben", "cai", "dee"}),
    ursus.ValuesNullable("score",
        []int64{90, 40, 0, 75},
        []bool{true, true, false, true}),
)
kept, err := scores.Filter(ursus.Col("score").Ge(50)).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
removed, err := scores.Remove(ursus.Col("score").Ge(50)).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
missing, err := scores.Filter(ursus.Col("score").IsNull()).Collect(ctx)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(kept)
fmt.Println(removed)
fmt.Println(missing)
Output
shape: (2, 2)
┌────────┬───────┐
│ name   │ score │
│ String │ Int64 │
├────────┼───────┤
│ "ana"  │ 90    │
│ "dee"  │ 75    │
└────────┴───────┘

shape: (1, 2)
┌────────┬───────┐
│ name   │ score │
│ String │ Int64 │
├────────┼───────┤
│ "ben"  │ 40    │
└────────┴───────┘

shape: (1, 2)
┌────────┬───────┐
│ name   │ score │
│ String │ Int64 │
├────────┼───────┤
│ "cai"  │ null  │
└────────┴───────┘

Polars' remove keeps those rows

Polars' remove(p) keeps a row where p is null; ursus's drops it, as its Filter does. Write the null case out to keep it: Remove(p.And(p.IsNotNull())), or Filter(p.Not().Or(p.IsNull())).

docs.title: Sorting
docs.text:
Sort takes keys, Asc or Desc of an expression, the first key first:

df, err := sales().
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region")), ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("qty"))).
    Select(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 3)
┌─────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ region  │ product │ qty   │
│ String  │ String  │ Int64 │
├─────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ "east"  │ "apple" │ 12    │
│ "east"  │ "pear"  │ 2     │
│ "north" │ "apple" │ 10    │
│ "north" │ "pear"  │ 7     │
│ "north" │ "fig"   │ 3     │
│ "south" │ "fig"   │ 9     │
│ "south" │ "pear"  │ 6     │
│ "south" │ "apple" │ 4     │
└─────────┴─────────┴───────┘

A sort is stable, so rows equal on every key keep their order. Nulls come first in either direction, unless a key says NullsLast():

df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.ValuesNullable("x", []int64{3, 0, 1, 2}, []bool{true, false, true, true}),
).Sort(ursus.Desc(ursus.Col("x")).NullsLast()).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (4, 1)
┌───────┐
│ x     │
│ Int64 │
├───────┤
│ 3     │
│ 2     │
│ 1     │
│ null  │
└───────┘

docs.title: The largest rows
docs.text:
TopK(k, keys...) keeps the k largest rows by its keys, and BottomK the k smallest, without sorting the whole frame. Write each key Asc: TopK takes the largest by it, and a Desc key ranks that column the other way, as Polars' reverse does. Nulls never make the cut.

df, err := sales().
    TopK(3, ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("qty"))).
    Select(ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("product"), ursus.Col("qty")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌──────────┬─────────┬───────┐
│ order_id │ product │ qty   │
│ Int64    │ String  │ Int64 │
├──────────┼─────────┼───────┤
│ 6        │ "apple" │ 12    │
│ 1        │ "apple" │ 10    │
│ 5        │ "fig"   │ 9     │
└──────────┴─────────┴───────┘

docs.title: Unique rows
docs.text:
Unique(names...) keeps the first row of each distinct key, in the rows' order, or of each distinct row when no names are given:

df, err := sales().
    Unique("region").
    Select(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("order_id")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬──────────┐
│ region  │ order_id │
│ String  │ Int64    │
├─────────┼──────────┤
│ "north" │ 1        │
│ "south" │ 2        │
│ "east"  │ 4        │
└─────────┴──────────┘

UniqueKeep chooses which row a key keeps: KeepFirst, KeepLast, KeepAny, or KeepNone, which keeps only the keys seen once. New in 0.6.7.

df, err := sales().
    UniqueKeep(ursus.KeepLast, "region").
    Select(ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("order_id")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬──────────┐
│ region  │ order_id │
│ String  │ Int64    │
├─────────┼──────────┤
│ "east"  │ 6        │
│ "north" │ 7        │
│ "south" │ 8        │
└─────────┴──────────┘

docs.title: Slices
docs.text:
Head, Tail and Slice(offset, length) take rows by position. A negative offset counts from the end, as Polars counts it (new in 0.6.7), and Reverse turns the frame around:

ctx := context.Background()
ids := func(lf *ursus.LazyFrame) []int64 {
    df, err := lf.Collect(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    s, err := df.Column[int64]("order_id")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    return s.Values()
}
fmt.Println("head 3:     ", ids(sales().Head(3)))
fmt.Println("tail 2:     ", ids(sales().Tail(2)))
fmt.Println("slice 2, 3: ", ids(sales().Slice(2, 3)))
fmt.Println("slice -3, 2:", ids(sales().Slice(-3, 2)))
fmt.Println("reverse:    ", ids(sales().Reverse()))
Output
head 3:      [1 2 3]
tail 2:      [7 8]
slice 2, 3:  [3 4 5]
slice -3, 2: [6 7]
reverse:     [8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1]

New in 0.6.7. Gather(ctx, indices, nullOnOOB) takes the rows at positions, in their order, as Polars' gather; a negative position counts from the end, and one past the end is refused, or with nullOnOOB is a row of nulls. Row(i) is a row's values as Go values, RowNamed(i) the same by name, and RowWhere(ctx, predicate) the one row a predicate holds of. Item() is a one-value frame's value and ItemAt(row, column) any one, as Polars' row and item.

New in 0.6.7. HashRows(seed, columns...) is each row's hash over its columns, every column when none is named, as Polars' hash_rows: rows equal as a group-by sees them hash alike. The numbers are ursus's own, not Polars'.

visits := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("user", []string{"ada", "ben", "ada"}),
    ursus.Values("page", []string{"/home", "/home", "/home"}),
)
show(visits.WithColumns(ursus.HashRows(0).Alias("hash")))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌────────┬─────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ user   │ page    │ hash                 │
│ String │ String  │ Uint64               │
├────────┼─────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ "ada"  │ "/home" │ 15332602214641343754 │
│ "ben"  │ "/home" │ 17635480945181825081 │
│ "ada"  │ "/home" │ 15332602214641343754 │
└────────┴─────────┴──────────────────────┘

WithRowIndex(name, offset) numbers the rows, from offset:

df, err := sales().
    Filter(ursus.Col("region").Eq("south")).
    WithRowIndex("n", 1).
    Select(ursus.Col("n"), ursus.Col("order_id"), ursus.Col("product")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
│ n      │ order_id │ product │
│ Uint32 │ Int64    │ String  │
├────────┼──────────┼─────────┤
│ 1      │ 2        │ "apple" │
│ 2      │ 5        │ "fig"   │
│ 3      │ 8        │ "pear"  │
└────────┴──────────┴─────────┘

ursus has no index of its own, as pandas has: row order is a property of a frame, not a label space, and a row index is a column like any other.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
Text methods sit behind Str(). A method returns an expression, so a second one needs Str() again: Col("name").Str().StripChars(" ").Str().ToLower(). The examples read a small frame of people:

func people() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.Frame(
        ursus.Values("name", []string{
            "  ada LOVELACE",
            "Zoë Smith ",
            "ben o'brien",
        }),
        ursus.Values("contact", []string{
            "ada@example.com, +44 20 7946 0958",
            "zoe.smith@mail.example.org",
            "call 555-0100 or 555-0199",
        }),
        ursus.Values("joined", []string{"2024-03-01", "2025-11-17", "bad date"}),
    )
}

docs.title: Cleaning
docs.text:
name := ursus.Col("name").Str()
trimmed := name.StripChars(" ").Str() // a method gives an Expr: Str() again
show(people().Select(
    trimmed.ToTitlecase().Alias("name"),
    trimmed.ToLower().Alias("lower"),
    name.LenChars().Alias("chars"),
    name.LenBytes().Alias("bytes"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 4)
┌────────────────┬────────────────┬────────┬────────┐
│ name           │ lower          │ chars  │ bytes  │
│ String         │ String         │ Uint32 │ Uint32 │
├────────────────┼────────────────┼────────┼────────┤
│ "Ada Lovelace" │ "ada lovelace" │ 14     │ 14     │
│ "Zoë Smith"    │ "zoë smith"    │ 10     │ 11     │
│ "Ben O'Brien"  │ "ben o'brien"  │ 11     │ 11     │
└────────────────┴────────────────┴────────┴────────┘
  • StripChars(chars) trims those characters from both ends, and StripCharsStart and StripCharsEnd from one; StripPrefix and StripSuffix remove a whole affix;
  • ToUpper, ToLower and ToTitlecase;
  • LenChars counts characters and LenBytes bytes of UTF-8: "Zoë Smith " is ten characters and eleven bytes.

docs.title: Matching
docs.text:
Contains(pattern, literal) tests a regular expression, or a literal string when literal is true. StartsWith and EndsWith take a literal, and CountMatches counts a pattern's matches:

contact := ursus.Col("contact").Str()
show(people().Select(
    ursus.Col("contact"),
    contact.Contains("@", true).Alias("email"),
    contact.Contains(`\d{3}-\d{4}`, false).Alias("us_phone"),
    contact.EndsWith(".org").Alias("org"),
    contact.CountMatches(`\d`, false).Alias("digits"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 5)
┌─────────────────────────────────────┬───────┬──────────┬───────┬────────┐
│ contact                             │ email │ us_phone │ org   │ digits │
│ String                              │ Bool  │ Bool     │ Bool  │ Uint32 │
├─────────────────────────────────────┼───────┼──────────┼───────┼────────┤
│ "ada@example.com, +44 20 7946 0958" │ true  │ false    │ false │ 12     │
│ "zoe.smith@mail.example.org"        │ true  │ false    │ true  │ 0      │
│ "call 555-0100 or 555-0199"         │ false │ true     │ false │ 14     │
└─────────────────────────────────────┴───────┴──────────┴───────┴────────┘

Patterns are Go's regular expressions, RE2, as Polars' are Rust's regex: the same syntax for nearly everything, and no backreferences or look-around in either. ContainsAny(patterns, ...) and ReplaceMany match many literal strings at once, in one pass.

docs.title: Extracting
docs.text:
Extract(pattern, group) takes a capture group of the first match, null where nothing matches; ExtractAll(pattern) takes every match, a list a row; ExtractGroups every named group, as a struct.

contact := ursus.Col("contact").Str()
show(people().Select(
    contact.Extract(`([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)`, 2).Alias("domain"),
    contact.ExtractAll(`\d{3}-\d{4}`).Alias("phones"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ domain             │ phones                   │
│ String             │ List(String)             │
├────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
│ "example.com"      │ []                       │
│ "mail.example.org" │ []                       │
│ null               │ ["555-0100", "555-0199"] │
└────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Replacing
docs.text:
Replace replaces the first match and ReplaceAll every one; ReplaceN the first n. With a regular expression, the replacement may refer to groups: $1, or ${name}.

contact := ursus.Col("contact").Str()
show(people().Select(
    contact.Replace(`\d`, "#", false).Alias("first_digit"),
    contact.ReplaceAll(`\d`, "#", false).Alias("every_digit"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ first_digit                         │ every_digit                         │
│ String                              │ String                              │
├─────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
│ "ada@example.com, +#4 20 7946 0958" │ "ada@example.com, +## ## #### ####" │
│ "zoe.smith@mail.example.org"        │ "zoe.smith@mail.example.org"        │
│ "call #55-0100 or 555-0199"         │ "call ###-#### or ###-####"         │
└─────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Splitting
docs.text:
Split(by) gives a list a row. SplitExact(by, n, inclusive) gives a struct of n + 1 fields, null where there are fewer parts, which Unnest turns into columns:

show(people().Select(
    ursus.Col("name").Str().StripChars(" ").Str().Split(" ").Alias("words"),
))
show(people().
    Select(ursus.Col("joined").Str().SplitExact("-", 2, false).Alias("parts")).
    Unnest("parts"))
Output
shape: (3, 1)
┌─────────────────────┐
│ words               │
│ List(String)        │
├─────────────────────┤
│ ["ada", "LOVELACE"] │
│ ["Zoë", "Smith"]    │
│ ["ben", "o'brien"]  │
└─────────────────────┘

shape: (3, 3)
┌────────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ field_0    │ field_1 │ field_2 │
│ String     │ String  │ String  │
├────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ "2024"     │ "03"    │ "01"    │
│ "2025"     │ "11"    │ "17"    │
│ "bad date" │ null    │ null    │
└────────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

SplitN(by, n) splits at most n − 1 times, the rest in the last part.

docs.title: Padding and slicing
docs.text:
code := ursus.Frame(ursus.Values("code", []string{"7", "42", "1234"}))
c := ursus.Col("code").Str()
show(code.Select(
    ursus.Col("code"),
    c.ZFill(5).Alias("zfill"),
    c.PadEnd(5, ".").Alias("pad_end"),
    c.Head(2).Alias("head"),
    c.Slice(1, 2).Alias("slice"),
    c.Reverse().Alias("reverse"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 6)
┌────────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ code   │ zfill   │ pad_end │ head   │ slice  │ reverse │
│ String │ String  │ String  │ String │ String │ String  │
├────────┼─────────┼─────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ "7"    │ "00007" │ "7...." │ "7"    │ ""     │ "7"     │
│ "42"   │ "00042" │ "42..." │ "42"   │ "2"    │ "24"    │
│ "1234" │ "01234" │ "1234." │ "12"   │ "23"   │ "4321"  │
└────────┴─────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┘

ZFill, PadStart and PadEnd pad to a width; Slice(offset, length), Head and Tail count characters, not bytes, and Reverse reverses them.

docs.title: Parsing
docs.text:
Strptime(type, format, strict) parses dates and times with a strftime format; ToInteger parses integers:

joined := ursus.Col("joined").Str()
show(people().Select(
    ursus.Col("joined"),
    joined.Strptime(ursus.Date, "%Y-%m-%d", false).Alias("date"),
    joined.Head(4).Str().ToInteger().Alias("year"),
))
Output
shape: (3, 3)
┌──────────────┬────────────┬───────┐
│ joined       │ date       │ year  │
│ String       │ Date       │ Int64 │
├──────────────┼────────────┼───────┤
│ "2024-03-01" │ 2024-03-01 │ 2024  │
│ "2025-11-17" │ 2025-11-17 │ 2025  │
│ "bad date"   │ null       │ null  │
└──────────────┴────────────┴───────┘

ToInteger, ToDate and ToDatetime turn what does not parse into a null. Polars' to_integer and to_date fail the query by default instead. For that, ask for strictness: Strptime(..., true), or ToIntegerWith(base, type, true).

New in 0.6.7: ToTime(format, strict) parses a time of day, by a format or, with none, each value as it comes, and ToDecimal(scale) a number into a Decimal(38, scale), rounded half away from zero, as Polars' to_time and to_decimal.

JsonDecode(type) parses JSON into a value of a type, a struct or a list, and Encode and Decode convert to and from hex or base64.

docs.title: Joining
docs.text:
ConcatStr(sep, exprs...) joins columns row by row, and Format fills a template; Str().Join(sep) in an aggregation joins a group's values into one string:

show(sales().Head(3).Select(
    ursus.ConcatStr("/", ursus.Col("region"), ursus.Col("product")).Alias("path"),
    ursus.Format("{} x {}", ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("product")).Alias("line"),
))
show(sales().
    GroupBy(ursus.Col("region")).
    Agg(ursus.Col("product").Str().Join(", ").Alias("products")).
    Sort(ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("region"))))
Output
shape: (3, 2)
┌───────────────┬──────────────┐
│ path          │ line         │
│ String        │ String       │
├───────────────┼──────────────┤
│ "north/apple" │ "10 x apple" │
│ "south/apple" │ "4 x apple"  │
│ "north/pear"  │ "7 x pear"   │
└───────────────┴──────────────┘

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────────┬────────────────────┐
│ region  │ products           │
│ String  │ String             │
├─────────┼────────────────────┤
│ "east"  │ "pear, apple"      │
│ "north" │ "apple, pear, fig" │
│ "south" │ "apple, fig, pear" │
└─────────┴────────────────────┘

A null in ConcatStr's inputs makes the row null, as in Polars; ConcatStrIgnoreNulls skips nulls instead.

docs.title: Window functions
docs.text:
A window function computes over a group of rows and gives an answer back on every row, so the frame keeps its height. GroupBy reduces each group to one row; a window keeps the rows and puts each group's answer beside them.

The examples read the quick start's orders, and a series of two tickers' closing prices over six trading days, a weekend before the sixth:

func prices() *ursus.LazyFrame {
    return ursus.ScanCSV("testdata/prices.csv",
        ursus.WithSchemaOverrides(map[string]ursus.DataType{"date": ursus.Date}))
}

docs.title: An aggregate beside every row
docs.text:
Over(keys...) computes an expression within each partition of rows with the same keys. An aggregate under Over is its partition's value on each of its rows, which an expression can then use, here for each order's share of its region:

qty, region := ursus.Col("qty"), ursus.Col("region")
df, err := sales().
    Select(
        ursus.Col("order_id"),
        region,
        qty,
        qty.Sum().Over(region).Alias("region_qty"),
        qty.Div(qty.Sum().Over(region)).Round(2).Alias("share"),
        qty.Sum().Over().Alias("all_qty"),
    ).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (8, 6)
┌──────────┬─────────┬───────┬────────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ order_id │ region  │ qty   │ region_qty │ share   │ all_qty │
│ Int64    │ String  │ Int64 │ Int128     │ Float64 │ Int128  │
├──────────┼─────────┼───────┼────────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 1        │ "north" │ 10    │ 20         │ 0.5     │ 53      │
│ 2        │ "south" │ 4     │ 19         │ 0.21    │ 53      │
│ 3        │ "north" │ 7     │ 20         │ 0.35    │ 53      │
│ 4        │ "east"  │ 2     │ 14         │ 0.14    │ 53      │
│ 5        │ "south" │ 9     │ 19         │ 0.47    │ 53      │
│ 6        │ "east"  │ 12    │ 14         │ 0.86    │ 53      │
│ 7        │ "north" │ 3     │ 20         │ 0.15    │ 53      │
│ 8        │ "south" │ 6     │ 19         │ 0.32    │ 53      │
└──────────┴─────────┴───────┴────────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

Over() with no keys is the whole frame as one partition: all_qty is the grand total on every row. Rows keep their order, whatever the partitions.

docs.title: Ordered windows
docs.text:
Cumulative functions, shifts and ranks depend on the rows' order. Without one of its own a window takes the rows as they come. OverWith gives a partition its order with a WindowSpec, whatever order the frame is in:

byTicker := ursus.WindowSpec{
    PartitionBy: []ursus.Expr{ursus.Col("ticker")},
    OrderBy:     []ursus.SortKey{ursus.Asc(ursus.Col("date"))},
}
df, err := prices().
    WithColumns(
        ursus.Col("close").CumMax(false).OverWith(byTicker).Alias("high"),
        ursus.Col("close").CumCount(false).OverWith(byTicker).Alias("day"),
    ).
    Filter(ursus.Col("ticker").Eq("ACME")).
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (6, 5)
┌────────────┬────────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────┐
│ date       │ ticker │ close   │ high    │ day    │
│ Date       │ String │ Float64 │ Float64 │ Uint32 │
├────────────┼────────┼─────────┼─────────┼────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ "ACME" │ 10      │ 10      │ 1      │
│ 2026-01-06 │ "ACME" │ 11      │ 11      │ 2      │
│ 2026-01-07 │ "ACME" │ 10.5    │ 11      │ 3      │
│ 2026-01-08 │ "ACME" │ 12      │ 12      │ 4      │
│ 2026-01-09 │ "ACME" │ 12      │ 12      │ 5      │
│ 2026-01-12 │ "ACME" │ 13.5    │ 13.5    │ 6      │
└────────────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┴────────┘

CumSum, CumProd, CumMin, CumMax and CumCount each take a reverse flag, to accumulate from the end.

docs.title: Shift, diff and percent change
docs.text:
Shift(n) moves values n rows later within each partition, nulls where they were; Diff(n) is the difference from n rows before, and PctChange(n) the change as a fraction:

t := ursus.Col("ticker")
df, err := prices().
    WithColumns(
        ursus.Col("close").Shift(1).Over(t).Alias("previous"),
        ursus.Col("close").Diff(1).Over(t).Alias("change"),
        ursus.Col("close").PctChange(1).Over(t).Round(3).Alias("pct"),
    ).
    Filter(t.Eq("BOLT")).
    Drop("ticker").
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (6, 5)
┌────────────┬─────────┬──────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ date       │ close   │ previous │ change  │ pct     │
│ Date       │ Float64 │ Float64  │ Float64 │ Float64 │
├────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ 20      │ null     │ null    │ null    │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 19      │ 20       │ -1      │ -0.05   │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 21      │ 19       │ 2       │ 0.105   │
│ 2026-01-08 │ 21      │ 21       │ 0       │ 0       │
│ 2026-01-09 │ 22      │ 21       │ 1       │ 0.048   │
│ 2026-01-12 │ 20      │ 22       │ -2      │ -0.091  │
└────────────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

ShiftFill(n, value) shifts with a value instead of nulls.

docs.title: Rank
docs.text:
Rank(method, descending) numbers the rows by value. The methods differ only on ties, here two 9s and two 7s:

x := ursus.Col("points")
df, err := ursus.Frame(
    ursus.Values("team", []string{"a", "b", "c", "d", "e"}),
    ursus.Values("points", []int64{7, 9, 7, 3, 9}),
).WithColumns(
    x.Rank(ursus.RankOrdinal, true).Alias("ordinal"),
    x.Rank(ursus.RankMin, true).Alias("min"),
    x.Rank(ursus.RankMax, true).Alias("max"),
    x.Rank(ursus.RankDense, true).Alias("dense"),
    x.Rank(ursus.RankAverage, true).Alias("average"),
).Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (5, 7)
┌────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┬─────────┐
│ team   │ points │ ordinal │ min    │ max    │ dense  │ average │
│ String │ Int64  │ Uint32  │ Uint32 │ Uint32 │ Uint32 │ Float64 │
├────────┼────────┼─────────┼────────┼────────┼────────┼─────────┤
│ "a"    │ 7      │ 3       │ 3      │ 4      │ 2      │ 3.5     │
│ "b"    │ 9      │ 1       │ 1      │ 2      │ 1      │ 1.5     │
│ "c"    │ 7      │ 4       │ 3      │ 4      │ 2      │ 3.5     │
│ "d"    │ 3      │ 5       │ 5      │ 5      │ 3      │ 5       │
│ "e"    │ 9      │ 2       │ 1      │ 2      │ 1      │ 1.5     │
└────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴─────────┘
Method Ties get RankOrdinal distinct ranks, in the rows' order RankMin the lowest rank of the tie RankMax the highest rank of the tie RankDense the same rank, with no gap after them RankAverage the mean of the tie's ranks, as a Float64

Under Over, a rank is within its partition: the expressions page ranks each order in its region. A null's rank is null, and the values are ranked among themselves, as Polars ranks them. Changed in 0.6.7: a null ranked as the least value before, and took a position.

docs.title: Rolling windows by rows
docs.text:
RollingMean(n) is the mean of each row and the n − 1 before it, and so on for RollingSum, RollingMin, RollingMax, RollingStd, RollingVar, RollingMedian, RollingQuantile, RollingSkew, RollingKurtosis and RollingRank:

t, c := ursus.Col("ticker"), ursus.Col("close")
df, err := prices().
    WithColumns(
        c.RollingMean(3).Over(t).Alias("mean3"),
        c.RollingMean(3, ursus.MinSamples(1)).Over(t).Alias("mean3_min1"),
        c.RollingMax(3, ursus.RollingCenter()).Over(t).Alias("max3_centred"),
    ).
    Filter(t.Eq("ACME")).
    Drop("ticker").
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (6, 5)
┌────────────┬─────────┬────────────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────┐
│ date       │ close   │ mean3              │ mean3_min1         │ max3_centred │
│ Date       │ Float64 │ Float64            │ Float64            │ Float64      │
├────────────┼─────────┼────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ 10      │ null               │ 10                 │ null         │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 11      │ null               │ 10.5               │ 11           │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 10.5    │ 10.5               │ 10.5               │ 12           │
│ 2026-01-08 │ 12      │ 11.166666666666666 │ 11.166666666666666 │ 12           │
│ 2026-01-09 │ 12      │ 11.5               │ 11.5               │ 13.5         │
│ 2026-01-12 │ 13.5    │ 12.5               │ 12.5               │ null         │
└────────────┴─────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────┘
  • a window needs all n values by default, so the first n − 1 rows are null; MinSamples(k) answers from k;
  • RollingCenter() centres the window on its row.

New in 0.6.7: RollingMap(name, type, n, fn) calls a Go function on each row's window, as Polars' rolling_map; see Go functions.

docs.title: Rolling windows by time
docs.text:
A window by rows counts rows; a window by time counts time. RollingSumBy(by, period) sums the rows whose by lies in the period up to each row's, (t − period, t] by default. Across the weekend the two differ: Monday's three rows reach back to Wednesday, and its three days only to Saturday.

t, c := ursus.Col("ticker"), ursus.Col("close")
df, err := prices().
    WithColumns(
        c.RollingSum(3, ursus.MinSamples(1)).Over(t).Alias("last_3_rows"),
        c.RollingSumBy(ursus.Col("date"), ursus.Every("3d")).Over(t).
            Alias("last_3_days"),
    ).
    Filter(t.Eq("ACME")).
    Drop("ticker").
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (6, 4)
┌────────────┬─────────┬─────────────┬─────────────┐
│ date       │ close   │ last_3_rows │ last_3_days │
│ Date       │ Float64 │ Float64     │ Float64     │
├────────────┼─────────┼─────────────┼─────────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ 10      │ 10          │ 10          │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 11      │ 21          │ 21          │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 10.5    │ 31.5        │ 31.5        │
│ 2026-01-08 │ 12      │ 33.5        │ 33.5        │
│ 2026-01-09 │ 12      │ 34.5        │ 34.5        │
│ 2026-01-12 │ 13.5    │ 37.5        │ 13.5        │
└────────────┴─────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘

A period is an Every interval: "3d", "2h", "1mo", or a combination such as "1d12h"; m is minutes and mo months. WindowClosed says which ends of the window belong to it.

The By forms take a Date, Datetime or Time column, which need not be sorted: a window is found by value, and rows tied with a row's instant are in its window. Unlike the windows by rows they answer from one value by default. New in 0.6.7: RollingRankBy(by, period, method) ranks each row's value among its window's, as Polars' rolling_rank_by; over one partition past a memory limit it is refused, as its window's values are not yet walked. New in 0.6.7: by can be an integer of 32 or 64 bits, a step rather than an instant, whose period counts it in Polars' integer unit: Every("3i") is three steps, as in Dates and times.

New in 0.6.7: e.Rolling(index, o) is any aggregate expression over each row's window, as Polars' Expr.rolling: Col("x").Max().Sub(Col("x").Min()).Rolling(Col("t"), ursus.RollingOptions{Period: ursus.Every("2d")}) is each row's range over the two days ending at it, the window placed as the frame's Rolling places it, and Over(keys) rolls within each partition. Where every aggregate in it is a sum, a mean, a minimum, a maximum, a variance, a standard deviation, a median or a quantile, and no offset is given, each is rolled by its own window above, found by value, so the index need not be sorted, and in an aggregation it is a list a group. Anything else, a row's value, which is the list of its window's, or a first, is rolled by the frame's rolling group, whose index is checked sorted, within each partition under Over, and is refused in an aggregation; under Over it holds its windows until the input ends.

docs.title: Exponentially weighted
docs.text:
EwmMean, EwmStd, EwmVar and EwmSum weight recent rows more. The decay is EwmAlpha, EwmSpan, EwmCom or EwmHalfLife, as Polars' parameters are, and EwmAdjust(false) uses the recursive form:

t, c := ursus.Col("ticker"), ursus.Col("close")
df, err := prices().
    WithColumns(
        c.EwmMean(ursus.EwmAlpha(0.5)).Over(t).Round(4).Alias("ewm"),
        c.EwmMean(ursus.EwmAlpha(0.5), ursus.EwmAdjust(false)).Over(t).Round(4).
            Alias("ewm_unadjusted"),
    ).
    Filter(t.Eq("ACME")).
    Drop("ticker").
    Collect(context.Background())
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Println(df)
Output
shape: (6, 4)
┌────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬────────────────┐
│ date       │ close   │ ewm     │ ewm_unadjusted │
│ Date       │ Float64 │ Float64 │ Float64        │
├────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼────────────────┤
│ 2026-01-05 │ 10      │ 10      │ 10             │
│ 2026-01-06 │ 11      │ 10.6667 │ 10.5           │
│ 2026-01-07 │ 10.5    │ 10.5714 │ 10.5           │
│ 2026-01-08 │ 12      │ 11.3333 │ 11.25          │
│ 2026-01-09 │ 12      │ 11.6774 │ 11.625         │
│ 2026-01-12 │ 13.5    │ 12.6032 │ 12.5625        │
└────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴────────────────┘

EwmMeanBy(by, halfLife) decays by time between rows rather than by rows, or by the steps of an integer by, its half-life such as Every("2i").

docs.title: Without Over
docs.text: A window function with no Over runs over the whole frame in the rows' order: Col("close").CumSum(false) is a running total from the first row to the last.

docs.title: A window inside a window
docs.text: New in 0.6.7: a window function's input may hold another, and an aggregate, each computed first in the outer window's partitions and order, as Polars computes them: Col("x").Shift(1).CumSum(false).Over(Col("g")) shifts within each g and then sums within each g, and Col("x").Sub(Col("x").Mean()).CumSum(false).Over(Col("g")) sums each row's distance from its group's mean. A window with an Over of its own inside another is computed within the outer one's partitions, so Col("x").Sum().Over(Col("g")).CumSum(false).Over(Col("h")) sums g's values within each h. An aggregate whose answer depends on the order, First, under an OrderBy is refused, as an ordering over an aggregate is.

docs.title: Under a memory limit
docs.text: Windows spill to disk under a memory budget, over many partitions or one huge one, and give the answer they give in memory. A rolling window by time whose period holds more than the budget fails rather than exceed it. See Memory and spilling.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The reference for every package, type and method is generated from the source on pkg.go.dev, for this version of ursus:

github.com/advenn/ursus@master on pkg.go.dev

Its doc comments say why a thing is the way it is, not only what it does, and the runnable examples beside the methods are run by go test, as this site's are.

The packages:

Package What it holds ursus frames, expressions, scans and sinks: everything a query needs ursus/dtype the type system, re-exported by ursus as ursus.Int64, ursus.Schema and the rest ursus/ursustest assertions for tests: frames equal, and golden plans ursus/i128 the 128-bit integer behind Int128 and Decimal

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
ursus is on ZeroVer: 0.x, and a stable 1.0 is not expected yet. Go's rule for v0 applies, so a minor version may change behaviour, and an API may be renamed, removed or reshaped when the result is better, without being deprecated first. Each release below therefore says what a user of the previous one can trip on, not only what is new; from 0.6 on, each lists its breaks with their replacements.

Every step of construction has an as-built record in context_files/, with the measurements behind each change. Step numbers below point at those records.

docs.title: Unreleased — toward v0.6.7
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.6 (2026-10-19): steps 288–339, so far. v0.6.7-scope.md set the scope: feature completeness, part 3 — frame operations.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
• A null's rank is null (335), as Polars': Rank ranked a null as the least value and gave it a position, so [5, null, 4] ranked [3, 1, 2]; it ranks [2, null, 1] now, the values among themselves, by every method, in a window and over the frame, streamed past a memory limit and in List().Eval. A rank's column is nullable where its input is.
  • A float cast to text is Polars' text (325): 2.0 is "2.0", -0.0 "-0.0", 1e-7 "1e-7", 1e16 "1e+16" and +Inf "inf", where they were Go's "2", "-0", "1e-07", "1e+16" and "+Inf". A pivot named by a float's text names its column so too, 2.0 where it was 2.
  • An as-of tolerance of zero admits only an exact match (315), as Polars' does: AsOfTolerance(ursus.FromDuration(0)) admitted any distance.
  • An as-of join keeps both ordering keys when they are named apart (315), as Polars' does: AsOfLeftOn(ts) with AsOfRightOn(quote_ts) gives ts and quote_ts, where quote_ts was merged into ts.
  • JoinMaintainOrder takes a JoinOrder (314), Polars' maintain_order, where it took a Boolean: JoinMaintainOrder(true) is JoinMaintainOrder(ursus.JoinOrderLeft).
  • RollingOptions.Offset is where a window starts (313), as Polars' offset: (t + Offset, t + Offset + Period], minus the period when unset, as before. It moved the window's end, so an offset of e is now e less the period: Every("15m") at a period of 2h is Every("-1h45m"). NoOffset() is Polars' offset="0d", a window after its row. A window whose offset is as long as its period, behind its row, ends at the row, as Polars', a month counted as 28 days.
  • A null condition takes Otherwise (311), as Polars' when and SQL's CASE WHEN do: When(c).Then(a).Otherwise(b) of a null c is b, or the next When's, where it was null. A conditional's result is nullable only where a branch is. Clip with a null bound now leaves that side unclipped, as Polars' does, where it gave null; FillNan still leaves a null alone.
  • ConcatMode is ursus's own type (307), no longer the plan's, its String the name of Polars' mode: ConcatStrict prints "vertical", where it printed "strict". Code that names the constants is unchanged.
  • PivotOptions.On is a []string (303), for several columns whose values together name a new column: On: "quarter" is On: []string{"quarter"}.
  • A selection among a variadic function's operands is now its operands, as in Polars (302). SumHorizontal(All()) is each row's sum across every column, one column. Before, the function was repeated a column at a time, so MaxHorizontal(All()) gave each column itself. This holds for the six horizontal reductions, ConcatStr, ConcatStrIgnoreNulls, Struct, ConcatList, List().Concat and Coalesce. Format still formats a column at a time, as Polars' does.
  • FillStrategy is a uint64, where it was a uint8 (301): its bits above the rule carry a limit. A conversion to uint8 no longer compiles, and a strategy with a limit is not == the bare one, FillForward.Limit(1) != FillForward.
  • A slice whose window starts before the first element is cut by as much, as every Polars slice is (291): Str().Slice(-7, 2) of "012345" is "0", and List().Slice(-99, 2) of three elements is none. Both clamped the start to the first element and kept the whole length.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• A frame collected from several batches says its columns hold no null (321), where they hold none: concatenating the batches built each column a bitmap with every bit set, and every kernel after read it a bit a row.
  • A null instant decodes as the zero time.Time (317), in Rows and CollectInto, as a null decodes as every other field type's zero: it was the epoch, 1970-01-01, a plausible instant no row held. IsZero now tells it.
  • A conditional of Lists or Structs (310): When(...).Then(list).Otherwise(...), and Coalesce of Lists, were refused, "a conditional is not implemented for List(String)"; each row is now its branch's, as Polars' when/then gives.
  • An expression that reads no column is named as its first input is (309), as Polars names it: Len().Cast(Int64) and Len().Add(1) are "len", where they were "literal".
  • A pivot's cell that no value falls in is Agg of none (303), as Polars' is: a count's 0, where every such cell was null. A sum of none stays null, as ursus's every empty sum is.
  • A fold in a list's body (302): List().Eval(Fold(...)) and a Fold in CumulativeEval's body failed, "fold reached typing unexpanded", since folds came in (266). A body is lowered when it is written, before any schema, so a fold or a function across columns in it is now built over its expressions as written.
  • A printed frame aligns text outside ASCII (296). It padded each cell by its bytes, so a row holding "Zoë" came out a column short; it pads by the columns a terminal draws, two for a wide East Asian character and none for a combining mark, as Polars measures them.
  • WithMemoryLimit's doc said the default budget is Linux's alone; it has been macOS's and Windows's too since step 181 (294).
  • The expression Slice in a Select kept a row too many where its window began before the first row, Slice(-7, 2) of six rows two (291); and in an aggregation, a negative length, "to the end", failed.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• CorrSpearman spills its pairs (339): over a group larger than the memory limit, in a group-by, a window or a dynamic or rolling group, where it failed; its pairs go to disk sorted by one variable, are ranked as they come back, and sorted again by the other. Its sums are exact integers now, so its answer no longer depends on the order its pairs came in, spilled, merged from several threads or neither; and it is faster, 89 ms where it was 332 by a thousand groups of a million rows (Polars 123), and 98 where it was 909 over the frame (Polars 82).
  • RollingRankBy and RollingMap (338), Polars' rolling_rank_by and rolling_map: each row's value ranked among its window's by time, and a Go function over each row's window of rows, given its values and whether each is there, centred or not, within each partition under Over.
  • The rolling of an expression (337), Polars' Expr.rolling: e.Rolling(index, o) is any aggregate expression over each row's window, placed as the frame's Rolling places it, and the list of the window's values for a row's; under Over within each partition, its index sorted within it, the answer in the frame's rows' order. A sum, a mean, a minimum, a maximum, a variance, a deviation, a median and a quantile are rolled by their own windows by time, thirty times as fast as by the rolling group, and a rolling window by an index already sorted skips its sort.
  • A window inside a window, and an aggregate inside an aggregate (336), as Polars computes them: Col("x").Shift(1).CumSum(false).Over(g) shifts and then sums within each g, Col("x").Sum().Over(g).CumSum(false).Over(h) sums g within each h, and (x - x.Mean()).Abs().Sum() is each group's, or the frame's, sum of distances from its mean. In Agg a mix, x - x.Mean(), is a list a group, x.Sum().Mean() the group's sum, and SortBy takes an aggregate in its keys. Each inner one is computed beneath the outer in its partitions and order; an aggregate the order does not change takes none of it. (x - x.Mean()).CumSum(false).Over(g), which failed with an internal error, answers. A window over one integer key numbers its partitions as the group-by does, twice as fast: Sum().Over(g) over a million rows of 1000 groups in 15.5 ms, where it took 38.
  • NDJSON read (334): ScanNDJSON, ScanNDJSONFiles, ScanNDJSONGlob, ScanNDJSONFrom and ScanNDJSONBytes, as Polars' read_ndjson and scan_ndjson, types inferred as Polars infers them; WithNDJSONSchema of any type, WithInferSchemaLines and WithNDJSONIgnoreErrors. Each block of lines is parsed by every thread at once, faster than Polars: a million lines of four keys in 70 ms to its 79, nested ones 2.3 times as fast.
  • JSON written (333): WriteNDJSON, WriteJSON and SinkNDJSON, as Polars' write_ndjson, write_json and sink_ndjson, each value in Polars' own text, to the byte.
  • Arrow IPC (332), as Polars reads and writes it: ScanIPC, ScanIPCStream, WriteIPC, WriteIPCStream, SinkIPC, uncompressed, LZ4 or Zstandard, and ReadIPCSchema; and ReadParquetSchema. Polars' own files read, string views and large lists in them, and Polars reads ursus's.
  • A list a group, and a window a group at a time (331): a non-aggregate in Agg is each group's values as a list, as Polars answers it, Agg(Col("x")) and Agg(Col("x").Mul(2)); and a window anywhere in Agg runs a group at a time, Agg(Col("x").CumSum(false)) a list and Agg(Col("x").CumSum(false).Max()) one value. They were refused, "expression is not an aggregate" and a hint to move the window into a WithColumns.
  • TopKBy and BottomKBy (330), Polars' top_k_by and bottom_k_by: the k values where another column is greatest or least, a List a group as TopK's, bounded, and parallel in a group-by: rows that tie are ordered by their values.
  • InterpolateBy (329), Polars' interpolate_by: a gap filled on the line at each row's by, a time or a number, sorted or not, to Polars' last bit.
  • MapRows, MapColumns, Show and Cache (328), as Polars' map_rows, map_columns, show and cache: a Go function of each row, typed by its struct or a []any, or of each named column; the first n rows drawn, every one; and a query run once where it is used twice, whatever it holds.
  • A frame's conveniences (327), as Polars' frame methods: Corr, NumPy's correlation of every pair of columns; Gather, Row, RowNamed, RowWhere, Item and ItemAt; GetColumnIndex, ReplaceColumn, DropInPlace, ToSeries and ToStruct; SumHorizontal, MeanHorizontal, MinHorizontal, MaxHorizontal and Fold across the columns; and a lazy frame's Columns, DTypes and Width.
  • The meta namespace (326), Expr.Meta(), as Polars' meta: RootNames, OutputName, HasMultipleOutputs, IsColumn, IsColumnSelection, IsLiteral, IsRegexProjection, UndoAliases, Eq, Pop and TreeFormat.
  • Str().ToTime, Str().ToDecimal and Dt().CastTimeUnit (325), as Polars' str.to_time, str.to_decimal and dt.cast_time_unit.
  • Polars' odds (324): Item, LowerBound, UpperBound and IsSorted, as aggregates; ToPhysical and Reinterpret; Arctan2, TrueDiv, Limit and Pipe.
  • The name namespace (323), Expr.Name(), as Polars' name: Keep, Map, Prefix, Suffix, ToLower, ToUpper, Replace, and a struct's PrefixFields, SuffixFields and MapFields; and Struct().Drop, as struct.drop.
  • Selectors (322), package ursus/selector, as Polars' polars.selectors: columns by their types, Numeric, Integer, Float, Temporal, String and the rest; by name, StartsWith, EndsWith, Contains, Matches, ByName; by place, ByIndex, First, Last; and their Union, Intersect, Difference, SymmetricDifference, Complement and Exclude, each an expression by Expr, its names by Expand.
  • A group-by's groups as frames (321): Groups, an iterator of each group's key and rows, and MapGroups, a Go function over each, as Polars' iteration and map_groups; and a frame's Extend, Glimpse and EstimatedSize, and WithColumnsSeq and SelectSeq, as Polars'. PartitionBy, which they are built on, is three and a half times as fast: its parts numbered with a group-by's tables and gathered in parallel.
  • ToDummies (320), as Polars' to_dummies, on a frame and on a Series: a Uint8 column for each distinct value, named by the value as Polars displays it and ordered by name, as Polars orders them. Unstack, as Polars' unstack, vertical or horizontal, with its fill values.
  • Transpose names its columns from a column, ColumnNamesFrom, as Polars' column_names, and meets text beside numbers at text, as Polars does, where it refused them (320).
  • A Series with operations (319), as Polars': Sort, Unique, Reverse, DropNulls, FillNull, Cast[U], Head, Tail, Slice, Rename, and the aggregates. Series is ursus's own type now, the view it was embedded, so every method it had is there still.
  • Rows out (318): RowsByKey, as Polars' rows_by_key; ToMaps, as its to_dicts; and IterRows, a query's rows as structs streamed a batch at a time, as its iter_rows.
  • FromRows (317), a frame from Go structs, as Polars builds one from dataclasses: a column a field, named as Rows reads it, pointers nullable, slices Lists and structs Structs; and Rows decodes a Struct column into a struct field, so the two round-trip.
  • Update (316), as Polars' DataFrame.update: another frame's values written over this one's, matched by keys or by place, a null leaving the value unless IncludeNulls, keeping the frame's rows, all of them, the matched ones or other's new ones too, in an order, under a memory limit as well.
  • An as-of join's numeric tolerance and its coalesce (315), as Polars': AsOfTolerance(5) on an integer key, AsOfTolerance(0.5) on a float one, and AsOfCoalesce(false) keeping the right frame's key; and JoinWhereSuffix, Polars' join_where(suffix=).
  • A join's order, Polars' maintain_order (314): JoinOrderLeft and JoinOrderRight, and Polars' left_right and right_left, for every kind of join: the left or the right frame's rows in their order, each row's matches in the other's, and the unmatched rows of the other after them. The order holds under a memory limit, where a join's never did: a join whose table spills sorts its rows back. A join that fits pays nothing for the left order; the right one hashes the left frame.
  • An integer index (312), Polars' "3i": GroupByDynamic and Rolling over an Int32 or Int64 index, its windows cut from its values and its type kept, and Upsample and the rolling windows and ewms by a column over one. All but GroupByDynamic take a UInt32 or a UInt64 too, as Polars' do. "i" mixes with no unit of time, and Truncate, Round, OffsetBy, a range or an as-of tolerance refuses it, where Polars moves nothing, panics, or reads it as nanoseconds.
  • FirstNonNull and LastNonNull (310), Polars' first(ignore_nulls=True) and last(ignore_nulls=True), of an expression and as group-by shorthands, and a group-by's All(), each column a List a group, as Polars' group_by().all().
  • Having (309), as Polars' GroupBy.having and SQL's HAVING: the groups whose predicates, aggregates of their own, all hold, for Agg, the shorthands, Head, Tail, and dynamic and rolling groups.
  • A group's Head(n) and Tail(n) (308), as Polars' group_by().head() and tail(): each group's first or last rows as rows, the keys first, the groups in the order each first appears, spilling past a memory limit with the order kept.
  • Concat's modes (307), Polars' eleven: ConcatRelaxed and ConcatDiagonalRelaxed, meeting a column's types at Polars' supertype; ConcatHorizontal and ConcatHorizontalExtend, side by side, a shorter frame padded with nulls; and ConcatAlign, ConcatAlignInner, ConcatAlignLeft and ConcatAlignRight, frames joined on the columns every frame has and sorted by them. ConcatFrames concatenates DataFrames in any mode.
  • Upsample (306), as Polars' upsample, and lazy: a row at every step from each group's first instant to its last, nulls where the frame has none, its rows in the grid's order with or without a memory limit.
  • PartitionBy (305), as Polars' partition_by: a frame split into a part for each distinct key, in the order the keys first appear, each part's typed Key beside its Frame, with or without the key columns.
  • Unpivot without On (304), as Polars' on=None: every column not in Index melted, every column with no Index either, and nothing, no rows, when Index names every column.
  • A lazy Pivot (303), as Polars' LazyFrame.pivot: its new columns given in OnColumns, so the plan knows them before it runs. A group-by of the index and the On values reduces the rows, streaming them and spilling past a memory limit. A DataFrame's pivot takes OnColumns too, or finds them; and several On columns, whose values together name a new column, {"q1","web"}.
  • InsertColumn and HashRows (302), as Polars' insert_column and hash_rows: a column, an expression or Go values, put at a place counted from either end; and each row's hash over its columns, an expression, and a Series of a frame.
  • A fill strategy's limit (301), Polars' fill_null(strategy="forward", limit=1): FillForward.Limit(1) and FillBackward.Limit(n), for an expression or every column of a frame at once.
  • A frame's DropNans and Interpolate (301), as Polars': the rows with a NaN in the named or every float column dropped, a null kept; every column a line can fill interpolated, numbers and instants, text and Booleans left as they are.
  • Interpolate of instants, durations and times (301), on their ticks in integers, keeping their type, as Polars': halfway from January 1 to January 4 is January 2. It was refused.
  • A frame's aggregates (300), as Polars': Sum, Mean, Median, Min, Max, Std, Var, Quantile, Product and NullCount on both frames, one row, every column kept, a null where the aggregate does not take the column, as Polars answers: a Boolean's mean is the share of its trues, a text column's sum is null.
  • Quantile of instants, durations and times (300), one of them as their median is, a Date's a Datetime(us), as Polars'. It was refused.
  • MatchToSchema (299), as Polars' match_to_schema: a frame made to a schema's columns, order and types, its missing columns inserted or refused, its extra ones dropped or refused, a narrower number widened where nothing can be lost, a struct's fields matched by name at any depth, each option for one column too, and a missing column computed by an expression.
  • A frame's cast (298), as Polars' frame cast: Cast by column name, CastTypes by type, CastAll every column, on both frames; CastStrict(false) turns what does not convert into nulls. A column of its own type is left out of the plan, and the plan is the frame's order whatever the map's.
  • A documentation site (294), advenn.github.io/ursus: a quick start, the concepts, a page for Polars users and the benchmarks, versioned by release from 0.6.6 on. Every code block on it is an example in docs/examples that go test runs. Its user guide has chapters on selecting and filtering, aggregation, window functions and joins (295); reshaping, strings, lists and structs, and dates and times (296); and missing data, Go values in and out, Go functions, and CSV, Parquet and Arrow (297).
  • Row shortcuts (293): a frame's Shift, ShiftFill, GatherEvery, Clear, First and Last; DataFrame.IsEmpty and Equals(other, nullEqual).
  • A frame's sample (292): SampleN, SampleFraction and Shuffle on both frames, every column's values of the same rows, seeded.

  • Slice with a negative offset (291), counted from the end as Polars counts it: Slice(-3, 2) is the last three rows' first two. It holds the rows Tail holds.

  • Duplicates over several columns (290): IsDuplicated(exprs...) and IsUnique(exprs...), a Boolean a row; DataFrame.IsDuplicated and IsUnique of whole rows; DataFrame.NUnique(subset...).

  • UniqueKeep(keep, subset...) (289): the first, last, any or none of each key's rows, kept in their order, as Polars' unique(keep=, maintain_order=True).

docs.title: v0.6.6 — 2026-10-19
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.5 (2026-10-15): steps 262–287. v0.6.6-scope.md set the scope: feature completeness, part 2 — namespaces and generators. Frame operations are 0.6.7 and I/O 0.6.8; feature-gaps.md lists what is missing. Step 287 checked the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Polars' namespaces and generators:
  • generators, temporal ranges and values from their components; folds; selection by position; List().Eval;
  • the .list, .str and .dt methods that were missing, .cat on an Enum, .bin, and struct fields of several names;
  • the statistics, integers as bits, search, hashing and counts of values, run lengths and sequences, and rounding modes;
  • rolling skew, kurtosis, rank, cov and corr, ewm_sum and the ewms by time, hist and cumulative_eval.
  • Each answers as Polars 1.44.1 does, checked against its answers on the same inputs.
  • Many hold to the bit, the rounding, the moments, the ewms and hist ported from Polars' own source.
  • The exceptions: Hash, Sample and ApproxNUnique, which cannot, and the differences feature-gaps.md §9 records.
  • Each spills or streams where its pieces do. A per-row function streams a batch at a time, a reshape in a Select spills through the frame operator it is written in, and an aggregate spills with the group-by. The rolling and ewm functions stream over one partition. What refuses under a limit is listed below.
  • Nothing the benchmarks run changed:
  • the optimized plans of the 22 PDS-H and 15 h2o queries are byte-identical to v0.6.5's, once step 287 named Len() without the Alias node that showed in gb9's plan. So no timing ran, and 0.6.4's figures stand.
  • Every PDS-H answer at SF=0.1, at every step, and every h2o answer at 10,000,000 rows over Parquet match DuckDB's.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
• Str().SplitN(by, n) is a Struct, fields field_0 to field_{n-1}, as Polars' splitn (270). It was a List, n <= 0 unlimited: Str().Split(by) is every part.
  • A struct's field is named after the field, as Polars names it (275): Col("s").Struct().Field("b") is b, where it was s. So WithFields of a field read sets that field, where it added one named after the struct.
  • A null bound of Clip is no bound, for its row, as Polars' None is (283). It was a null result, and a null literal bound nulled the whole column.
  • Str() refuses a Binary column, as Polars' .str does (274). It read one as text, and a text function such as Slice split its bytes as runes; Bin() has the byte functions.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Generators (263): IntRange, LinearSpace, Repeat, Ones and Zeros, a column of their own length, e.g. WithColumns(IntRange(0, Len(), 1).Alias("i")); and their per-row forms IntRanges, LinearSpaces and Expr.RepeatBy, a List a row. LinearSpace agrees with Polars' to the bit.
  • Temporal ranges (264): DateRange, DatetimeRange and TimeRange, and DateRanges, DatetimeRanges and TimeRanges a row, by an Interval or a time.Duration, each value start plus k intervals as Polars counts them.
  • Values from their components (265): MakeDate, MakeDatetime, MakeTime and MakeDuration, Polars' pl.date and its kin, from constants or expressions; FromEpoch; and BusinessDayCount with a BusinessCalendar.
  • Folds and constructors (266): ConcatList, Fold, Reduce, CumFold, CumReduce, CumSumHorizontal and Format. A fold's function builds the expression once, when the query is planned, over a selection's columns too: Fold(0, func(acc, x Expr) Expr { return acc.Add(x) }, All()).
  • Selection by position and the index functions (267): Nth, First() and Last() as column selectors; ArgWhere, ArgSortBy, and ArgSort, ArgTrue and ArgUnique on an expression, UInt32 indices, a list a group in an aggregation.
  • List().Eval and Element() (268), an expression over each list's elements: values an element, aggregates, reshapes, filters and window functions, e.g. Col("l").List().Eval(Element().Sub(Element().Mean())). And List().Agg and List().Filter.
  • The list namespace's missing methods (269): Concat, Shift, Diff, CountMatches, Any, All, Item, SampleN, SampleFraction, and SortWith for nulls last.
  • Matching, splitting and forms of strings (270): ContainsAny, ReplaceMany, ExtractMany and FindMany over many patterns, by Polars' matching rules; ExtractGroups and SplitExact, a Struct; SplitInclusive; ToTitlecase; and Normalize to NFC, NFD, NFKC or NFKD.
  • Encodings, integers in a base, and JSON (271): Str().Encode and Decode, hex or base64; ToIntegerWith(base, dtype, strict), the base a constant or a column; ReplaceN, the first n matches; ConcatStrIgnoreNulls; JsonPathMatch(path); and JsonDecode(dtype), to a type given, with Polars' conversions.
  • The temporal namespace's missing functions (272): IsoYear, Century and Millennium; BaseUtcOffset and DstOffset; WithTimeUnit; TotalMilliseconds, TotalMicroseconds and TotalNanoseconds, and every total and the second with its fraction, TotalSecondsFractional and the rest; EpochIn, EpochDays and Timestamp in a unit; IsBusinessDay and AddBusinessDays with a BusinessCalendar and a Roll; and Replace(DateTimeParts{...}), setting components.
  • The categorical namespace on an Enum (273): Cat().GetCategories, StartsWith, EndsWith, LenBytes, LenChars, Slice and Physical; and Str() reads an Enum as its text, where it refused one.
  • The binary namespace (274): Bin().Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, Get, Head, Tail and Slice, each argument a constant or an expression; Size, Encode, Decode, and Reinterpret to a number or an instant, little- or big-endian.
  • Histograms and prefixes (286): Hist(opts...), bins by count or edges, a count or a Struct with each bin's edge and interval; CumulativeEval(body), an aggregate of Element() over each row's prefix.
  • Exponential weights (285): EwmSum, and EwmMeanBy and EwmSumBy by time, each Polars' to the bit; over the whole frame they stream under a memory limit.
  • Rolling statistics (284): RollingSkew, RollingKurtosis and RollingRank, and RollingCov and RollingCorr of two expressions. The moments are Polars' algorithm, a kurtosis Polars' to the bit.
  • Numeric odds (283): Round(decimals, RoundHalfToEven), Polars' default mode; Truncate(decimals); RoundSigFigs(digits); Cot(); ClipLower and ClipUpper. Rounding is Polars' algorithm, so each answer is Polars' to the bit.
  • Sequences (282): Append(other, upcast), ExtendConstant(value, n), SampleN, SampleFraction and Shuffle(seed), each a column of its own length in a Select and a list a group in an aggregation.
  • Run lengths (281): RleID(), a window function, and Rle(), a Struct of each run's length and value.
  • Counts of values (280): UniqueCounts() and ValueCounts(sort, normalize, name...), a Struct of each value and its count, a column of its own length in a Select and a list a group in an aggregation.
  • Search, peaks and hashing (279): SearchSorted(value, side, descending), IndexOf, PeakMax, PeakMin and Hash(seed), each comparing in the total order Sort uses, NaN above every number, as Polars'.
  • Integers as bits (278): And, Or, Xor and Not of integers are their bits', at their common type, as Polars' &, |, ^ and ~; a Go integer beside one keeps its type where it fits. A Boolean beside an integer is refused.
  • Entropy, mode and Spearman's correlation (277): Entropy(base, normalize); Mode(maintainOrder), a column of its own length or a list a group; and CorrSpearman(a, b).
  • Skew, kurtosis and small aggregates (276): Skew(bias) and Kurtosis(fisher, bias), kept online and merged pairwise; BitwiseAnd, BitwiseOr and BitwiseXor of integers or Booleans; NanMin and NanMax; HasNulls, IsEmpty, ApproxNUnique (exact) and Dot.
  • Struct().Field of several names (275), or a regex between ^ and $, or "*": a column a field, in the struct's order, as Polars' struct.field.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• A list's eval over an aggregate in a Select, Col("a").Implode().List().Eval(...), failed as an internal error (271).
  • Len() is named len, as Polars' pl.len() is; in most plans it was named literal (273). Alias of an alias now replaces the name. Since step 287 the name is OutputName's, not an Alias node's, so every plan that holds Len() renders as at v0.6.5.
  • Unnest().Suffix(...) keeps its suffix (275); each field's name undid it.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.5's, except:

  • Refused under a memory limit, each by name:
  • CorrSpearman and Mode in a group-by past the limit: their per-group pairs and values do not spill;
  • RleID and Rle over a partition larger than the limit;
  • SampleN, SampleFraction, Shuffle and Hist in a Select, which implode the column, as implode refuses;
  • CumulativeEval over a partition larger than the limit;
  • a generator whose argument is an aggregate of the frame, beside a string column, such as WithColumns(IntRange(0, Len(), 1)). WithRowIndex streams.
  • Last bits:
  • a rolling var, std, skew, kurtosis, cov or corr streamed under a limit can differ from the answer in memory;
  • a float aggregate's depend on the thread count, Sum's and Var's as the new moments'; a spilled run is the one-thread run's.
  • Refused where Polars answers:
  • a window inside a window, Col("a").Shift(1).CumSum();
  • an aggregate inside an aggregate's input;
  • CumulativeEval in GroupBy(...).Agg, as every window is.
  • .arr waits for an Array type, in a release of types after I/O.
  • A count reads every column: Select(Len()) over Parquet projects them all; Polars reads none.

docs.title: v0.6.5 — 2026-10-15
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.4 (2026-10-14): steps 248–261. v0.6.5-scope.md set the scope: feature completeness, part 1 — the bugs, and the expression model. The rest of 0.6 is feature completeness, and 0.7 performance; feature-gaps.md lists what is missing. Step 261 checked the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Expressions work where Polars' do. An aggregate is a scalar in Select, WithColumns and Filter. Expr.Filter is an aggregate's input. A length-changing expression is a list a group in an aggregation, and a column of its own length in Select and WithColumns. Arguments take expressions, and a Go slice is a List literal. Explode and Unnest are expressions, as DropNulls and DropNans became.
  • Each answers as Polars 1.44.1 does, checked against its answers on the same inputs, but for the differences feature-gaps.md §9 records.
  • Each spills or streams where its pieces do: a broadcast aggregate as a window, a filtered aggregate through the same accumulators, a column of another length as a plan of its own over the frame. A group's values in an aggregation are held by its implode, which refuses past the limit, as it did.
  • Nothing the benchmarks run changed: the optimized plans of the 22 PDS-H and 15 h2o queries are byte-identical to v0.6.4's, so no timing ran; 0.6.4's figures stand. Every PDS-H answer at SF=0.1, at every step, and every h2o answer at 2,000,000 rows match DuckDB's.

docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
• List().Get, and Str()'s Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, StripPrefix, StripSuffix, Split, Replace and ReplaceAll, are generic methods now, over a constant or an Expr. A call compiles as before; a method value needs its type argument: l.Get[int], not l.Get. IsIn, OffsetBy and Lit were generic already and take a wider type set.
  • Expr.Explode, Unnest, DropNulls and DropNans no longer refuse; code that relied on the refusal to catch a mistake gets an answer.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • lf.FillNull(ursus.FillForward) fills by the strategy (249). It filled every null with the constant 2: FillStrategy is a uint8, so it was taken for a value. Expr.FillNullWith(strategy) did the same. With no subset, forward and backward fill every column, min and max every ordered one, and zero, one and mean every numeric one; Polars fills a String with "" and a Bool with false for zero, and refuses a String for one and mean.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Dt().Date() and Dt().Time() (249), Polars' dt.date and dt.time: the date and time of day on the column's zone's wall clock. Cast(Date) reads the UTC one, as Polars' cast does.
  • An aggregate in Select, WithColumns and Filter is a scalar (250), as in Polars: Select(Col("x"), Col("x").Sum()) gives each row the total, WithColumns(Col("x").Sub(Col("x").Mean())) centres x, and Filter(Col("x").Gt(Col("x").Mean())) keeps the rows above the mean. A Select of aggregates, with or without literals, is one row. It was refused. The broadcast streams past a memory limit.
  • A window in Filter (250), SQL's QUALIFY: Filter(Col("x").Sum().Over(Col("g")).Gt(10)). It was refused.
  • Expr.Filter as an aggregate's input (251), a conditional aggregate: Col("a").Filter(Col("b").Gt(0)).Sum(), in a group-by, a window, a rolling or dynamic group, and as a scalar. The aggregate reads only the rows that pass, so Len counts them. Anywhere else a filter is refused for now.
  • Sort, SortDesc, Head, Tail, Slice, Reverse, Unique, DropNulls and Get on an expression (252), as Polars has them: in an aggregation a list a group, and an aggregate over one a value, Col("a").Head(2).Sum(), there and in Select, WithColumns, Filter and .Over. Expr.DropNulls was a refusal. Alone outside an aggregation they are refused for now.
  • SortBy, SortByDesc, GatherEvery and DropNans on an expression, and median, std, var and quantile over any of them (253). Expr.DropNans was a refusal. The list namespace gains Median, Std, Var, Quantile, DropNans, GatherEvery, SortBy and SortByDesc.
  • IsIn(Col("tags")), a value in each row's own list, and List().Get and List().Contains of an expression, a per-row index and value (254). IsIn now takes Operands, and Get an int or an Expr.
  • String patterns as expressions (255): Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, StripPrefix, StripSuffix and Split take a pattern a row, and Replace and ReplaceAll a value a row, inserted as written. A null replacement value gives null, where Polars keeps the string.
  • Dt().OffsetBy of an expression (256): an offset a row, a String such as "1mo2d". One that does not parse, or that the type cannot hold, is an error naming its row.
  • List literals (257): Lit([]int64{1, 2}) and the other slices are one List value, e.g. Col("x").IsIn(Lit([]int64{1, 2})). And Expr.Gather in an aggregation, by a List literal or a column of indices.
  • Length-changing expressions in Select (258): a reshape or an Expr.Filter is a column of its own length, e.g. Select(Col("a").Sort(), Col("b").Head(3)) is refused for its two lengths and Select(Col("a").Head(3), Col("b").Sum()) is three rows. Each is a plan of its own over the frame, so it spills as the frame-level operation does.
  • WithColumns takes them at the frame's height, and Expr.Explode is an expression (259), in Select, in an aggregation and under an aggregate; it was a refusal.
  • Expr.Unnest (260): a struct's fields, a column each named after its field, in Select, WithColumns and under an operation, as Polars' struct.unnest(); it was a refusal. StructExpr.Unnest spells it as Polars does.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.4's, except:

  • Of the expression model, each refused by name:
  • IsIn(Col("b").Implode()), membership among a column's values: 0.7's scalar subqueries;
  • a length-changing expression in Filter;
  • Gather in Select;
  • a reshape of a selection of several columns, Col("a", "b").Sort();
  • DropNans of a column that is not a float, and Explode of one that is not a List, where Polars returns them as they were.
  • A Select of literals alone is a row for each of the frame's rows; Polars' is one row.
  • A column of another length in Select reads the frame again: each is a plan of its own over it. A frame that joins, aggregates or sorts is computed once and replayed; a scan is read once a plan.

docs.title: v0.6.4 — 2026-10-14
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.3 (2026-10-12): steps 234–247. v0.6.4-scope.md set the scope: out of core, the leftovers — what still refuses under a memory budget, made to spill or stream. Step 247 measured the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Every window function streams past a memory limit, over one huge partition too; a rolling window by time holds the rows of its period. Keyed Rolling and GroupByDynamic hand their answer out. n_unique, and a median, quantile or n_unique in a window or a temporal group, spill their values; a large top-k spills.
  • Out of core, measured: each new path under a tenth of its input gives the answer it gives without a limit, the same to the byte, peaking at 1.01 to 2.11 times the limit (step 247 §3).
  • Against v0.6.3, both built alike and alternated: level. PDS-H at SF=1 takes 1.4% less wall time by geomean and 0.4% more CPU, at SF=0.1 2% less; h2o's gb1, gb4, gb5 and j1 move by −8% to +2%. 0.6.4 changed what happens past a limit, and these run without one.
  • Against Polars, in one session, every answer validated against DuckDB's:
suite ursus Polars ratio at v0.6.3 PDS-H SF=1 158 ms 79 ms 2.01× 1.94× PDS-H SF=0.1 20 ms 9 ms 2.29× 1.82× h2o 10M, Parquet 697 ms 531 ms 1.31× 1.20× h2o 10M, CSV 1,784 ms 1,088 ms 1.64× 1.77×

The builds are level, so the ratios move with the session: both engines ran h2o faster than in 0.6.3's, which was short of memory, Polars by more over Parquet and ursus by more over CSV. - CI's race job, which had timed out since step 237, has twenty minutes, and its heaviest budget tests run smaller under the race detector (244).

docs.title: Out of core
docs.text:
• A window with an order_by streams over one huge partition (235), with no partition_by or over one hot key: its rows' order keys and inputs are sorted, the functions walked over them, and the answers sorted back beside the rows. It refused.
  • A reversed cumulative function and a backward fill with no limit stream over one huge partition (236), walked backward through a reverse of that stream. They refused.
  • Rank, every method, streams over one huge partition (237), in its child's order: max and average from the peer group's first position counted both ways. It refused.
  • Interpolation, linear and nearest, streams over one huge partition (238), from a walk each way finding the values on either side and their positions. It refused.
  • A sort merges its spilled runs as they gather, sixteen of one level into one of the next (239), so its final merge holds a batch of fewer than sixteen runs a level. A window's sorted pass peaked at 6.7× its limit and now at 1.2×.
  • A window with no partition_by beside a keyed one spills (240), its keyless functions one more pass of the keyed spill. It refused. Of windows over one huge partition, only a rolling window by time still refuses.
  • n_unique over a few huge groups, or with no key, spills its values (241), as sorted runs of their bytes, counted as they merge back. It refused. Implode, whose answer is every value, still does.
  • A median, quantile or n_unique in a window spills its values over one huge partition (242), as a group-by's does. It refused. A run of spilled values, a group-by's too, is now written a batch at a time, so the merge back holds a batch of each run rather than a chunk of 8,192 values.
  • Keyed Rolling and GroupByDynamic hand their answer out (243) as their windows close, and a sort that spills puts it in bucket order. They held every window, and refused past the limit. In memory a keyed group is a little slower: over 2,000,000 rows under 1,000 keys, +4% rolling and +13% dynamic.
  • A median, quantile or n_unique in Rolling or GroupByDynamic spills its values (244), keyed or not, as a group-by's does. Windows that overlap hold a value for every (window, row) pair, many times their input, and refused past the limit. Implode still does.
  • Sort(...).Head(k) with a large k spills (245): past the limit its best k rows go to disk as runs, and the first k of their merge are the answer, ties in input order. It held them past the limit.
  • A rolling window by time streams over one huge partition (246), in a sorted pass by its by, each function's state carried from batch to batch so that the answers match the in-memory ones to the bit. It refused. It holds the rows of its period, and refuses, naming the period, only when one period is past the limit. Every window function now streams past the limit.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
As v0.6.3's, except:

  • Operators that do not spill, each failing under a budget with an error naming itself:
  • a rolling window by time one of whose periods holds more rows than the limit;
  • implode over a group, a window partition or a temporal window larger than the limit: its answer is every value;
  • join_asof's read-ahead: a left by-key the right side lacks reads that side to its end and holds it;
  • a dynamic group's long gap in its index makes every empty window in it at once, under the window ceiling.
  • A keyed Rolling or GroupByDynamic is a little slower in memory, +4% and +13% over 2,000,000 rows under 1,000 keys: its windows go out in segments and are put in bucket order at the end.
  • Speed: 2.01× Polars on PDS-H at SF=1. The widest gaps are q12 at 4.3×, q19 at 3.5× and q16 at 2.9×; over h2o, gb4 at 2.3× over Parquet and 3.1× over CSV, the joins at 1.7 to 2.1×.
  • Memory: with no limit set, h2o's gb10 peaks at 7.7 GB over Parquet and 6.4 GB over CSV; Polars' highest is 5.0 GB.
  • A large top-k is slower in memory than under a limit: the best half of two million rows takes 1.35 s as a heap, and 0.42 s as spilled sorted runs.

docs.title: v0.6.3 — 2026-10-12
docs.text: Everything since v0.6.2 (2026-10-12): steps 213–232. v0.6.3-scope.md set the scope: wall-time speed, out-of-core, and features. Each step was timed against 0.6.2's code, alternated in one session, and step 232 measured the whole.

docs.title: Where it ends
docs.text:
• Against v0.6.2, both built alike and alternated over PDS-H at SF=1: 7.6% less wall time by geomean, 2.2% more CPU, the Parquet reader decoding ahead. q11 takes 30% less time, q4 22%, q15, q21 and q12 15 to 17%. Over h2o, gb1 takes 31% less, gb4 24%, gb5 8%.
  • The scope's claims: PDS-H at least 7% faster by wall time, no query slower beyond about 5%, and q1's and gb4's peak memory within +100 MB, met; gb4 at least 35% faster, not met, at 24%: it is bound by this laptop's four cores.
  • Against Polars, in one session, every answer validated against DuckDB's:
suite ursus Polars ratio at v0.6.2 PDS-H SF=1 148 ms 76 ms 1.94× 2.07× PDS-H SF=0.1 18 ms 10 ms 1.82× 2.76× h2o 10M, Parquet 928 ms 774 ms 1.20× 1.52× h2o 10M, CSV 2,535 ms 1,434 ms 1.77× 1.65×

The laptop was short of memory, and both engines ran h2o slower than in 0.6.2's session, by different amounts. The h2o ratios measure that session, and the alternated runs what 0.6.3 changed: faster than 0.6.2 over Parquet and CSV. - Out of core: tail, hstack, a keyless WhereExists with a predicate, a median or quantile over a few huge groups, and ewm and a reversed cum_count over one huge partition, each past a limit that refused it before. - Features: the list namespace's set operations, Gather, ToStruct, NUnique, ArgMin and ArgMax; six horizontal reductions; Replace and its strict forms; rolling median and quantile; eager Pivot and Transpose; DaysInMonth, Combine, RenameFields and JsonEncode. Each answers as Polars does, checked against its answers, except where its docs say otherwise.

docs.title: Faster
docs.text:
• The Parquet reader reads ahead (214). A row group not at the head decoded three batches and waited, so most of each decoded only once it was the head, one at a time. Each now decodes ahead while what the workers hold stays under a read-ahead of a thirty-second of the memory limit, at most 256 MiB. h2o gb1 takes 28% less time, PDS-H q6 10% and q1 8%; peak memory grows by up to about 90 MB.
  • A sum or mean of an integer of 32 bits or fewer adds in int64 (215), folding into its exact 128-bit sum every 2³⁰ rows and at the end, where every value was widened to 128 bits first. h2o gb4 takes 15% less time, gb5 8%.

docs.title: Out of core
docs.text:
• Tail spills (217). The last rows it holds go to run files past the budget, the oldest dropped as later rows cover them, and come back in order a batch at a time. It refused.
  • Hstack streams (218), pairing a batch of each frame at a time, sliced to the fewest rows any has left. It held every frame whole, and refused. Frames of different heights are still refused, after the rows paired before.
  • A WhereExists or WhereNotExists of a predicate alone spills (219): a keyless Semi or Anti join with a residual writes its build side to a file and reads it for each probe batch until each row is decided. It refused.
  • A median or quantile over a huge group spills its values (220): over a few hot keys, or over no key, past the budget its values go to sorted run files, which are merged as they gather and read back in one pass at the end. A group-by partitions keys, never the values of one, so it refused. n_unique and implode over a hot key still refuse.
